Tools are model-controlled: Claude reads their descriptions and chooses to call them mid-turn. Resources are application-controlled: the host application (or the user through it) selects a resource and the client reads it, then places the content into context. Prompts are user-controlled: reusable templates that a person explicitly invokes, for example as a slash command. A server author picks the primitive by asking which party should hold the trigger, because the protocol wires each primitive to a different set of methods: tools/list and tools/call for tools, resources/list, resources/templates/list, and resources/read for resources, and the prompt methods for templates.

Read-only reference documents that the application attaches as context are the textbook case for resources. The client can enumerate them, fetch one by URI, and hand the content to the model without any tool round trip, and the server can advertise updates through subscription mechanisms. This is why an MCP-capable client such as Claude Code lets users reference server resources with @server:protocol://path, fetching them as attachments rather than waiting for the model to request them.

Modelling the documents as a tool works mechanically but changes the control model: the model now has to notice that it should call the tool, and the application loses the ability to deterministically supply the context. Prompts are the wrong shape because they are templates for instructions, not carriers of arbitrary documents, and each would need explicit invocation. Embedding documents in tool descriptions is an anti-pattern that bloats every tool listing and every request's context while still leaving the content coupled to tool selection. Choosing the primitive whose control model matches the requirement keeps the server predictable for every host that connects to it.

See the MCP server concepts page for the tools, resources, and prompts primitives and their control models, and the architecture overview for how hosts, clients, and servers relate.
option_feedback: Resources are the application-controlled MCP primitive: passive, read-only context sources that the host or user selects and the client reads through resources/list and resources/read. That matches documents the application attaches as context without the model deciding to act, which is exactly how Claude Code surfaces server resources through @ mentions.

Tools are model-controlled executable functions that Claude chooses to invoke during a turn. Wrapping passive reference material in a tool hands the decision to the model, which is the opposite of the requirement that the application attach the content as context.

Tool descriptions exist to tell the model what a tool does and when to use it, not to store documents. Stuffing reference material into descriptions inflates every tools/list response and every request's context, and it still ties the content to tools the model may or may not call.

Prompts are user-controlled reusable templates that must be explicitly invoked, and they are meant for parameterized instructions rather than for serving raw reference documents. Turning every document into a prompt misuses the primitive and forces a separate command invocation per document.

question: A team is in the system design phase for a Claude-based contract review assistant. Which TWO activities belong to this phase?
options: Triage user-reported errors from the live deployment and roll out corrective prompt fixes.
Define the prompt structure and where cache breakpoints separate static from dynamic content.
Interview reviewers to determine the acceptable turnaround time for a checked document.
Select between synchronous Messages API calls and the Message Batches API for the workload.
answer: Define the prompt structure and where cache breakpoints separate static from dynamic content.
Select between synchronous Messages API calls and the Message Batches API for the workload.
explanation:
Classic systems life cycle frameworks separate the work of building an IT system into phases that answer different questions. Requirements analysis asks what the system must do and how well it must do it: stakeholders are interviewed, business goals are decomposed into functional and non-functional requirements, and success criteria are made specific and measurable. System design asks how the system will satisfy those requirements: which architecture, which components, which integration patterns. Implementation builds and tests what the design specifies, and operations and maintenance keeps the live system healthy, fixes defects, and manages controlled upgrades.

For a Claude application, design-phase decisions have a recognizable shape. Deciding whether the workload runs through synchronous Messages calls or the Message Batches API is a direct consequence of a turnaround requirement that was already captured: a latency-tolerant, high-volume workload fits batch processing at reduced cost, while an interactive reviewer waiting on a result needs synchronous calls. Likewise, defining the prompt architecture, placing stable content such as instructions and shared reference material first and per-request content last, and choosing where cache_control breakpoints sit, is how the design meets cost and latency targets with prompt caching. Neither decision can be made sensibly before requirements exist, and both must be settled before the code that implements them is written.

The other activities sit on either side of design in the life cycle. Interviewing reviewers about acceptable turnaround produces a requirement; it is an input to design, not part of it, and Anthropic's guidance on defining success criteria reflects this ordering: measurable criteria come first, then the system and its evaluations are shaped around them. Triaging errors reported by users of the deployed assistant and shipping corrective prompt fixes is the defining work of operations and maintenance, which only exists once there is a live system to sustain.

The value of keeping these phases distinct is traceability: every design choice can be justified by a stated requirement, and every production fix can be checked against the design it is meant to preserve. For the mechanics behind the two design decisions here, see Batch processing and Prompt caching.
option_feedback: Responding to defects in a running system and shipping fixes is sustaining work on a live product. It belongs to the operations and maintenance phase, which begins only after the system has been implemented and deployed.

Laying out the prompt architecture, including which content is stable and where prompt caching breakpoints sit, determines how the system will meet its cost and latency requirements. This is a design-time decision that shapes what implementation later builds.

Discovering how quickly a reviewed document must be returned is requirements elicitation, which produces the constraints that design must satisfy. It belongs to the requirements analysis phase that precedes system design.

Choosing the invocation pattern is an architectural decision that translates already-known requirements, such as acceptable turnaround and cost targets, into how the system will be built. Deciding how the application will call Claude is core system design work.

question: A service built directly on the Messages API reads each reply as response.content[0].text. After the team adds a custom tool definition to the request, the parser intermittently fails with missing-attribute errors. What is the appropriate code fix?
options: Iterate over every block in the content array and branch on each block's type field before reading its fields.
Set tool_choice to none on every request so the reply always arrives as a single text block.
Wrap the access in a try/except and retry the same request until a text block appears at index zero.
Add a system prompt instruction requiring the model to always place a text block before any tool_use block.
answer: Iterate over every block in the content array and branch on each block's type field before reading its fields.
explanation:
The failure here is a modeling mistake about the shape of the API response, not a model behavior problem. A Messages API reply does not return a string; it returns a content array of typed content blocks. With no tools defined, that array is usually a single text block, so content[0].text appears to work. As soon as tools are present, the model may emit a tool_use block first, or only a tool_use block with no accompanying text, and index zero no longer has a text attribute. The intermittent nature of the errors is exactly what you would expect: sometimes the model comments before calling the tool, sometimes it does not.

The array-of-blocks design exists so that one response can carry heterogeneous output (prose, tool invocations, and thinking) without the client having to parse free text to find structured data. The correct mental model is therefore a dispatch loop: iterate over content, switch on each block's type, append text to the user-visible reply, and route each tool_use block to the matching handler so a tool_result can be returned. Checking stop_reason (for example tool_use versus end_turn) complements this by telling the loop whether another round trip is needed. The official client SDKs expose these blocks as typed objects, which makes the dispatch pattern natural and catches this class of bug at development time.

The distractors are all attempts to make reality fit brittle code. Instructing the model to always lead with text cannot be guaranteed; the documentation states that code should treat these responses like any other assistant-generated text and not rely on specific formatting conventions. Wrapping the access in a retry converts a valid response into a fake transient error and throws away the tool calls the application is supposed to act on. Setting tool_choice to none stabilizes parsing only by disabling the feature that motivated the change.

See Handle tool calls for parsing tool_use blocks and formatting tool_result responses, and Using the Messages API for the request and response structure.
option_feedback: A Messages API response carries a list of typed content blocks, and once tools are defined that list can contain tool_use blocks (and possibly thinking blocks) in any position. Dispatching on the type field of every block is the only parsing approach that stays correct regardless of what the model chooses to emit.

Forcing tool_choice to none does make the parser stable, but it prevents the model from ever calling the tool the team just added, which defeats the reason for defining it. This trades away the feature to avoid fixing brittle response handling.

Retrying spends tokens and latency to force a response shape the code happens to expect, and it silently discards legitimate tool_use blocks that the application should be handling. It treats a correct API response as an error, which is a design bug rather than a transient failure.

Prompt instructions influence phrasing but cannot bind the structure of the response, and the documentation explicitly warns against relying on specific formatting conventions in assistant output. Any request where the model goes straight to a tool call still breaks the parser.

question: A developer wants a chat interface to display Claude's reply progressively as text is generated, using an official Anthropic SDK against the Messages API. Which description of how the API delivers a streamed response is accurate?
options: Send the request with a small max_tokens value and re-issue it in a loop, appending each partial reply to the next prompt.
Submit the request through the Message Batches API and poll its results endpoint repeatedly while the reply is generated.
Set stream to true so the API returns server-sent events over the HTTP response, which the SDK parses into typed events.
Build a websocket relay in front of the SDK, since the Messages API only returns complete responses over plain HTTP.
answer: Set stream to true so the API returns server-sent events over the HTTP response, which the SDK parses into typed events.
explanation:
The Claude Messages API is a plain RESTful interface over HTTPS, and its incremental delivery mechanism follows from that design. Setting stream: true on a request tells the server to keep the HTTP response open and emit server-sent events (SSE) as generation proceeds. The event sequence is structured: a message_start event carries the message envelope and initial usage (including input and cache token counts), content_block_start and content_block_delta events carry the incremental text, tool input JSON, or thinking content, a final message_delta reports the stop_reason and output token usage, and message_stop closes the stream. Because SSE is one-directional (server to client) over ordinary HTTP, it fits a request-response model where the client sends a complete prompt and then only needs to receive; a bidirectional websocket would add connection-management complexity without adding capability the API needs.

This is where the official SDKs earn their place. Hand-parsing an SSE stream means handling event framing and stitching many small deltas back into content blocks. The SDKs wrap this in streaming helpers that yield typed events and accumulate deltas into a final message object, so application code can update the UI on each text delta and still receive the assembled response at the end. What the SDK helpers do not do is guarantee recovery from a connection that drops mid-stream: if a stream is interrupted, the application should capture the partial content it has received and, based on its own reliability requirements, issue a new request that asks the model to continue from where it left off. Streaming changes only the delivery of tokens, not what is generated or billed: the model, sampling, and pricing are identical to a non-streaming call.

The distractors each misplace the mechanism. Building your own websocket relay rests on a false premise, because the Messages API already delivers partial output over HTTP via SSE; websockets are a legitimate protocol for pushing updates to a browser, but they are not required to obtain incremental text from Claude, and a relay that forwards only finished responses would not render progressively at all. The Message Batches API is the opposite tool for this job: it trades latency for a 50% discount and returns results asynchronously after the batch finishes, with no partial output during generation. Looping with a small max_tokens and re-sending the prompt with each fragment appended reprocesses the growing prompt on every call, inflating input cost and adding round-trip latency for a worse result than a single streamed request.

See Streaming Messages and the Client SDKs overview.
option_feedback: Truncating each request with a low max_tokens and chaining continuations reproduces the full prompt on every call, multiplying input cost and latency while producing awkward seams in the output. Streaming exists precisely so a single request can deliver text incrementally without this workaround.

The Message Batches API is an asynchronous bulk-processing path designed for latency-tolerant workloads, with results retrieved after the batch completes. It does not surface partial output while a single reply is being generated, so it cannot drive a progressively rendering chat interface.

Streaming on the Messages API is enabled with the stream parameter, and the response is delivered as a sequence of server-sent events (message_start, content_block_delta, message_delta, message_stop, and others) over the same HTTP connection. The official SDKs parse these events into typed objects and offer helpers that accumulate deltas into a final message.

The premise is wrong: the Messages API already delivers incremental output over HTTP using server-sent events when stream is enabled, so a websocket layer is not needed to obtain partial text. A relay that only forwards a completed response would still leave the user waiting for the whole reply, which defeats the goal of progressive display.

question: A voice assistant reads Claude's replies aloud through a speech engine. The system prompt says "Do not use markdown," yet responses still contain bullet points and bold markers that the engine reads out literally. Which prompt change is most likely to fix this?
options: Raise the temperature so the model explores formatting choices beyond its default markdown style.
Describe the desired output positively, such as flowing prose paragraphs, and explain that the text will be read aloud.
Repeat the prohibition in capital letters at several points in the system prompt so the model treats it as higher priority.
Add asterisk and hash characters as stop sequences so any markdown formatting ends the response immediately.
answer: Describe the desired output positively, such as flowing prose paragraphs, and explain that the text will be read aloud.
explanation:
Output formatting is one of the most common places where prompt wording matters more than prompt volume. Claude's guidance on controlling response format is explicit: tell the model what to do instead of what not to do. A prohibition like "Do not use markdown" leaves the target undefined, and the model falls back on its default style, which for technical or list-like content leans heavily on markdown. Replacing it with a positive description such as "Your response should be composed of smoothly flowing prose paragraphs" gives the model a concrete shape to produce. You can reinforce this with an XML format indicator, for example asking for the prose inside a <smoothly_flowing_prose_paragraphs> tag, and by matching the prompt's own style to the desired output, since markdown in the prompt tends to invite markdown in the reply.

The second lever is adding context. The documentation's own example is almost this exact case: "NEVER use ellipses" is less effective than explaining that a text-to-speech engine will read the response and cannot pronounce them. Once Claude understands why a formatting rule exists, it generalizes to related cases it was never told about, such as avoiding headings, tables, or emphasis markers that would be spoken literally. Motivation turns a brittle rule into a goal the model can reason about.

The distractors each miss this. Repeating the prohibition in capitals is louder but not clearer; it still fails to specify the alternative and bloats the system prompt. Stop sequences are a hard truncation mechanism: the moment an asterisk appears the response ends, so the user hears a fragment. Temperature adjusts sampling randomness and has no bearing on instruction adherence; raising it makes formatting less consistent, not more compliant. A useful mental model is that Claude behaves like a capable new colleague: a prohibition with no stated alternative or reason is exactly the kind of instruction a colleague would interpret inconsistently. See Prompting best practices for the format-control and context-adding techniques.
option_feedback: Temperature controls sampling randomness, not adherence to formatting instructions, so raising it makes output less predictable without steering it toward prose. The formatting problem is one of instruction design, not of sampling diversity.

Claude steers far more reliably toward a stated target format than away from a prohibited one, so telling it what to produce (prose paragraphs) works better than telling it what to avoid. Adding the motivation, that a speech engine will read the text, lets the model generalize the rule to any markup that would sound wrong when spoken.

Repeating a negative instruction more loudly does not change the underlying problem that the model has been told what not to do without being told what to do instead. It adds tokens and noise to the prompt while leaving the format target unspecified.

Stop sequences truncate generation the moment the sequence appears, which would cut the reply off mid-sentence rather than produce a clean spoken answer. This is a mechanical workaround that damages output instead of shaping how the model writes.

question: A team schedules an unattended nightly job that calls the Claude API. Which TWO credential practices align with Anthropic's documented guidance?
options: Share one long-lived key across development, staging, and production so rotation only has to happen in a single place.
Store the key in an encrypted file committed to the repository so the CI runner can decrypt it during each build.
Set an expiration when creating the key and load it from a secrets manager at runtime.
Authenticate the job with a service account key or Workload Identity Federation instead of an engineer's personal key.
answer: Set an expiration when creating the key and load it from a secrets manager at runtime.
Authenticate the job with a service account key or Workload Identity Federation instead of an engineer's personal key.
explanation:
Credential design for an unattended workload starts with the question of whose identity the job acts under. Claude Console keys come in three types: a personal key acts as the user who created it, a service account key acts as a dedicated service account, and the legacy workspace key acts as no one. Because a nightly job is not a person, binding it to a personal key couples the pipeline to one engineer's account and blurs the audit trail. A service account gives the job its own identity that survives staff changes and can be reasoned about independently. Workload Identity Federation removes the static secret entirely: the job presents a token from its own platform identity to POST /v1/oauth/token, receives a short-lived access token, and sends it as Authorization: Bearer <token>, so there is nothing long-lived to leak or rotate.

When a static key is still needed, its lifecycle should be bounded and its storage controlled. The Console lets you set an expiration at creation, which caps the damage window if the key is ever exposed and forces periodic re-issuance rather than indefinite reuse. The key should be kept out of source control, client-side code, and prompts, and delivered to the process at runtime from a secrets manager. That separation is what makes rotation a configuration change rather than a code change.

The two rejected practices both trade security for convenience in ways the platform is designed to discourage. Committing an encrypted key still places the credential in version history on every clone, and the decryption secret becomes a second shared secret to protect. Reusing one key across environments collapses the isolation that workspaces provide: workspaces exist precisely to segment keys and control spend per use case, and a shared key means a compromise in development is a compromise in production with no way to attribute usage. See Authentication and the API overview for key types, headers, and Workload Identity Federation.
option_feedback: A single shared key means a leak in a low-trust development environment compromises production, and it defeats the purpose of workspaces, which exist to segment keys and control spend by use case. It also makes it impossible to tell from usage which environment generated a given request.

Encrypting the file does not change the fact that the credential now lives in version control, where it persists in history, is copied to every clone, and is decryptable by anyone holding the shared decryption secret. The documented practice is to keep keys out of source control entirely and supply them at runtime from a secrets manager.

Anthropic's guidance is to choose an expiration at key creation time and to keep the key out of source control, client-side code, and prompts. Injecting the key from a secrets manager at runtime keeps it off disk in the repository and makes rotation a configuration change rather than a code change.

A personal key acts as the user who created it, so tying an unattended workload to it means the job breaks when that person leaves and its activity is attributed to an individual. Service account keys are identity-backed credentials meant for shared or unattended workloads, and Workload Identity Federation goes further by exchanging a platform identity for a short-lived bearer token so no static key exists at all.

question: A lead agent's context fills with file contents during codebase exploration, and its independent searches run one after another. Which TWO subagent practices address these problems?
options: Route broad searches through subagents so intermediate file contents and search hits stay out of the lead agent's context.
Spawn separate subagents for independent exploration tasks so they run concurrently instead of one after another.
Rely on each subagent's fresh starting context to make its output for the same subtask deterministic across repeated runs.
Instruct each subagent to return the full text of every file it read in its final message so nothing needs summarizing.
answer: Route broad searches through subagents so intermediate file contents and search hits stay out of the lead agent's context.
Spawn separate subagents for independent exploration tasks so they run concurrently instead of one after another.
explanation:
The mental model for a subagent is a separate agent instance with its own conversation, its own system prompt, and its own tool permissions. When a lead agent hands off a subtask, the subagent does all of its reading, searching, and reasoning inside that separate context and returns only its final message. This is the core reason delegation improves task execution: the lead agent's context window is a scarce resource, and codebase exploration is exactly the kind of work that floods it with search results, logs, and file contents that will never be referenced again. Keeping that material out of the main conversation is what the Claude Code subagents documentation calls preserving context.

The second benefit is parallelization. Because each subagent is an independent instance, the lead can spawn several at once for subtasks that do not share state, and the whole set completes in roughly the time of the slowest one. A single conversation, by contrast, must interleave those steps sequentially. Subagents also allow specialized instructions and tool restrictions: an exploration subagent can be limited to read-only tools such as Read, Grep, and Glob, and given a focused prompt without cluttering the lead agent's instructions. The Agent SDK subagents guide lists these four benefits explicitly.

The tradeoff is that isolation cuts both ways. Because only the final message crosses back to the lead, anything the subagent learned but did not include in its summary is lost to the parent, and a resumed subagent is needed to continue that work rather than restarting. Instructing subagents to return the full text of everything they read inverts the design: the final message becomes as large as the exploration itself, and delegation saves no context at all. Likewise, running in a fresh context does not make outputs deterministic; model sampling stays probabilistic wherever it runs, so repeated delegations of the same subtask can still diverge. Delegation is a context-management and concurrency pattern, not a correctness guarantee, and the lead agent should still validate what comes back.
option_feedback: Each subagent runs in its own context window, so the dozens of files and search hits it reads never accumulate in the lead agent's conversation. The lead receives the subagent's final message, which keeps its own context small and focused on coordination.

Multiple subagents can execute concurrently, so a set of independent explorations finishes in roughly the time of the slowest one instead of the sum of all of them. A single conversation must perform those steps sequentially.

A fresh context isolates the subagent's work, but it does not make model output deterministic. Language model sampling remains non-deterministic regardless of where the conversation runs, so repeated runs can still produce different results.

Only a subagent's final message returns to the lead, so stuffing that message with every file it read pushes all of the exploration material back into the lead agent's context. This negates the context savings that motivated delegation in the first place.

question: A developer marks the final block of a system prompt with cache_control, and that block embeds the current timestamp. The stable instructions above it exceed the minimum cacheable length, yet cache_read_input_tokens stays at zero across hundreds of requests. What should the developer change?
options: Enable automatic caching at the top level, which hashes each block separately so stable blocks still hit.
Switch the breakpoint to the 1-hour TTL so the entry survives long enough to be read on later requests.
Keep the breakpoint where it is and rely on the 20-block lookback to match the stable blocks above the timestamp.
Move the breakpoint onto the last block that stays identical across requests, ahead of the timestamp.
answer: Move the breakpoint onto the last block that stays identical across requests, ahead of the timestamp.
explanation:
Prompt caching is prefix-based: the API hashes everything from the start of the prompt up to and including the block marked with cache_control, and a later request gets a hit only when that exact prefix has already been written. This design is what makes caching cheap and safe: the model's processed state for a prefix can be reused verbatim only if the prefix is byte-identical, so any variation, even a few characters of timestamp, produces a different hash and a cache miss.

The practical consequence is that the breakpoint belongs on the last block that stays identical across requests, not simply on the last block. When a prompt has a static prefix followed by per-request content (timestamps, session context, the incoming message), the breakpoint should sit at the end of the static portion. Placing it on the varying block means a write happens every time and a read never does, which shows up exactly as cache_creation_input_tokens being nonzero while cache_read_input_tokens stays at zero. Reading those two usage fields together is the fastest diagnostic for this class of problem.

The other adjustments misdiagnose the failure. Extending to the 1-hour TTL addresses expiry, which is not the issue when requests arrive constantly; it also doubles the write cost without producing a single read. The 20-block lookback only locates entries that earlier requests wrote at their own breakpoints, so it cannot recover stable content that was never written on its own. Automatic caching moves the breakpoint to the last cacheable block and otherwise behaves identically, so it would inherit the same mismatch. When the cause is unclear, cache diagnostics can compare consecutive requests and report where the prefix diverged.

See Prompt caching and Prompt caching pricing for the breakpoint rules and cost multipliers.
option_feedback: Automatic caching uses the same prefix-based infrastructure and simply moves the breakpoint to the last cacheable block; it does not hash blocks independently. With a varying timestamp in the prefix, the same mismatch would occur.

The requests are arriving continuously, so the 5-minute lifetime is not what is failing here. A longer TTL only extends how long an entry lives; it cannot make a prefix containing a fresh timestamp match one written on a previous request.

The lookback window only finds entries that earlier requests actually wrote at their own breakpoints. It does not discover stable content sitting behind a breakpoint that was never cacheable, so no entry exists for it to match.

Cache writes happen only at the marked block, and a hit requires the entire prefix up to and including that block to match exactly. Because the timestamp changes every request, the prefix hash never matches; placing the breakpoint on the last stable block lets subsequent requests read the entry that earlier requests wrote there.

question: A tutoring application sends only the learner's latest message to the Messages API on each request. Learners complain that Claude forgets facts they stated two messages earlier, even within the same lesson. Which change resolves the problem?
options: Enable prompt caching so the server keeps the conversation between requests.
Pass the id from the previous response so the server links the new turn to it.
Include the prior user and assistant turns in the messages array on every request.
Raise max_tokens so the model has room to carry earlier turns forward.
answer: Include the prior user and assistant turns in the messages array on every request.
explanation:
The Messages API (POST /v1/messages) is a stateless endpoint. Every request carries a structured list of prior messages, and Claude generates the next message based solely on that list plus the top-level system prompt and any tools. Nothing about the conversation is retained on Anthropic's side between calls, which is why the documentation describes it as supporting stateless multi-turn conversations: the multi-turn behavior exists only because the client re-sends the history each time.

The correct mental model is that the application owns conversation state. To let Claude remember what a learner said two messages ago, the client appends each user message and each assistant reply to a running messages array (alternating user and assistant roles) and sends the whole array on the next request. This design gives developers full control over what the model sees, which is what makes techniques such as trimming, summarization, and session hygiene possible; the tradeoff is that continuity is the client's responsibility rather than a server feature. By contrast, Claude Managed Agents persists event history server-side, which is a different product with a different tradeoff.

The distractors reflect common confusions about what other mechanisms do. Prompt caching speeds up and discounts processing of a prompt prefix that is byte-identical to one sent recently, but the prefix still has to be in the request; caching optimizes input the client provides and never supplies input the client left out. max_tokens caps output length and has no bearing on input context. Response id values identify individual messages for logging and correlation, not for threading; the API offers no parameter that links a new request to a previous response.

See Messages API reference, Using the Messages API, and Prompt caching.
option_feedback: Prompt caching reduces cost and latency by reusing processing of an identical prompt prefix that the client sends again; it does not store or reconstitute content the client omits. A cached prefix only helps when the same tokens are present in the request, so caching cannot replace the missing history.

Each Messages API response carries an id for identification, but the endpoint does not accept an id as a conversation handle or thread reference. There is no server-side linking of turns in the Messages API; continuity comes only from the messages the client includes.

The Messages API is stateless: each request is processed in isolation, and Claude sees only the messages array supplied in that call. Sending the accumulated conversation history with alternating user and assistant turns is how an application gives Claude memory of earlier exchanges.

The max_tokens parameter is an upper bound on how many output tokens Claude may generate in a single response. It has no effect on what input the model sees, so increasing it cannot restore conversation history that was never sent.

question: An application built on Claude Sonnet 4.5 ends each request with a partial assistant message containing an opening brace to force JSON replies. After the team changes only the model ID to claude-sonnet-4-6, every request fails with a 400 error. What should the team do?
options: Keep the trailing assistant message but move the brace into a system prompt line that tells the model to continue from it.
Lower the temperature to zero so the model reliably continues the seeded assistant turn on the newer model.
Remove the trailing assistant message and shape the output with structured outputs or system prompt instructions instead.
Raise max_tokens so the response has room to complete the JSON object that the seeded brace begins, keeping the request otherwise unchanged.
answer: Remove the trailing assistant message and shape the output with structured outputs or system prompt instructions instead.
explanation:
A model upgrade is a behavior change, not a drop-in swap, and some changes are hard API breaks rather than soft shifts in style. Prefilling (placing a partial assistant message in the last position of messages so Claude continues from it) was a common technique on earlier models such as Claude Sonnet 4.5 for forcing a format like JSON. The Messages API documentation states that prefilling is not supported on Claude 4.6 and later models and Claude Mythos Preview, and that requests using prefill with these models return a 400 error. The migration notes in the prompting best practices list this explicitly as Migrate away from prefilled responses: prefilled responses on the last assistant turn are no longer supported starting with the Claude 4.6 models. Changing only the model ID to claude-sonnet-4-6 therefore turns a working request into a rejected one, which is exactly what the team observed.

The right mental model is that format control has moved from steering the sampler to declaring a contract. Structured outputs let you supply a JSON schema under output_config.format with type: "json_schema" and a schema, and the API uses constrained sampling so the entire response conforms, which is stronger than a prefilled brace ever was because the whole object, not just its first character, is guaranteed to match. This comes with documented tradeoffs: the first request with a new schema pays grammar compilation latency, an additional system prompt is injected and billed as input tokens, and changing output_config.format invalidates the prompt cache for that conversation. Where structured outputs are not available, clear system prompt instructions describing the exact output shape are the documented fallback. Either way, the trailing assistant message must be removed; relocating the brace into the system prompt while keeping the partial assistant turn does not fix the request, raising max_tokens only matters for requests that pass validation and begin generating, and temperature only influences sampling on requests that are accepted in the first place.

More broadly, this is why teams should run their eval suite and review the migration notes before cutting over to a new release: removed parameters and unsupported request shapes surface as hard failures, while formatting and instruction-following differences surface as quality regressions. See Using the Messages API for the prefill limitation, Structured outputs for the replacement pattern, Prompting best practices for the migration considerations, and the Migration guide for the full list of changes between model generations.
option_feedback: The error is caused by the presence of a prefilled assistant turn in the last position of the messages list, not by what that turn contains. Any request that still ends with a partial assistant message will continue to fail on Claude 4.6 and later.

Temperature controls sampling randomness and has no bearing on whether the request is accepted. The request is rejected before any generation happens because the prefilled assistant turn itself is unsupported.

Prefilling is documented as not supported on Claude 4.6 and later models, and requests using prefill with these models return a 400 error. The documented replacements are structured outputs (a JSON schema in output_config.format) on models that support them, or system prompt instructions describing the required format.

max_tokens caps how much output the model may generate once a request is accepted; it has no effect on request validation. The request is rejected before generation starts because the trailing partial assistant turn is unsupported on Claude 4.6 and later, so a larger output budget changes nothing.

question: An agent that integrates with GitHub and Slack now exposes more than forty separately defined tools and often calls the wrong one. Which TWO changes improve tool selection accuracy?
options: Prefix each tool name with the service it belongs to, such as github_list_prs and slack_send_message.
Set tool_choice to {"type": "any"} so Claude is required to choose one of the tools on every turn.
Trim every tool description down to a single sentence so that the combined tool definitions consume fewer input tokens per request.
Consolidate related operations such as create, review, and merge into a single pull-request tool with an action parameter.
answer: Prefix each tool name with the service it belongs to, such as github_list_prs and slack_send_message.
Consolidate related operations such as create, review, and merge into a single pull-request tool with an action parameter.
explanation:
When a request includes a tools array, the API assembles a special system prompt that lists every tool's name, description, and JSON schema before the model ever sees the user's message. Claude selects a tool by matching the request against those definitions, so the shape of the tool surface directly determines how accurately it chooses. A library of forty overlapping, unprefixed tools presents the model with many candidates whose definitions look alike, and misrouting is the predictable result.

Two structural fixes address this. Consolidating related operations into a single tool with an action parameter (for example, one pull-request tool instead of separate create, review, and merge tools) collapses several near-duplicate choices into one clear decision, moving the fine-grained distinction into a parameter where a schema enum can constrain it. Namespacing tool names with a service prefix such as github_ or slack_ gives Claude an unambiguous signal about which system each tool touches, which matters increasingly as a library grows and is particularly important if you later adopt tool search to load definitions on demand. The tradeoff is a slightly larger per-tool schema for consolidated tools, but the reduction in selection ambiguity outweighs it.

The other approaches work against the mechanism. Trimming descriptions to a sentence reduces token cost but strips out the when to use and when not to use guidance that Anthropic identifies as the most important factor in tool performance; the recommended minimum is three to four sentences per tool. Setting tool_choice to any only forces Claude to call some tool rather than respond in text; it provides no help in distinguishing between tools and can surface more wrong calls when the underlying confusion is left in place.

See Implement tool use for the best practices on descriptions, consolidation, and namespacing, and Tool use with Claude for how Claude decides when to call a tool.
option_feedback: Service-prefixed names give Claude an immediate signal about which system a tool touches, which disambiguates similarly named operations across GitHub and Slack. Namespacing is recommended as a tool library grows and is especially valuable when tool search is in play.

The any setting forces Claude to call some tool rather than answer directly, but it does nothing to help Claude decide which of forty tools is appropriate. Forcing a call when the underlying ambiguity remains can increase wrong-tool invocations rather than reduce them.

Detailed descriptions are the single most important factor in tool performance, and Anthropic recommends at least three to four sentences covering what the tool does, when to use it, and its caveats. Shortening descriptions saves tokens but removes exactly the information Claude relies on to pick the right tool.

Grouping closely related operations into one tool with an action parameter reduces the number of near-identical candidates Claude must choose between. Fewer, more capable tools shrink the selection ambiguity that causes wrong-tool calls and make the tool surface easier to navigate.

question: A group must decide whether a fixed workflow or an autonomous agent should handle a newly automated task. Which TWO recommendations correctly identify when to build it as an agent?
options: Build it as an agent when the possible next actions cannot be enumerated in code and must be chosen from tool feedback.
Build it as an agent when every incoming request follows exactly the same, fully known sequence of processing steps.
Build it as an agent when predictable, low-cost execution matters more than adapting the path to each request.
Build it as an agent when the number and order of steps cannot be determined before the task begins.
answer: Build it as an agent when the possible next actions cannot be enumerated in code and must be chosen from tool feedback.
Build it as an agent when the number and order of steps cannot be determined before the task begins.
explanation:
The core architectural distinction is between workflows, where LLM calls and tools are orchestrated along code paths defined in advance, and agents, where the model itself directs the process and decides which tools to use and in what order. The decision criterion is whether the path through the task is knowable before execution. If it is, code should own the sequencing; if it is not, the model must.

Two task properties push toward an agent. First, when the number and order of steps cannot be fixed ahead of time, there is no sequence to hard-code, and only a runtime planner can proceed. Second, when the possible next actions cannot be enumerated in code and must be selected from environmental feedback, the task requires the observe-decide-act cycle that the agentic loop provides: the model gathers context, takes an action, checks the result, and chooses the next step based on what it learned. Note the qualification: a workflow can still branch on intermediate results (a router that classifies input and dispatches to one of several known paths is a workflow), because its author anticipated every branch. Agents earn their place only when the branches themselves cannot be written down in advance. Coding tasks, open-ended research, and debugging typically exhibit both properties, which is why harnesses such as the Claude Agent SDK are built around this loop rather than a predetermined pipeline.

The other two properties point the opposite way. A request that always follows the same processing steps is a workflow by definition; there is nothing for the model to plan, and letting it plan anyway introduces variance where none is needed. Likewise, when predictability and cost dominate, a fixed workflow wins: each step is a discrete call whose output can be validated, logged, and debugged in isolation, and total spend is bounded by the number of steps. Agents give up some of that determinism and cost control in exchange for flexibility, so the tradeoff should only be accepted when the task genuinely demands it. Practitioners often mitigate agent risk with turn or budget caps and deterministic hooks, but those controls do not turn an agent back into a workflow; they only bound its autonomy.

Further reading: Building effective agents and the Agent SDK agent loop.
option_feedback: A workflow can branch on intermediate results as long as its author can enumerate the branches ahead of time. When the set of possible next actions cannot be written down in code and must instead be chosen from whatever the environment returns, only the observe-decide-act cycle of an agent can proceed.
An identical, known sequence is the textbook case for a fixed workflow, not an agent. Giving the model autonomy to plan a process that never varies adds cost and unpredictability with no benefit.

Predictability and low cost are the strengths of a fixed workflow, where each step is a discrete call that can be validated and debugged in isolation. Agents trade those properties for flexibility, so prioritizing them argues against the agent pattern.

When the path through a task is unknown up front, a fixed sequence of LLM calls cannot be written in advance. An agent plans its own steps at runtime, which is exactly the capability an open-ended task requires.

question: A developer is building an agent that must view, create, and make targeted edits to source files on the machine where the agent runs. Which tool approach best fits this requirement?
options: Enable the server-side code_execution tool so Claude performs the edits inside Anthropic's sandboxed environment.
Write a custom edit_file tool with a bespoke input schema and execute each requested file operation in the agent's own process.
Provide the Anthropic-defined text_editor tool schema and execute each requested file operation in the agent's own process.
Package file-editing instructions as a Skill so Claude loads the editing procedure whenever a file task appears.
answer: Provide the Anthropic-defined text_editor tool schema and execute each requested file operation in the agent's own process.
explanation:
Choosing among Claude's extension mechanisms starts with one question: where does the work actually execute, and who owns that execution? Client tools run in your application: Claude returns a tool_use block, your code performs the operation, and you send back a tool_result. Server tools such as web_search and code_execution run on Anthropic's infrastructure, so you never touch the execution but you also have no access to your own machines from inside them. Skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and reference material that Claude loads progressively when a task matches their description; they supply know-how rather than a new execution surface. MCP servers package operations behind a shared protocol so many clients can reuse them.

Client tools split further into two kinds. With user-defined tools you author the schema and description from scratch, which is the right choice for proprietary business logic that has no standard shape. With Anthropic-schema client tools (bash, text_editor, memory, computer, browser) Anthropic publishes the interface and Claude has been trained on it, but your application still executes every call. Because file viewing and targeted editing are exactly the standard operations text_editor was designed for, adopting that schema gives the agent local filesystem access with the highest likelihood of well-formed calls and no bespoke schema to iterate on. See How tool use works and the Text editor tool reference.

A hand-rolled edit_file tool is not wrong so much as strictly weaker: it lands in the same execution location while giving up the trained-in interface and requiring more description work to match its reliability. The server-side code_execution tool fails the requirement outright, since its sandbox is not the host where the agent runs. Packaging editing instructions as a Skill confuses knowledge with capability; a Skill can tell Claude how to approach an edit, but on the API it executes in the isolated code execution container described in Using Agent Skills with the API, which has no reach into the developer's filesystem. The mental model to carry forward: pick the layer whose execution location matches where the effect must happen, then prefer a published schema over a bespoke one whenever the operation is a standard one.
option_feedback: Code execution runs in a container on Anthropic's infrastructure, not on the machine where the agent runs. Files edited there never touch the developer's host filesystem, so this approach cannot satisfy the requirement.

A custom tool would also run locally, but it discards the trained-in schema Claude already handles reliably for viewing and editing files. The documented guidance is to use the Anthropic-schema tools for these standard operations rather than reinventing equivalents that need extra description and testing to reach the same accuracy.

The text_editor tool is a client tool with an Anthropic-published schema, so the agent still executes every operation locally while benefiting from an interface Claude has been optimized to use. This gives direct access to the host filesystem without inventing and tuning a bespoke editing interface.

Skills package procedural knowledge and resources that load on demand; they are not the mechanism that gives Claude the ability to act on a specific host. On the API, Skills also run inside the isolated code execution container, which has no access to the agent's local files.

question: A document analysis service uses the Files API to store uploads from many customer tenants and references them in later Messages requests. No tenant may ever be able to read another tenant's files. Which design provides hard isolation?
options: Accept the file_id from the client on each request and validate its format server-side before forwarding it.
Set a short expires_in_seconds on every upload so files disappear before another tenant could reference them.
Issue each tenant its own API key in the Default Workspace so a key can only reference files it uploaded.
Create a separate workspace per tenant and keep the user-to-file mapping as server-side references.
answer: Create a separate workspace per tenant and keep the user-to-file mapping as server-side references.
explanation:
The key mental model for the Files API is that an uploaded file belongs to a workspace, not to an end user, a conversation, or the specific API key that performed the upload. Every API key assigned to that workspace can reference every file in it, and all keys share an organization's Default Workspace until they are explicitly assigned elsewhere. That design keeps the API simple for single-tenant backends, but it means the platform has no notion of which of your users owns which file. Tenant isolation therefore has to be built from two pieces: a platform boundary and application-side ownership.

The platform boundary is the workspace. Creating a separate workspace per tenant makes each tenant's files unreachable from any other tenant's keys, which is the secure-by-design property the scenario demands rather than a policy the application merely tries to enforce. On top of that, the application should treat file_id values as server-side references: the backend stores which files belong to which user and injects the correct IDs into Messages requests itself. A file_id arriving from a client is untrusted input in exactly the same sense as any other user-controlled identifier, and checking that it is well formed does nothing to establish authorization.

The other approaches fail for instructive reasons. Per-tenant API keys inside a single workspace feel like least privilege, but keys are not the scoping unit for files, so the separation is illusory. Aggressive expires_in_seconds values shrink the exposure window without closing it, and expiration is documented as a lifecycle mechanism rather than a guaranteed-deletion or access control. Both are examples of substituting a mitigation for a boundary, which is the core distinction guardrail layering is meant to preserve. See Files API for the workspace-scoped access warning and Workspaces for how keys and resources are scoped.
option_feedback: Accepting file IDs from end users is explicitly warned against, because a user-supplied ID would let one tenant read content another tenant uploaded. Validating the format only confirms the string looks like a file ID; it says nothing about who is entitled to reference it.

Expiration is a lifecycle feature, not an access control, and content may be retained for a period after expires_at. While a file is live, any key in the workspace can reference it, so a short expiry narrows the window but never establishes isolation.

Files are scoped to the workspace, not to the individual API key that uploaded them. Any key in the same workspace can reference any file uploaded there, so distinct keys within one workspace provide no isolation between tenants.

The workspace is the isolation boundary for uploaded files, so a workspace per tenant gives each tenant's data hard separation from every other tenant. Keeping file IDs as server-side references, never accepted from clients, ensures the application, not the caller, decides which files a request may reference.

question: An application lets users attach long PDFs and several images to a question. The developer wants to check that the assembled request is likely to fit within the model's context window and show users an input token estimate before the request is sent for generation. Which approach fits?
options: Call the count_tokens endpoint with the messages, base64 attachments, and client tools before sending.
Estimate the count locally by dividing the combined character length of the text and captions by four.
Submit the request through the Message Batches API first and read the token counts from its results.
Send the request with max_tokens set to 1 and read input_tokens from the usage field in the response.
answer: Call the count_tokens endpoint with the messages, base64 attachments, and client tools before sending.
explanation:
The Messages API is stateless: every request carries the full input the developer wants Claude to see, and that input, plus the generated output, must fit inside the model's context window. Text, images, PDF pages, and tool definitions all consume tokens, and image and document tokenization does not follow the simple characters-per-token rule that works reasonably for plain English text. When a request assembles many heavyweight attachments, the developer cannot know in advance whether it will fit or roughly what it will cost.

Anthropic exposes a dedicated endpoint for this: POST /v1/messages/count_tokens. It takes the system prompt, the messages, and client tools and returns an input token count without creating a Message. The count is a tokenizer-based estimate: the input_tokens reported when the real request runs can differ by a small amount, so treat it as a preflight figure rather than a guaranteed exact number. The endpoint also does not accept every input shape the Messages API does. Images and PDFs must be supplied as base64 to be counted, blocks with URL or file sources are not supported, and most server tools and MCP connector inputs are excluded. Within those bounds, the estimate reflects how the model tokenizes the attachments, which makes it a sound basis for a context-window check and a cost preview. See Count Message tokens.

The tempting shortcut of sending the real request with a tiny max_tokens and reading usage.input_tokens has a different cost profile. max_tokens is an upper bound on output, not a preview switch: the request still creates a Message, the entire input is processed and billed, up to one output token may be generated, and an oversized input fails with an error before any usage is reported. Local character-based estimates are cheap but inaccurate once images and PDFs dominate the payload. The Message Batches API is a throughput and cost optimization for asynchronous workloads that still fully generates a response; it is not an inspection mechanism. See Create a Message for the request structure and the semantics of max_tokens.
option_feedback: The token counting endpoint accepts system prompts, client tool definitions, and image and PDF blocks supplied as base64, and returns a tokenizer-based input token estimate without creating a Message. The figure can differ slightly from the input_tokens later reported by the real request, but it is the supported preflight check for context-window fit and cost display without triggering generation.

Four characters per token is only a rough heuristic for English prose and ignores how images and PDF pages are tokenized. For a request dominated by documents and images the estimate can be far off, which defeats the purpose of a reliable fit check.

The Batches API processes the request asynchronously and produces a real generated response, billed at the batch rate, within a window of up to 24 hours. It is a processing path for latency-tolerant workloads, not a way to inspect a request's token count before generation.

This still creates a real Message: the full input is processed and billed, and Claude may generate up to one output token. If the input already exceeds the context window, the request fails with an error instead of returning a usage count, so it cannot serve as a safe pre-flight check.

question: An incident-investigation agent uses tool result clearing to keep long sessions under the context limit. After older results are cleared, it re-runs log queries it already completed and loses key findings. Which change preserves those findings without keeping every result in context?
options: Raise the clearing trigger threshold so tool results remain in context until the window is almost completely full.
Pair context editing with the memory tool so Claude writes key findings to memory files before results are cleared.
Instruct Claude in the system prompt to memorize cleared tool results so it can recall them later.
Configure keep to retain every tool result and rely on prompt caching to offset the added token cost.
answer: Pair context editing with the memory tool so Claude writes key findings to memory files before results are cleared.
explanation:
The failure here comes from treating context editing as a complete memory strategy when it is only a pruning strategy. The clear_tool_uses edit removes the oldest tool results server-side and replaces each with placeholder text, which keeps the window small, but anything that lived only in those results is gone from the model's view. An agent that had learned a root cause from a log query no longer has that fact, so it plausibly re-runs the query. Your client still holds the full unmodified history, but Claude does not see it.

The intended mental model is a two-tier system: the context window is fast, expensive working memory, and the memory tool provides durable storage outside it. When both are enabled in a request, Claude receives an automatic warning as the conversation approaches the clearing threshold, giving it the chance to write essential information (findings, decisions, failed approaches) to memory files before the underlying results are cleared. Later, Claude can read those files back on demand rather than carrying every payload forward. This is the same principle behind pruning and compaction generally: keep the window full of signal, offload bulk, and retain the distilled facts somewhere retrievable.

The distractors each misunderstand one part of that model. Raising the trigger threshold defers the problem while letting stale output accumulate, which invites the recall degradation that grows with token count. Keeping every tool result and leaning on prompt caching confuses cost with capacity: cached prefixes are cheaper, but they still count toward the context window in full. Asking the model to memorize cleared content assumes a memory the model does not have; once tokens are removed from the request, no instruction can restore them.

See Context windows, Context editing, and Memory tool.
option_feedback: Delaying clearing only postpones the same loss, and it keeps large volumes of spent tool output in context, which degrades recall and accuracy as token count grows. Once clearing eventually fires, the findings embedded in those results are still gone.

Context editing and the memory tool are designed to work together: as the conversation approaches the clearing threshold, Claude receives a warning to preserve important information, and it can write essential facts from tool results to memory files. The verbose raw results are then cleared while the distilled findings remain retrievable on demand.

The model has no memory outside its context window, so content that has been cleared cannot be recalled by instruction. A system prompt cannot make removed tokens available again; persistence requires an external store such as memory files.

Retaining every tool result defeats the purpose of context editing and drives the session back toward the context limit. Prompt caching lowers the price of repeated prefixes, but cached tokens still occupy the context window, so caching does not create room for accumulating results.

question: A prompt classifies customer feedback into five categories using four few-shot examples. All four examples are short complaints labelled "billing". In production, Claude labels most feedback as billing, including praise and feature requests. Which change to the examples is recommended?
options: Add ten more billing examples so the labelling convention is reinforced strongly enough to apply to every category.
Replace them with three to five examples spanning different categories, lengths, and edge cases, wrapped in example tags.
Delete the examples and rely on the category names alone, since any example set will bias Claude toward its labels.
Keep the four examples but raise the temperature so the classifier's label distribution becomes more varied.
answer: Replace them with three to five examples spanning different categories, lengths, and edge cases, wrapped in example tags.
explanation:
Few-shot (multishot) prompting works because Claude infers the rule behind the examples, not just their surface. That inference is powerful and indiscriminate: if every example shares an incidental property, such as being short, negative, and labelled billing, Claude treats that property as part of the task definition. The observed behaviour, praise and feature requests collapsing into billing, is the direct signature of an unintended pattern learned from a homogeneous example set.

Anthropic's guidance is that examples should be relevant (mirroring the real inputs), diverse (covering edge cases and varying enough that Claude does not pick up unintended patterns), and structured (wrapped in <example> tags, with multiple examples inside <examples>, so they are unambiguous relative to the instructions). Three to five well-chosen examples usually outperform a larger set of similar ones, and Claude itself can be asked to critique an example set for coverage or to generate additional varied cases. The mental model is that examples define the boundary of the task, so they should sit at different points along that boundary rather than clustering in one corner.

The alternatives fail for distinct reasons. Adding more billing examples makes the accidental rule even more dominant. Removing examples entirely throws away a reliable steering mechanism when the fix is simply better examples, and the classifier would then depend on category names alone for tone and formatting consistency. Raising temperature changes sampling randomness, which affects variability rather than correctness; a classifier with a biased prompt becomes a noisier biased classifier. Once the example set is fixed, the change should still be verified against a consistent eval set of real feedback, since prompt engineering remains an empirical process.

See Prompting best practices for the full guidance on using examples effectively and structuring prompts with XML tags.
option_feedback: More examples of the same kind strengthen the unintended pattern rather than correcting it. Claude generalizes from what the examples have in common, so a larger homogeneous set makes the billing bias worse.

Few-shot examples steer Claude toward whatever pattern they share, and four short billing complaints teach the pattern "feedback is billing". A small, diverse set that covers several categories and input shapes, clearly delimited so Claude can tell examples from instructions, shows the actual decision boundary instead of an accidental one.

Examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer output format and labelling consistency, and removing them discards that leverage. The problem is not that examples exist but that these examples are homogeneous; well-chosen diverse examples improve accuracy rather than biasing it.

Temperature controls sampling randomness, not which label is correct for a given input. Raising it adds noise to every classification while leaving the misleading examples in place, so accuracy on praise and feature requests does not improve.

question: A team using Claude Code wants to guarantee that the agent never reads the repository's .env files, no matter how a developer phrases a request during a session. Where should this constraint be configured?
options: Add a Read deny rule for the .env paths under permissions in the project's settings.json.
Add an instruction to the project CLAUDE.md telling Claude never to open or read .env files.
Add the .env paths to the repository's .gitignore so Claude Code skips ignored files.
Pin the session to a dated model snapshot in settings.json so tool behavior stays consistent.
answer: Add a Read deny rule for the .env paths under permissions in the project's settings.json.
explanation:
Claude Code has two distinct layers of configuration, and choosing the right one depends on whether you need enforcement or guidance. settings.json (at user, project, local, or managed scope) is read by Claude Code itself and drives deterministic behavior: which tools may run, which paths may be read or edited, whether the sandbox is on, and which environment variables are set. CLAUDE.md, by contrast, is markdown injected into the context window at session start. The model sees it and usually follows it, but nothing in the runtime checks that it did.

For a hard constraint such as never reading secrets, the permission system is the correct home. A rule like "deny": ["Read(./.env)", "Read(./.env.*)"] under permissions is evaluated before the Read tool executes, so the call is blocked even if a developer explicitly asks Claude to open the file. Because settings follow a precedence hierarchy, an organization can also place the same rule in managed settings so that user and project files cannot override it. This is exactly why the documentation maps concerns to layers: blocking tools, commands, or file paths belongs in permissions.deny; code style, data-handling reminders, and other behavioral instructions belong in CLAUDE.md.

The distractors each confuse a neighboring mechanism with enforcement. A CLAUDE.md instruction is advisory: it reduces the likelihood of a read but cannot guarantee it, and adherence degrades as CLAUDE.md files grow. A .gitignore entry is a version-control concern; it keeps a file out of commits, not out of a tool's reach on disk. Pinning a dated model snapshot is sound configuration management for a different reason (it prevents ambient behavior changes when a new model ships) but has nothing to do with file access. The general mental model: when a rule must hold every time, encode it where the harness can check it; when a rule shapes judgment, encode it where the model can read it.

See Claude Code settings, Configure permissions, and Manage Claude's memory with CLAUDE.md.
option_feedback: Permission rules in settings.json are enforced by Claude Code's permission system before a tool call executes, so a deny rule such as Read(./.env) blocks the read regardless of what the prompt says. This is the mechanism designed for technical enforcement of tool and file-path restrictions.

CLAUDE.md content is loaded into the context window as guidance, not enforced configuration, so adherence depends on the model following the instruction. It is the right place for conventions and style rules, but it cannot guarantee a file is never read.

A .gitignore entry controls what git tracks, not what Claude Code's tools are permitted to open. A file that exists on disk can still be read by the Read tool, so this does not enforce the constraint.

Model pinning makes upgrades deliberate and keeps behavior stable across releases, but it does not restrict which files any model version may read. It addresses a different configuration concern entirely.

question: A project's CLAUDE.md has grown past 500 lines, mostly step-by-step runbooks for occasional tasks such as releases and schema migrations. Engineers notice Claude now overlooks the short coding standards at the top. Which restructuring best addresses both problems?
options: Move each runbook into a skill under .claude/skills/ and keep only concise standards in CLAUDE.md.
Move the runbooks into separate markdown files in .claude/rules/ without any paths frontmatter.
Split each runbook into its own file and pull all of them back in with @path imports from CLAUDE.md.
Copy the runbooks into the project's .claude/settings.json so they load as project configuration.
answer: Move each runbook into a skill under .claude/skills/ and keep only concise standards in CLAUDE.md.
explanation:
Claude Code separates always-loaded context from on-demand context, and choosing the right container for each kind of instruction is what keeps a project's guidance both cheap and effective. CLAUDE.md files are concatenated into the context window at the start of every session, so everything in them is paid for on every turn. The documentation recommends keeping each file under roughly 200 lines because longer files consume more context and measurably reduce adherence; the model has more competing text to weigh, and short standards near the top get diluted by hundreds of lines of procedure.

Skills exist for exactly the material that overflowed here. At session start Claude sees only each skill's name and description; the full SKILL.md body is loaded when a skill is invoked with /skill-name or when Claude judges it relevant to the task. A release runbook that is needed once a month therefore costs almost nothing on the other days, and when it is needed it arrives in full. The guidance is explicit: create a skill when a section of CLAUDE.md has become a procedure rather than a fact, and reserve CLAUDE.md for standing rules such as build commands, conventions, and architectural decisions.

The other options fail to reduce what loads at launch. @path imports are expanded at startup, so splitting a large file into imported pieces improves maintainability but not context usage or adherence. Files in .claude/rules/ without paths frontmatter also load at launch with the same priority as .claude/CLAUDE.md; only rules scoped with paths load conditionally, which suits file-type conventions rather than task runbooks. Finally, settings.json is a strict JSON configuration file for permissions, hooks, environment variables, and similar keys; it is not a place Claude reads instructions from, and free-form prose there would not function as guidance.

See How Claude remembers your project, Extend Claude with skills, and Claude Code settings.
option_feedback: A skill's body enters context only when the skill is invoked or Claude decides it is relevant, so long procedures stop consuming tokens on every session. CLAUDE.md shrinks back to the concise, always-relevant facts and rules that adherence depends on.

Rules without paths frontmatter load at launch with the same priority as .claude/CLAUDE.md, so every runbook is still in context every session. Only path-scoped rules load conditionally, and task runbooks are not tied to specific file patterns.
Imported files are expanded and loaded into context at launch alongside the CLAUDE.md that references them. This helps organization but leaves the context cost and the adherence problem unchanged.

settings.json is strict JSON that holds configuration such as permissions, hooks, and environment variables, not instructions for Claude to follow. Prose runbooks placed there would not be read as guidance and would likely break parsing.

question: An application runs a Claude model with adaptive thinking and sets the thinking display to omitted so that no reasoning text is returned. Reviewing invoices, the team finds output token charges far exceed the visible response length. How should the team account for the billing?
options: Attribute the overage to the specialized system prompt that supports thinking, which is injected on every request and billed as output tokens.
Attribute the overage to omitted thinking being billed at the cache write rate instead of the output rate, reflecting the cache premium.
Conclude that the display setting was ignored because summarized thinking is still produced, and summary generation carries a surcharge.
Explain that thinking tokens are billed as output tokens in full regardless of the display setting, since omitting them only hides the content.
answer: Explain that thinking tokens are billed as output tokens in full regardless of the display setting, since omitting them only hides the content.
explanation:
Thinking is a generation process, not a display feature. When Claude reasons before answering, it produces thinking tokens in the same way it produces response text: one next-token step at a time, each consuming compute. The API therefore bills those tokens as output tokens at the moment they are generated, and the total appears in usage.output_tokens. A separate read-only breakdown, usage.output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens, reports how many of the billed output tokens were internal reasoning, so an engineer can subtract it from output_tokens to approximate the visible portion.

The display setting sits on top of this. With summarized, the response carries a condensed version of the reasoning; with omitted, the thinking field is empty. In both cases the billed count is identical, because what changed is what the client sees, not what the model did. This is also why the billed output count never matches the visible token count when thinking is active: you pay for the full reasoning, not the summary or the blank field.

The distractors each misplace the cost. Cache write pricing applies to input prefixes stored for reuse and has nothing to do with thinking output. Summary generation carries no charge in either display mode, and omitted does suppress returned thinking text rather than being ignored. The specialized system prompt that accompanies thinking is real, but it is input, so it cannot inflate output charges.

The practical lever for a team that wants lower thinking spend is not the display setting but output_config.effort, which steers how often and how deeply Claude thinks, or max_tokens as a hard ceiling on total output including reasoning. See Steering thinking for the pricing and cost-control mechanics and Models overview for per-model thinking support.
option_feedback: A specialized system prompt is included when thinking is active, but system prompt content is input to the model, not output. It cannot account for elevated output token charges.

Thinking tokens are always billed as output tokens when generated, never as cache writes. Prompt caching pricing applies to input prefixes, and the display setting has no connection to caching mechanics.

Summary generation is not charged separately in either display mode, and the omitted setting does suppress the returned thinking text. The overage is not a surcharge but the raw reasoning tokens themselves.

Claude generates its full internal reasoning whether or not the text is returned, and every one of those tokens is billed as output. The display setting changes only what is visible in the thinking field, not what is generated or charged, and the usage.output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens field shows how much of the output was reasoning.
