Add the tool deny rules that must be technically enforced regardless of how Claude is prompted.
Document the code style guidelines and architectural conventions the whole team follows.
Commit the build, test, and lint commands everyone working in the repository relies on.
answer: Document the code style guidelines and architectural conventions the whole team follows.
Commit the build, test, and lint commands everyone working in the repository relies on.
explanation:
Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md files into the context window at the start of every session, which makes them a configuration surface for behavior: the instructions shape what Claude does, but only as context, not as enforced policy. That distinction drives what belongs in a project-level file. Shared, team-wide guidance such as build and test commands, coding standards, and architectural conventions fits well, because the file lives in the repository, is reviewed like any other change, and reaches every contributor identically. Concrete instructions ("run npm test before committing", "API handlers live in src/api/handlers/") are followed far more reliably than vague ones, and because the file consumes context tokens in every session, it should stay focused on guidance the whole team actually needs.

The scoping model is layered on purpose. A user-level file in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md carries one developer's preferences across all projects, and CLAUDE.local.md holds project-specific personal notes without being committed, so individual habits never crowd a shared file. Organizations can additionally deploy a managed CLAUDE.md that loads before user and project files for company-wide behavioral guidance.

Anything that must hold no matter how a request is phrased is a different kind of requirement. Because instructions in CLAUDE.md compete with everything else in context, they mitigate but do not guarantee. Blocking tools, commands, or file paths belongs in permissions.deny in settings.json, where the permission system enforces the rule on each tool call; sandboxing, environment variables, and login restrictions likewise belong in settings. The practical rule is: settings for technical enforcement, CLAUDE.md for behavioral guidance.

See Manage Claude's memory and Claude Code settings.
option_feedback: Content in a committed project CLAUDE.md applies to every contributor, so one person's preferences add noise and consume context for the whole team. Individual preferences belong in a user-level CLAUDE.md or a CLAUDE.local.md that stays out of version control.

CLAUDE.md is context, not enforced configuration, so an instruction in it can be outweighed by other prompting. Hard restrictions such as blocking reads of specific files belong under permissions in settings.json, which the permission system enforces on every tool call.

Behavioral guidance such as naming conventions, architectural decisions, and style rules is the intended use of a committed CLAUDE.md. Because the file is checked in, the whole team reviews and evolves these conventions together rather than each developer drifting independently.

A project CLAUDE.md is loaded at the start of every session and shared through version control, so commands every contributor relies on are exactly the standing context it exists to carry. Concrete, verifiable instructions such as which test command to run before committing are what Claude follows most reliably.

question: A data-extraction service running on an older Claude model prefilled the assistant turn with an opening brace to force JSON output. After moving to Claude Sonnet 4.6, every request fails with a 400 error. Which adjustment is recommended?
options: Move the opening brace to the end of the user message so Claude treats it as the start of its own reply and continues from it.
Remove the prefill and use the structured outputs feature, supplying a JSON schema that the response must conform to.
Keep the prefilled assistant turn but follow it with a user message such as 'Continue' so the prefill is no longer the last turn.
Lower the temperature to zero and add retry logic that regenerates the response whenever the returned text fails to parse.
answer: Remove the prefill and use the structured outputs feature, supplying a JSON schema that the response must conform to.
explanation:
Prefilling worked by placing a partial assistant message in the last position of messages, so the model had to continue from text you chose. Developers leaned on it for two jobs: forcing an output shape (a leading { for JSON, a tag name for XML) and suppressing preambles. Starting with the Claude 4.6 generation, a prefilled final assistant turn returns a 400 error. The rationale is that instruction following has improved enough that the trick is rarely needed, and where a strong guarantee is required there is now a purpose-built mechanism.

That mechanism is structured outputs. Supplying a JSON schema through the structured outputs feature makes the API use constrained decoding, so in normal operation the response text is schema-compliant JSON, including required fields and types. This is a considerably stronger promise than a prefilled brace, which only nudged the first token and left everything after it to the model, and it largely removes the downstream failures (parse errors, missing keys, wrong types) that the old approach still needed retry loops to handle. The guarantee is not unconditional, though: a refusal produces no schema-conformant object, a response cut off by max_tokens can be truncated mid-structure, and the documentation notes caveats around capitalization for enum and const values, so consumers should still check stop_reason and validate before trusting the payload. Other boundaries to note: the first request with a new schema pays a grammar-compilation latency, the injected format instructions add a few input tokens, and structured outputs cannot be combined with citations or with prefilling itself. For lighter-weight cases, a direct system prompt instruction such as respond only with the JSON object, no preamble often suffices on current models, and structured outputs are the right choice when schema conformance matters.

The other approaches all miss the mechanism. Appending a brace to the user message changes what the user said, not how the model begins its reply. Following the prefill with another user message is legal (assistant turns earlier in history are fine), but it turns the prefill into inert history rather than a constraint on the next generation. Temperature and retries operate after a request is accepted, so they cannot address a request the API rejects outright, and they only ever reduce the odds of bad output rather than constraining it at decode time.

See Prompting best practices for the prefill migration patterns and Structured outputs for the schema-constrained JSON feature and its documented limitations.
option_feedback: Text at the end of a user message is read as part of the user's input, not as the beginning of Claude's response, so the model has no reason to continue from it. This removes the 400 error but provides no output constraint and does not reliably produce JSON.

Prefilling the last assistant turn is not supported on Claude 4.6 and later models, which is why the requests now return 400. Structured outputs are the recommended replacement: supplying a JSON schema constrains decoding so the response is schema-compliant JSON in normal operation, with documented exceptions such as refusals and max_tokens truncation, which is far stronger than what a prefilled brace ever provided.

Assistant messages earlier in the conversation are allowed, so this sidesteps the error, but the brace is then just a fragment of prior history rather than a constraint on the next output. Claude generates a fresh response to 'Continue' with no guarantee of JSON structure.

Sampling settings and retries have no effect on a request that is rejected with a 400 error before any generation happens. Even once the prefill is removed, this approach leaves output validity to chance and burns tokens on retries when a schema-constrained mechanism exists.

question: An async service exposes a chat endpoint and a health-check endpoint. Chat handlers call the Messages API through the SDK's synchronous client. Under load, health checks stall whenever a chat call is in flight, although the API itself responds promptly. What is the correct fix?
options: Replace the synchronous client with the SDK's asynchronous client and await each Messages call inside the handler.
Route the chat handlers' requests through the Message Batches API so the service never blocks waiting on a call.
Wrap each synchronous call in exponential backoff with jitter so transient errors no longer hold up the handler.
Enable streaming on the existing synchronous call so the handler starts yielding tokens while the response arrives.
answer: Replace the synchronous client with the SDK's asynchronous client and await each Messages call inside the handler.
explanation:
An asyncio server runs every request handler as a coroutine on a single event loop thread. That design gives high concurrency cheaply, but it rests on one contract: coroutines must yield control whenever they wait on I/O. A call made through a synchronous HTTP client never yields; the thread sits inside a blocking socket read until the full response arrives. While that happens, nothing else on the loop runs, so a lightweight health check queued behind a twenty-second model call looks, to the load balancer, like a dead instance. The symptom in the stem (health checks stall exactly when a chat call is in flight, while the API itself is healthy) is the signature of a blocked event loop rather than a capacity or error problem.

The official Client SDKs ship both synchronous and asynchronous clients with the same request surface; the asynchronous client issues its network calls through non-blocking I/O, so awaiting a Messages call suspends only that handler and hands the loop back to other coroutines. This is why the fix belongs in the handler code, not in request parameters. An acceptable alternative when an async client is unavailable is to offload the blocking call to a worker thread (for example with asyncio.to_thread), which keeps the loop free at the cost of an extra thread per in-flight call.

The other options misdiagnose the failure. Streaming reduces perceived latency for the person reading the reply, but a synchronous stream is still consumed with blocking reads, so the loop stays frozen. The Message Batches API trades immediacy for a discount and a completion window of up to 24 hours, which is the wrong product for interactive chat and in any case does not change how the handler waits. Exponential backoff with jitter is the correct discipline for 429 and 529 responses, yet the stem rules out server-side errors, and sleeping between retries of a blocking call would make the stall longer, not shorter.

The general engineering lesson is to match the concurrency model of the client library to the concurrency model of the host process: async servers need async clients, and sync code paths need either sync clients or explicit thread offloading. See Client SDKs overview and Using the Messages API.
option_feedback: The synchronous client performs blocking network I/O, and a blocking call inside an asyncio handler freezes the entire event loop until the response returns, so every other coroutine, including the health check, waits. Awaiting the asynchronous client releases the loop while the request is in flight, letting unrelated endpoints keep serving.

The Batches API is designed for latency-tolerant bulk work that completes within a 24-hour window, which is unsuitable for a user waiting on a chat reply. It also does not address the underlying problem, which is blocking I/O running on the event loop thread.

Backoff and jitter are the right response to 429 and 529 errors, but the scenario states the API responds promptly, so errors are not the cause. Retrying a blocking call still blocks the loop, and adding waits between attempts would lengthen the stall.

Streaming changes how the response is delivered, not how the handler waits for it. Iterating a synchronous stream still performs blocking reads on the event loop thread, so the health check remains stalled for the duration of the call.

question: A team's backend service is written in Go. They want that service to drive the same agent loop and built-in tools that power Claude Code, without reimplementing the tool loop themselves. What is the appropriate integration approach?
options: Call the Messages API through the Go client SDK and write the tool dispatch and iteration logic in the Go service.
Wrap the Go service as an MCP server and register it so Claude Code calls into the service for each tool.
Run the Claude Code CLI as a subprocess with the -p flag and --output-format json, and parse the structured result in Go.
Import the Go package of the Claude Agent SDK and call query() with the same options that the TypeScript SDK exposes.
answer: Run the Claude Code CLI as a subprocess with the -p flag and --output-format json, and parse the structured result in Go.
explanation:
The Claude Agent SDK is best understood as Claude Code packaged as a library: it runs the agent loop, tool execution, context management, and retries inside your own process, and both the Python and TypeScript packages bundle a native Claude Code binary to do that work. Because the SDK is only published for those two languages, a service written in Go, Java, Rust, or any other language cannot import it directly. The documented path for those languages is to treat the CLI itself as the harness: spawn claude as a subprocess with -p (or --print) so it runs one prompt to completion without an interactive terminal, and add --output-format json so the calling process receives a structured result instead of free text. The CLI exits with code 0 on success and a non-zero code on failure, so the Go service can branch on the exit status, and options such as --allowedTools pre-approve the tools the run may use. In scripted and CI contexts, adding --bare skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, and CLAUDE.md so the run behaves the same on every machine.

This design keeps a single agent runtime regardless of the host language: the same loop, permissions model, and built-in tools are available whether you consume them through the Python or TypeScript library or through the CLI's process boundary. The tradeoff is fidelity of integration. The library route gives typed message objects, callback hooks, and tool-approval callbacks in-process, while the subprocess route exchanges JSON over stdout and stdin, which is coarser but language-agnostic.

The other approaches confuse different layers of Anthropic's tooling. The Anthropic client SDKs, including the Go one, wrap the Messages API and give direct model access; using them means implementing tool dispatch and the iteration loop yourself, which is the opposite of reusing Claude Code's harness. A Go package for the Agent SDK does not exist, so building on it is not an option. Wrapping the Go service as an MCP server is a valid way to give Claude tools, but it makes the service something Claude calls rather than something that drives agent runs. See the Agent SDK overview for the comparison of the Agent SDK, CLI, client SDK, and Managed Agents, and Run Claude Code programmatically for the -p and --output-format details.
option_feedback: The Go client SDK provides direct access to the Messages API, so the team would have to implement the tool loop, tool execution, and context management themselves. That is exactly the work the scenario says the team wants to avoid, and it would not reuse Claude Code's built-in tools.

Exposing the service as an MCP server makes it a tool provider that Claude Code can call, which inverts the desired direction of control. The requirement is for the Go service to launch and drive agent runs, not to be invoked as a tool by an interactive session.

The Claude Agent SDK is published as a library for Python and TypeScript only, and the documented way to reach the same agent loop from another language is to run the CLI non-interactively as a subprocess. The -p flag runs a single prompt to completion and --output-format json returns a structured result the calling process can parse.

There is no Go distribution of the Claude Agent SDK; the SDK ships only as Python and TypeScript packages. A Go client SDK exists for the Messages API, but that is a different product that gives direct model access rather than the Claude Code agent loop and tools.

question: A developer adds Anthropic's web_search tool to an existing agent loop that already runs client-defined tools. The loop is written to execute every tool request it receives and return a tool_result. How should the loop treat web_search requests?
options: Route any turn that requests web_search to the Message Batches API, because search results are only delivered asynchronously once the batch finishes processing.
Redefine web_search as a custom tool with its own input_schema so the loop can dispatch it through the same handler it already uses for client-defined tools.
Implement a search function client-side, run it whenever a web_search server_tool_use block appears in the response, and return the fetched results in a tool_result block on the next turn.
Leave web_search to Anthropic's infrastructure; the search runs during the request and its results arrive in the response, so the loop sends no tool_result for it.
answer: Leave web_search to Anthropic's infrastructure; the search runs during the request and its results arrive in the response, so the loop sends no tool_result for it.
explanation:
Tool use with Claude is a contract: the model emits a structured request describing what it wants done, and something else carries it out. What that something is depends on where the tool executes. For client tools (user-defined tools plus Anthropic-schema tools such as bash, text_editor, memory, and computer), the response stops with stop_reason: "tool_use", your application performs the operation, and you send the outcome back as tool_result blocks in a new user message. For server tools such as web_search, web_fetch, and code_execution, Anthropic's infrastructure performs the operation while the request is still being processed, and the record of that activity (a server_tool_use block followed by the tool's result block) is placed directly into the response content.

The practical consequence for a hand-built loop is that it must distinguish the two kinds of tool activity. When a turn uses only server tools, there is no pending work for the client and no tool_result to construct; the loop simply reads the response as it would any other completed turn. When a turn mixes server and client tools, the loop still handles only the client-tool tool_use requests and returns results for those alone. A loop that blindly treats every tool-related block as something it must execute will either error out or send spurious tool results the API does not expect.

This split exists so that common, infrastructure-heavy capabilities like live web search do not have to be re-implemented by every developer, while still leaving anything that touches your own systems (files, shells, databases) under your control. Redefining web_search as a custom tool throws away the hosted capability, and moving traffic to the Message Batches API changes the delivery model for cost reasons without having anything to do with how server tools return results. See How tool use works for the full description of client versus server execution and the stop_reason-driven loop.
option_feedback: Server tools work in ordinary synchronous Messages API calls and their results come back in the same response. The Message Batches API is a cost and throughput mechanism for latency-tolerant workloads, not a requirement for using server-executed tools.

Redefining the tool as a custom schema would replace the Anthropic-provided search capability with one the application has to implement itself. The point of the server tool is that Anthropic supplies both the definition and the execution, so no custom handler is needed.

This treats the server-side web_search trace like a client tool request, which it is not. A server_tool_use block records a search Anthropic has already executed on its infrastructure, so there is no pending request for the application to fulfil and no tool_result to send back.

web_search is a server-executed tool: Anthropic runs the search while processing the request and returns the search results inside the response content. The application never executes it and must not construct a tool_result for it; only client-defined tools in the same turn still require tool_result blocks.

question: A team submits 5,000 product reviews for sentiment labeling as a single Message Batch. When the batch completes, they join each result to its source review by its line position in the results file, and some labels land on the wrong reviews. What should they change?
options: Join each result to its review using the custom_id echoed in the result rather than its position.
Split the workload into several smaller batches so that each batch preserves submission order.
Embed a review number in every prompt and instruct Claude to repeat it at the start of its answer.
Move the workload to synchronous Messages API calls so responses come back in request order.
answer: Join each result to its review using the custom_id echoed in the result rather than its position.
explanation:
The Message Batches API is built for high-volume, latency-tolerant work: you submit many independent Messages requests in one batch, the API processes them asynchronously within a 24-hour window at a discounted price, and you retrieve the outputs when the batch finishes. Because the requests are processed independently and in parallel on Anthropic's side, the API makes no promise that results are written in the same order you submitted them. That design is what lets the batch system schedule work efficiently, and it is why ordering is not part of the contract.

To make the join deterministic, every request in a batch must include a unique custom_id, and each line of the results file (a .jsonl document reachable through the batch's results_url) echoes that custom_id alongside the result. The correct mental model is a key-value lookup, not a positional array: read each result line, extract its custom_id, and look up the corresponding source record. Joining by line position works only by coincidence and silently corrupts data when it does not, which is exactly the symptom in the scenario.

The alternatives do not fix the underlying defect. Shrinking batch sizes changes nothing about the ordering guarantee. Asking Claude to echo an identifier in its generated text substitutes a probabilistic mechanism for a deterministic one the API already provides. Moving to synchronous POST /v1/messages calls throws away the cost and throughput advantages of batching for a job that has no user waiting on it, and a robust integration should still key results on an application-controlled identifier rather than on the order in which network responses happen to arrive.

See Batch processing for how batches are created, polled, and retrieved, and Create a Message for the request shape each batch entry wraps.
option_feedback: Every request in a batch carries a unique custom_id, and each result in the output file echoes that identifier back. Because the Message Batches API does not guarantee that results appear in submission order, the custom_id is the only reliable key for joining outputs to inputs.

Batch size has no effect on result ordering; the API processes requests independently and may write results in any order regardless of how many requests a batch contains. Smaller batches also add management overhead without fixing the join logic.

Relying on the model to echo an identifier in its generated text is fragile and can fail if the output format drifts or the model omits it. The API already provides a deterministic identifier for exactly this purpose, so a prompt-level workaround is unnecessary.

Switching to realtime calls gives up the batch discount and the ability to hand off a large latency-tolerant job, and it does not address the real defect, which is joining by position instead of by identifier. Even with synchronous calls, a correct join should be keyed on an identifier the application controls.

question: A developer is authoring an MCP server whose tools will be called by Claude through several different MCP clients. Which TWO server-side practices improve how reliably Claude uses those tools?
options: Return the complete raw payload from every tool so the client never needs a follow-up call.
Define each tool's input schema as a root-level anyOf union so one tool accepts several argument shapes.
Declare accurate tool annotations, such as readOnlyHint on tools that have no side effects.
Return failures as tool results flagged as errors, with a message describing what went wrong.
answer: Declare accurate tool annotations, such as readOnlyHint on tools that have no side effects.
Return failures as tool results flagged as errors, with a message describing what went wrong.
explanation:
An MCP server is consumed by clients the author does not control, so the quality of the server is measured by how well an arbitrary MCP client, and the model behind it, can act on what the server returns. Two things the server fully controls are the shape of its tool results and the metadata it attaches to each tool in its tools/list response. Both directly shape the model's decisions on every call.

Error handling is the clearest case. When a tool fails, the model sees nothing except the result content. Marking the result as an error (isError in MCP tool results) and describing the failure turns a dead end into information the model can reason about: a bad parameter suggests a retry with corrected input, a missing record suggests a different lookup, and an outage suggests telling the user. Empty strings, empty objects, or stale cached data all hide the failure and push the model toward fabrication or endless identical retries.

Tool annotations serve the client rather than the model directly. Hints such as readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, and idempotentHint let a client make informed decisions about how to treat a call: a tool declared read-only is a safer candidate when the client is configured to execute tool calls concurrently, and a client can reasonably ask for confirmation before a destructive tool runs. Because these are hints, clients must not treat them as a security boundary, but accurate annotations still make the server behave predictably across surfaces.

The remaining practices work against the model. Dumping full raw payloads fills the shared context window and can exceed client limits; Claude Code warns when a single MCP tool output passes 10,000 tokens and caps MCP output at a configurable maximum, 25,000 tokens by default, through the MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS environment variable. Root-level anyOf unions are a problem in Claude Code's MCP handling specifically: the client flattens the schema and moves requiredness into the tool description, or drops the tool when it cannot produce an acceptable schema; combinators belong nested inside properties, or the tool should take an action parameter that selects the argument group.

See the MCP server concepts for how tools, resources, and prompts are exposed, the MCP architecture overview for the host, client, and server roles that make server-side discipline matter, Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP for output limits and schema handling on the Claude Code client, and Tool use with Claude for how the model decides when and how to call tools.
option_feedback: Large payloads consume the shared context window and can run into client output limits; Claude Code, for instance, warns when an MCP tool output exceeds 10,000 tokens and enforces a configurable maximum (25,000 tokens by default via MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS). Tools should return the fields the model actually needs, with pagination or targeted queries for the rest.

Claude Code's MCP handling does not pass anyOf, oneOf, or allOf at the root of a tool's input schema through unchanged; it flattens the schema and moves each branch's required list into the tool description, or skips the tool entirely when it cannot produce an acceptable schema. A single object schema, or an action parameter with nested combinators inside properties, is the portable choice.

Annotations are behavioral hints that clients use to make informed decisions about how to treat a tool; a tool marked readOnlyHint does not modify its environment, so it is a safer candidate when a client is configured to run tool calls in parallel or to apply lighter approval flows. Accurate hints help every client behave sensibly, although they are hints and should not be relied on for security enforcement.

The tool result is the only feedback channel the model has, so a result marked as an error with an informative message lets Claude retry with different arguments, choose another tool, or report the failure honestly. Silent or empty results leave the model guessing and invite hallucinated data or repeated identical calls.

question: A developer implements the client-side handler for Claude's memory tool, mapping the /memories prefix onto a per-user directory on the application's server. Which safeguard must the handler apply to the path in every command Claude sends?
options: Skip validation on view commands, since only create and str_replace can modify files on disk.
Reject any path containing the literal string ../ and accept everything else without further checks.
Canonicalize every requested path and reject any that resolves outside the /memories directory.
Add a system prompt instruction telling Claude to use only /memories paths and trust the paths it requests.
answer: Canonicalize every requested path and reject any that resolves outside the /memories directory.
explanation:
The memory tool is an Anthropic-schema client tool: Anthropic publishes the command schema and trains Claude on it, but the application executes every operation and returns a tool_result. Claude requests view, create, str_replace, insert, delete, and rename operations against paths under /memories, and the handler maps that prefix onto real storage such as a per-user directory or database keys. This design keeps the data entirely in the developer's infrastructure, which is the tradeoff that makes memory usable in production: Anthropic never holds the memory files, so the developer owns both the storage and the security of it.

Because the handler runs whatever path it is given, path traversal is the central risk. A request for /memories/../../secrets.env starts with the expected prefix yet resolves to a file outside the memory root. The correct defense is to resolve each path to its canonical form (for example with Python's pathlib.Path.resolve() and relative_to()) and reject anything that lands outside the mapped directory. This must run on every command: a view with a bad path exfiltrates data just as effectively as a create with a bad path overwrites it.

The other approaches fail for instructive reasons. Prompt-level instructions are behavioral guidance, not enforcement, and the boundary between what the model reads and what it does is exactly where instructions can be influenced by task content. Exempting read-only commands ignores the data-exposure half of the threat. A substring blocklist for ../ misses backslash and URL-encoded variants and never checks the resolved destination. The general mental model is the same one that applies to any client-side tool: treat tool inputs as untrusted input arriving at a system boundary and validate them in code.

See Memory tool and Handle tool calls.
option_feedback: A view command with a traversal path can read arbitrary files outside the memory directory, which is a data exposure risk even though nothing is written. Every command, including read-only ones, needs the same path check.

A literal substring match misses variants such as backslash sequences and URL-encoded forms like %2e%2e%2f, and it does not confirm where the path ultimately resolves. Canonical resolution followed by a containment check is the robust approach; a substring blocklist is not.

The memory tool is client-side, so the application executes whatever file operation Claude requests, and a path such as /memories/../../secrets.env would otherwise escape the memory directory. Resolving each path to its canonical form and verifying it remains inside the mapped memory root is the check that closes directory traversal on every command.

Prompt instructions shape behavior but do not enforce it, and requested paths can also be influenced by content Claude has read during the task. Security boundaries for file operations belong in handler code, not in guidance the model may or may not follow.

question: A team building a Claude-based document summarizer began writing and iterating prompts on the first day, judging quality by informal impressions. Weeks later, nobody can say whether the summaries are good enough because no definition of success was ever agreed. Which systems life cycle activity was skipped?
options: Operations and maintenance tracking production cost and quality dashboards.
Implementation writing the prompt and the Messages API integration code.
System design selecting the model, API mode, and prompt structure.
Requirements analysis defining measurable success criteria for the summaries.
answer: Requirements analysis defining measurable success criteria for the summaries.
explanation:
The systems life cycle orders work deliberately: requirements analysis establishes what the system must do and how well, system design decides how to achieve it, implementation builds it, testing verifies it against the requirements, and operations and maintenance keeps it healthy once live. Each later phase depends on the artifacts of the earlier ones. A team that jumps straight to prompt iteration has effectively started implementation without the requirements that make iteration meaningful.

For LLM applications this ordering matters more than usual, because output quality is subjective unless it is pinned down. Anthropic's guidance is to define success criteria first and then build evaluations that measure performance against them. Good criteria are specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant; typical dimensions include task fidelity, consistency, relevance and coherence, tone, latency, and price. Once those exist, the eval suite becomes the objective test that turns informal impressions into pass or fail signals, and every prompt change can be judged as an improvement or a regression rather than a matter of opinion.

The other phases do not fit the gap described. Design choices about model, API mode, and prompt structure were being made all along, just without a target. Implementation is what the team has been doing since day one. Operations and maintenance presumes a deployed system with dashboards to watch, and even then, a quality dashboard needs criteria to report against. The missing piece is the requirements work that defines what a successful summary is, which is why the team cannot answer the question of whether it is done.

See Define your success criteria for how to write measurable criteria and design evaluations around them.
option_feedback: Operations and maintenance applies to a live system and involves monitoring, triage, and controlled upgrades. The summarizer has not reached that phase, and dashboards cannot report quality against criteria that were never defined.

Implementation is the build activity, and the team has been doing exactly this since the first day. Having working prompts and integration code does not tell anyone whether the output meets a defined standard.

System design translates agreed requirements into architectural choices such as model selection and prompt layout. The team has clearly been making prompt design decisions; what is missing is the yardstick those decisions should be measured against.

Requirements analysis is where a team establishes what the system must achieve, expressed as specific, measurable criteria such as task fidelity, latency, or cost targets. Without that step there is nothing to evaluate prompts against, which is exactly the situation described.

question: A custom tool takes a nested, format-sensitive input object, and Claude's calls sometimes fail validation in the application. Which TWO changes to the tool definition address this?
options: Add schema-valid examples in the input_examples field to show Claude the expected nested format.
Set strict to true on the tool definition so tool calls must match the input_schema exactly.
Move the schema into the system prompt as prose and remove input_schema from the tool definition.
Raise max_tokens on the request so Claude has enough room to emit the complete nested input object.
answer: Add schema-valid examples in the input_examples field to show Claude the expected nested format.
Set strict to true on the tool definition so tool calls must match the input_schema exactly.
explanation:
A tool definition is a contract between your application and the model, and the input_schema is the machine-readable half of that contract. By default Claude reads the schema and usually complies, but compliance is probabilistic: nested objects, enums, and date or identifier formats are where inputs most often drift. Two complementary controls exist for this. Strict tool use (strict: true on the tool definition) turns the schema from guidance into an enforced constraint, so the tool call Claude produces is guaranteed to validate against input_schema. Input examples (input_examples) improve the model's understanding of the intended shape and typical values; each example is itself validated against the schema, and invalid examples are rejected with a 400 error, so they cannot contradict the contract.

The mental model is that descriptions and examples improve selection and interpretation, while strictness guarantees conformance. Anthropic's guidance is to prioritize detailed descriptions, then reach for input_examples when inputs are complex or format-sensitive, and to combine strictness with tool_choice when both the call and its exact shape must be guaranteed. Examples do add prompt tokens (roughly tens of tokens for simple cases and up to a few hundred for nested objects), which is the tradeoff for the extra clarity.

Replacing input_schema with prose in the system prompt fails on two counts: the schema is a required field of a user-defined tool, and prose cannot be validated by the API or your application. Raising max_tokens targets a different failure entirely; it governs how much output Claude may generate, and a truncated call is reported through the max_tokens stop reason rather than as an input that violates the schema. See Implement tool use, Strict tool use, and Tool use with Claude.
option_feedback: The input_examples field exists for exactly this case: tools with nested objects or format-sensitive parameters where a description alone leaves room for interpretation. Each example is validated against the input_schema, so it teaches Claude the concrete shape without introducing inconsistent guidance.

Strict tool use makes the API enforce schema conformance on the tool call itself, so the input Claude emits is guaranteed to match the declared input_schema. This removes the class of failures where a well-intended call still arrives with a missing field or wrong type.

A user-defined tool must include an input_schema; it is a required part of the definition, not optional metadata. Describing the shape in prose removes the machine-checkable contract and makes conformance worse, not better.

The max_tokens parameter bounds the length of the response, not whether the emitted input satisfies a schema. A truncated call would surface as a max_tokens stop reason, which is a different symptom from a structurally invalid input that the application rejects.

question: A recruiting assistant uses the MCP connector to reach an applicant-tracking MCP server that exposes delete_candidate and merge_profiles alongside read-only tools. The assistant must never modify data, yet a review found one delete_candidate call despite a system prompt forbidding it. What enforces the restriction?
options: Set tool_choice to {"type": "none"} on requests where the user's message appears likely to trigger a write.
Set defer_loading to true on delete_candidate and merge_profiles so Claude only sees them after a tool search.
Disable delete_candidate and merge_profiles in the server's mcp_toolset configs so they are never offered to Claude.
Rewrite the system prompt with emphatic, repeated instructions never to invoke delete_candidate or merge_profiles.
answer: Disable delete_candidate and merge_profiles in the server's mcp_toolset configs so they are never offered to Claude.
explanation:
The MCP connector lets a Messages API request attach remote MCP servers without a separate client, and the tools those servers expose are governed by an mcp_toolset entry in the tools array. That toolset is where the application, not the model, decides which capabilities exist for the request: default_config sets the baseline for every tool on the server, and configs overrides individual tools by name. Setting enabled: false on a tool removes it from Claude's tool surface entirely, which is why denylisting destructive or write operations is the documented approach for read-only assistants or for flows that need a human confirmation step before state changes.

The mental model worth holding is the split between steering and enforcement. System prompt wording, tool descriptions, and phrasings such as "use your judgment about whether to call a tool" all shift how readily Claude reaches for a tool, and they are the right lever when the goal is better selection. But the model still makes the final choice on each turn, so a rule that must hold every time belongs in a mechanism that removes the option. The failing review in the scenario is the expected outcome of relying on steering for an invariant: it usually works, and occasionally it does not.

The distractors each miss that boundary in a different way. Stronger prompt language raises compliance without guaranteeing it. defer_loading is a context-management setting that delays when a tool definition enters context; the tool stays enabled and remains callable once discovered. tool_choice: {"type": "none"} is enforcement, but it is far too blunt: it blocks every tool on the request, including the reads the assistant needs, and choosing which requests to apply it to reintroduces guesswork about user intent. Only the per-tool enabled: false configuration removes exactly the two dangerous tools while leaving the rest of the server available.

See MCP connector for the allowlist, denylist, and per-tool configuration patterns, and Tool use with Claude for how tool_choice and system prompt steering shape when Claude calls tools.
option_feedback: A tool_choice of none prevents Claude from calling any tool on that request, including the read tools the assistant depends on. Deciding in advance which messages might lead to a write is itself a guess, so the restriction would be neither reliable nor targeted.

The defer_loading setting controls when a tool's definition is loaded into context, not whether the tool is callable. A deferred tool is still enabled and can be discovered and invoked, so this hides the tool without removing the capability.

The MCPToolset object in the tools array supports per-tool configuration, and setting enabled to false on a tool removes it from what Claude can call in that request. A denylist of write or destructive tools is the documented pattern for read-only assistants because it is enforced by the API rather than by the model's compliance.

Prompt instructions steer how readily Claude calls tools, but they remain probabilistic and the scenario already shows a prompt-only restriction failing once. A hard requirement that a tool is never called should not rest on the model choosing to comply.

question: A developer is adding one capability to a single Claude application: computing a quote from the application's own pricing rules and a private database that is reachable only inside the application's process. Nothing else will consume this capability. Which approach fits best?
options: Package the pricing rules and database queries as a Skill so Claude executes them inside the code execution container on demand.
Define a custom client tool with an input schema and run the quote calculation in the application's own code when Claude calls it.
Deploy a separate MCP server that exposes the quote operation and connect the application to it as an MCP client over a transport.
Add the code_execution server tool and instruct Claude to write code that queries the private database directly from the sandbox.
answer: Define a custom client tool with an input schema and run the quote calculation in the application's own code when Claude calls it.
explanation:
The core question in agentic customization is where the code that does the work should run, and who else needs it. Claude never executes a capability on its own; it emits a structured request that either the developer's application fulfils (a client tool) or Anthropic's infrastructure fulfils (a server tool). When the operation depends on business logic and data that exist only inside one application's process, the only place that operation can actually execute is that process. A user-defined client tool is the direct expression of that: the developer writes a name, description, and input_schema, Claude returns a tool_use block, the application runs the quote calculation against its own database, and the result goes back in a tool_result block. See How tool use works.

MCP is a protocol for exposing capabilities to many clients through a server that can be owned, versioned, and maintained independently of any one consumer. That is a real benefit when several Claude surfaces or applications need the same integration. It is pure overhead when exactly one application needs the capability and the data is already in that application's memory: the team would be building a server, choosing a transport, and running a client to reach code sitting a function call away. Choosing MCP here is not wrong in the sense of being impossible; it is the wrong tradeoff for the stated scope.

Skills and server-side code execution fail for a more concrete reason. Skills are filesystem-based packages of instructions and optional scripts that Claude loads progressively and runs in the code execution container; they excel at repeatable procedures and domain knowledge, and on the Claude API that container has no network access, so it cannot reach a private database (see Agent Skills and Using Agent Skills with the API). The same isolation applies to the code_execution server tool: it runs on Anthropic's infrastructure and is suited to computation over data already present in the request, not to querying systems inside the developer's process.

A useful mental model: server tools for capabilities Anthropic can run for you, Anthropic-schema client tools for standard local operations the model is trained on, custom client tools for your own application logic and data, Skills for reusable know-how, and MCP when a capability must be shared or independently maintained across consumers.
option_feedback: Skills package procedural knowledge and scripts that run in the code execution container, which on the Claude API has no network access and cannot reach a database inside the application's process. Skills are for know-how loaded on demand, not for invoking live application-side operations.

A user-defined client tool is exactly the mechanism for application-specific business logic and proprietary data: Claude returns a tool_use block, the application executes the operation in its own process where the database is already reachable, and returns a tool_result. With one consumer and no sharing requirement, it adds no extra infrastructure.

MCP earns its overhead when a capability must be shared across multiple clients or maintained independently of any one application. Here there is a single consumer and the data lives inside that application's process, so a separate server, transport, and client add moving parts without delivering the reuse MCP exists to provide.

Code execution runs on Anthropic's infrastructure in a sandbox that cannot reach systems inside the developer's application process. Server tools suit computation over data already in the request, not access to private in-process resources.

question: A team's cost dashboard prices output_tokens correctly but computes input cost as usage.input_tokens times the base input price. After enabling prompt caching on a long shared system prompt, the dashboard's input totals fall far below the invoice. How should the team correct the input-side cost model?
options: Switch every request to streaming, since the usage object reports token counts only on streamed responses.
Add a fixed per-request cache storage fee to every response, since that charge never appears in the usage object.
Sum input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens, and cache_creation_input_tokens, each priced at its own multiplier.
Price the cached prefix tokens at the output token rate, since cache hits are billed as output rather than input.
answer: Sum input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens, and cache_creation_input_tokens, each priced at its own multiplier.
explanation:
When prompt caching is active, the input side of a request is reported across three fields in usage, and each maps to a different price. cache_read_input_tokens counts the prefix retrieved from an existing cache entry (billed at 10% of the base input price). cache_creation_input_tokens counts the prefix written to the cache on this request (billed at 1.25x base for the 5-minute TTL, or 2x for the 1-hour TTL). input_tokens counts only what comes after the last cache breakpoint: the tokens that were neither read from nor written to cache. The spatial mental model is a prompt split at the breakpoint: everything before it lands in one of the two cache fields, everything after it lands in input_tokens. Output tokens are reported separately in output_tokens and are always billed at the normal output rate; caching never discounts them.

This is why a dashboard that treats input_tokens as the whole input systematically undercounts as soon as caching is turned on. The correct input total is cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens, and an accurate cost model applies a separate multiplier to each term. The same three fields also feed rate limits and the context window, so the breakdown matters for capacity planning, not only for billing.

The API is designed this way so that you can see caching's economics directly: a large read count with a small write count means the cache is paying off, while repeated large write counts signal that the prefix is being invalidated and rewritten. The other remedies misplace the cost: cached tokens are never billed at output rates, breakpoints carry no fixed storage fee, and the usage object is returned on every response whether or not streaming is used (in a stream, input and cache counts arrive on message_start and the final output count on a later message_delta).

See Tracking cache performance and Prompt caching pricing.
option_feedback: Every Messages API response includes a usage object regardless of whether streaming is used; with streaming, the input and cache fields arrive on the message_start event and the final output usage arrives on a later message_delta event. Delivery mode has no effect on whether usage is reported, so changing it would not fix the model.

There is no per-request storage fee for prompt caching; cache breakpoints themselves are free. All caching charges are token-based and are fully visible in the usage object through the cache read and cache creation fields.

Once caching is active, input_tokens reports only the uncached tail of the prompt that follows the final breakpoint. The cached prefix is reported in cache_read_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens, which are billed at 0.1x and 1.25x the base input price respectively (2x for a 1-hour write), so pricing all three fields with their own multipliers reconciles the input side of the dashboard with the invoice.

Cached prefix tokens are input tokens and are never billed at output rates. A cache hit is billed at a fraction of the base input price, so applying the output rate would overstate cost rather than explain the gap.

question: A lead agent delegates a dependency audit to a subagent, which inspects dozens of manifest files but reports back only that four outdated packages were found. Which change lets the lead name the packages while preserving the context isolation that justified delegating?
options: Raise the lead agent's max_tokens so its final answer has room to list every outdated package.
Have the lead agent reread every manifest file itself after the subagent returns its summary.
Have the subagent's prompt require the package names and file paths in its final report to the lead.
Move the subagent to a model with a larger context window so its findings fit in the lead's context.
answer: Have the subagent's prompt require the package names and file paths in its final report to the lead.
explanation:
In a manager/supervisor hierarchy, each subagent is a separate agent instance with its own context window. When the lead delegates, the subagent gathers context, calls tools, and reasons inside that isolated window; the intermediate reads, search hits, and tool results accumulate there and nowhere else. When it finishes, a single final message crosses back to the parent. That boundary is the whole point of the pattern: the lead can farm out a task that touches dozens of files without any of that material consuming its own context.

The tradeoff is that the boundary is opaque. The supervisor sees only what the subagent chooses to write in its closing report, so the quality of the supervisor's aggregation is capped by the quality of the summaries it receives. A subagent that silently knows the answer but reports only a count leaves the lead unable to act. The design remedy is to treat the return message as an interface contract: the delegation prompt (or the subagent's system prompt) should state exactly what the report must contain, such as each finding with its identifier and file location. Anthropic's own guidance for forked research skills models this by instructing the subagent to summarize findings with specific file references.

The distractors each misread where the information lives. Having the lead reread every manifest would surface the names, but it discards the context savings and duplicates work that was already done, which is exactly the benefit the question asks to preserve. Raising the lead's max_tokens only lengthens the response the lead is allowed to write; it cannot conjure names the lead never received, because the limit governs output length, not what a subagent returns. Enlarging the subagent's model window changes how much the subagent can hold, not what it transmits, so the lead would be no better informed.

The mental model to carry: a subagent is a function call with an isolated stack frame. Everything it computed is local, and only its return value is visible to the caller, so the caller must specify what that return value should include. See Subagents in the SDK and Create custom subagents for how context isolation and the returned result work.
option_feedback: max_tokens caps how long the lead's own response can be; it has no effect on what the subagent transmits back. The lead cannot list names it never received, so a larger output allowance leaves the final answer just as uninformative.

This would recover the names, but it throws away the context isolation that justified delegating in the first place, filling the lead's window with the very file contents the subagent was meant to absorb. It fails the stated requirement to preserve isolation and doubles the work without changing what the subagent returns.

A subagent runs in its own context window, and only its final message returns to the parent. Whatever the lead needs must therefore be written into that final report, so the delegation prompt should specify the required detail explicitly while the manifest contents stay inside the subagent's window.

The subagent's context window governs how much the subagent itself can hold, not what is transmitted to the lead. The findings are missing because they were not included in the final message, not because they did not fit anywhere.

question: A contract-summarization service occasionally returns summaries that stop mid-sentence. The API returns HTTP 200 with no error, and the text before the cut-off is coherent and on topic. What should the developer do?
options: Inspect stop_reason and raise max_tokens when it reports max_tokens.
Enable streaming so the remaining text is delivered after the initial chunk.
Retry the request with exponential backoff, treating the cut-off as a transient error.
Add a system prompt instruction telling Claude to always finish its sentences.
answer: Inspect stop_reason and raise max_tokens when it reports max_tokens.
explanation:
Every successful Messages API response includes a stop_reason field that tells the application why generation ended. Common values include end_turn (Claude finished naturally), max_tokens (the output cap was reached), stop_sequence (a configured stop string was emitted), and tool_use (Claude is requesting a client tool call). Reaching the cap is a normal outcome, not a failure, so the HTTP status is 200 and no error object appears. Code that only checks the status code will treat a truncated summary as complete, which is exactly the bug in this scenario.

The mental model is that max_tokens is an upper bound, not a target. Claude may stop well before max_tokens when it finishes naturally, in which case stop_reason is end_turn; other stop reasons such as stop_sequence or tool_use should still be handled separately. When the bound is hit mid-thought, the text simply ends, coherent up to that point. The fix is to size max_tokens for the longest output the task legitimately needs and to check stop_reason on every response so truncation is detected rather than silently passed downstream. If a response is truncated on a Claude 4.6 or later model, the documented recovery is to send a follow-up user message containing the partial output and an instruction to continue from where it left off.

The distractors misdiagnose the mechanism. Exponential backoff is the correct discipline for transient capacity errors such as 429 and 529, but it does nothing for a successful response that ran out of output budget; the retry would truncate at the same place. Streaming changes delivery, letting tokens render progressively, but the total generated is still bounded by max_tokens; a stream ends with the same message_delta reporting max_tokens. A prompt instruction cannot override the cap because the limit is enforced by the API after the model has already committed to its answer, so Claude has no way to "finish its sentences" once the budget is exhausted.

See Stop reasons and fallback for the full list of values and recommended handling, and the Messages API reference for the semantics of max_tokens.
option_feedback: A mid-sentence cut-off with a successful response is a common symptom of hitting the output token cap, which the API reports as stop_reason max_tokens rather than as an error. Reading stop_reason confirms the cause, and increasing max_tokens to fit the expected summary length removes it.

Streaming changes how tokens are delivered, not how many the model is allowed to generate. A stream ending with stop_reason max_tokens is truncated at exactly the same point as a non-streamed response.

Backoff and retry is the right response to 429 and 529 capacity errors, but this response succeeded with HTTP 200. Resending the same request with the same output cap produces the same truncation and doubles the cost.

The max_tokens limit is enforced by the API, so generation halts when the cap is reached regardless of what the prompt says. No instruction can extend a hard output ceiling; only the request parameter can.

question: A service wraps every Messages API call in a retry loop that retries any non-2xx response with exponential backoff. Logs show a request with a misspelled top-level field being retried five times, receiving HTTP 400 invalid_request_error each time. What should the client do differently?
options: Route the failing request through the Message Batches API so it is queued rather than rejected outright.
Add random jitter to the backoff schedule so the repeated 400 attempts are not sent in lockstep.
Stop retrying this 400, log the returned error body, and fix the request construction that produced it.
Raise the maximum retry count and lengthen the backoff so the 400 has more time to clear on its own.
answer: Stop retrying this 400, log the returned error body, and fix the request construction that produced it.
explanation:
A robust client for a REST API treats HTTP status codes as a signal about where a failure lives, not simply as success or failure. Statuses such as an ordinary 429 (rate limit), 529 (overloaded), and 500 indicate conditions on the server side or in capacity that can change from moment to moment; the same request may well succeed a few seconds later, which is exactly what retries with exponential backoff and jitter exist to exploit. A 400 invalid_request_error returned for a malformed body, as in this scenario, is a different category: the server parsed the request, found it did not conform to the Messages API contract (here, a misspelled top-level field), and rejected it. Resending the same bytes reproduces the same rejection, so retrying is pure waste and, worse, hides the defect behind a generic "request failed after five attempts" message.

The engineering fix is therefore to build a retry policy that classifies errors. Transient statuses go through the backoff path, honouring any retry-after guidance and capping total attempts. Validation-type 400s are surfaced immediately with the error body, which the API returns as a structured JSON object naming the error type and a human-readable message. That message is what lets an engineer find and correct the request-construction bug. Good practice is to inspect the error type and message in the response body rather than keying solely on the numeric status, because even the retryable family is not uniform: an ordinary rate-limit 429 typically carries a retry-after header and is worth retrying, but a 429 rate_limit_error returned because the organization has reached its monthly spend cap may carry no retry-after and will not clear by retrying; it needs the account limit resolved, so the client should surface it rather than back off indefinitely. Reading the error body keeps those cases distinguishable from each other and from a genuinely malformed request.

The distractors all misapply tools meant for a different failure class. Longer backoff and more attempts only help if the server's answer might change, which it will not for an invalid payload. Jitter solves the thundering-herd problem when many clients retry transient errors together, but it does not alter the outcome of an individual request the server will always reject. The Message Batches API trades immediacy for a cost discount on large asynchronous workloads; it validates request shape just as the synchronous endpoint does, so a malformed request fails there too. The official Messages API reference defines the request schema that the client must satisfy, and the Errors page describes the error types and status codes a client should distinguish when deciding whether to retry.
option_feedback: The Message Batches API is designed for large, latency-tolerant workloads at reduced cost, not as a workaround for validation failures. A request with a malformed body is invalid in a batch as well, so moving it changes the delivery mechanism without addressing the defect.

Jitter is a sound technique for spreading retries of transient capacity errors across many clients so they do not all retry simultaneously. It has no bearing on a request the server rejects as invalid, which fails regardless of when or how spread out the retries are.

A 400 caused by a malformed request body is deterministic: the server rejected the payload itself, so resending the identical payload yields the identical rejection. The right behaviour is to classify this error as non-retryable, surface the error message so the defect in request construction can be fixed, and reserve backoff retries for transient statuses such as 500, 529, and ordinary rate-limit 429s.

Waiting longer only helps when the failure is a transient server-side condition such as rate limiting or overload. A misspelled field in the request body does not change between attempts, so more retries and longer waits just delay the same rejection and waste capacity.

question: A team migrates a classification service from Claude Sonnet 4.6 to Claude Opus 5, leaving temperature set to 0.2 and top_p in the request body to keep outputs consistent. Every request now fails with a 400 error. What should the team change?
options: Route the requests through the Message Batches API, where the sampling parameters remain accepted.
Enable adaptive thinking on the request, which restores support for the sampling parameters on the newer model.
Set temperature to exactly 0, since the newer model rejects only non-zero sampling parameter values.
Remove the temperature and top_p fields from the request and guide output consistency through the prompt instead.
answer: Remove the temperature and top_p fields from the request and guide output consistency through the prompt instead.
explanation:
Sampling parameters such as temperature, top_p, and top_k shape how a model selects each next token from its probability distribution. On earlier Claude models they were the standard lever for trading creativity against consistency. Starting with the Claude 4.7 generation, and continuing through Claude Opus 5, these parameters are not supported: sending any non-default value returns a 400 error rather than being silently ignored. A request that worked unchanged on Claude Sonnet 4.6 therefore fails immediately after a model swap, which is exactly the failure the team observes.

The mental model to carry forward is that model upgrades are behavior and interface changes, not drop-in replacements. The documented remedy is to omit the sampling parameters from the payload and use prompting to guide the model's behavior. For a classification service, that means clear instructions, a fixed label set, and multi-shot examples that demonstrate the exact output, backed by an eval that confirms consistency on the target model. Even on models that accept temperature, generation was never guaranteed deterministic, so designing for validation rather than exact repetition was already the robust pattern.

The distractors each misread the constraint. Setting temperature to 0 still sends a non-default value and still fails. Adaptive thinking governs reasoning depth, not token sampling, so enabling it changes nothing about parameter acceptance. The Message Batches API applies the same per-model request rules asynchronously; it is a delivery and pricing model, not a way to unlock retired parameters. See Using the Messages API for the parameter note and Models overview for the current lineup.
option_feedback: The Message Batches API processes the same Messages request format asynchronously at a discount; it does not change which parameters a given model accepts. Requests with unsupported sampling parameters would fail there as well.

Adaptive thinking controls whether and how much Claude reasons before answering; it has no relationship to sampling parameter support. The sampling parameters remain unsupported regardless of the thinking configuration.
The rejection applies to any non-default value, and 0 is not the default temperature, so the request would still fail. There is no special exemption for greedy sampling on these models.

Claude 4.7 and later models, including Claude Opus 5, do not support the temperature, top_p, and top_k sampling parameters, and any non-default value returns a 400 error. Omitting them and using prompting to shape the model's behavior is the documented migration path.

question: A long-running Claude API agent built on a tool-use loop regularly approaches the context window limit before its task is finished. Which TWO mechanisms address this directly?
options: Use context editing to clear older tool results from the conversation as the agent works.
Enable prompt caching on the stable prefix so cached tokens no longer count toward the window.
Raise max_tokens on each request so the model has more room before the context window fills.
Enable server-side compaction so earlier turns are summarized and the conversation can continue.
answer: Use context editing to clear older tool results from the conversation as the agent works.
Enable server-side compaction so earlier turns are summarized and the conversation can continue.
explanation:
Every turn of a tool-use loop appends to the conversation: the assistant's tool_use blocks, the tool_result blocks your application returns, and the model's reasoning and text. For a long-running agent that reads files, runs searches, or executes commands dozens of times, the tool results dominate that growth, and most of them are only relevant for a few turns after they arrive. The context window is a hard ceiling, so an agent that never manages it will eventually fail mid-task. The mental model is that context is a working buffer, not an archive, and the harness has to decide what stays in it.

Two documented Claude API mechanisms attack the problem from different angles. Server-side compaction has the API summarize earlier parts of the conversation so the exchange can continue past the window limit; the tradeoff is that fine detail from early turns is replaced by a structured summary, which is why the default summary prompt captures task overview, current state, discoveries, and next steps. Context editing is more surgical: its tool result clearing strategy removes old tool outputs (and thinking block clearing removes thinking blocks when extended thinking is in use) while leaving the rest of the conversation intact. Compaction suits conversations that must run indefinitely; context editing suits agentic loops where the bulk is stale tool output. Delegating exploratory work to subagents that return only summaries and persisting durable state to an external memory store are complementary patterns that reduce how fast the window fills in the first place.

The distractors confuse adjacent parameters with the context window. max_tokens bounds the output of one response and has no effect on how much of the window the accumulated conversation occupies; hitting it produces a truncated response with stop_reason: max_tokens, not more room. Prompt caching lowers the cost and latency of reprocessing a stable prefix, but cached tokens are still part of the prompt and still count toward the window, so caching does not defer the limit at all.

See Compaction, Context editing, and How tool use works.
option_feedback: Context editing provides a tool result clearing strategy that removes stale tool outputs from the conversation in agentic workflows. In a tool-use loop, accumulated tool results are usually what consumes the window, so clearing them frees space for further turns.

Prompt caching reduces cost and latency for repeated prefixes, but cached tokens still occupy the context window in full. Caching changes how tokens are billed and processed, not how many of them the conversation contains.

The max_tokens parameter caps the number of output tokens in a single response; it does not change the size of the context window or how much of it the conversation occupies. Raising it can even make the problem worse by allowing longer responses that consume more of the window.

Server-side compaction summarizes earlier parts of the conversation on Anthropic's servers so the conversation can continue past the context window limit. It is designed precisely for conversations that regularly approach the limit mid-task.

question: A developer finds that an Anthropic API key was hardcoded in a Python script and pushed to a shared Git repository three weeks ago. The key has since been deleted from the current version of the file. What should the team do next?
options: Add the script to .gitignore so that future edits to the file are never pushed to the shared repository again.
Move the key into a .env file committed alongside the script so it no longer appears inline in the source code.
Rewrite the repository's Git history to purge the key from every past commit and continue using the same key.
Revoke the key in the Console, issue a replacement, and supply it through an environment variable or secrets store.
answer: Revoke the key in the Console, issue a replacement, and supply it through an environment variable or secrets store.
explanation:
API keys are credentials, and the governing rule for a leaked credential is simple: once it has been visible to anyone who should not hold it, its lifetime is over. Git makes this especially unforgiving. A commit is immutable content that is copied wholesale to every clone, fork, mirror, and CI runner that fetched it, so deleting the string from the working tree, or even rewriting history on the origin, cannot recall the copies that already exist. The only remediation that actually closes the exposure is to revoke the key in the Claude Console and issue a new one, which is why key management there lets you delete keys and set an expiration at creation time.

The second half of the fix is structural. Anthropic's client SDKs read the credential from the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable by default, and the SDK does not load .env files on its own, so the intended pattern is that the runtime environment, a secrets manager, or a deployment pipeline injects the key at process start. Configuration that varies by environment and must stay confidential belongs outside the repository; configuration that defines behaviour, such as prompts and pinned model versions, belongs inside it under review. Keeping those two categories separate is the mental model that prevents this class of incident from recurring.

The distractors each address a symptom rather than the exposure. Purging history without rotating the key leaves the compromised credential live everywhere the old commits were fetched. Committing a .env file merely relocates the secret within version control. Adding the script to .gitignore neither invalidates the key nor removes it from past commits, and it removes application code from source control in the process. Only rotation plus environment-based injection resolves both the immediate breach and the design flaw that caused it.

See the Claude API overview for how API keys are issued and used with the SDKs, and Authentication for key lifecycle options such as expiration.
option_feedback: Ignoring the script does not remove the key from the commits already in the repository's history, and it does not invalidate the credential that was exposed. It also breaks the workflow by keeping application code out of version control, which trades one configuration problem for another.

Committing a .env file to the repository stores the secret in version control just as surely as an inline string, so anyone with repository access still obtains it. Environment files are useful only when they are excluded from source control and populated per environment, and this option also does nothing about the already exposed key.

Rewriting history only cleans the canonical repository; every existing clone, fork, mirror, and build log still holds the original commits and the key inside them. Continuing to use the same credential leaves the exposure fully in place, so history rewriting is at best optional hygiene after rotation, not a substitute for it.

A secret that has spent three weeks in a shared repository must be treated as compromised, because clones, forks, CI logs, and local checkouts may already contain it. Revoking the key removes the exposure regardless of where copies exist, and loading the replacement from the environment or a secrets store keeps it out of source control going forward.

question: A team wants a PreToolUse hook that blocks force-pushes and recursive deletes to apply to every engineer who clones a repository, without each person configuring anything. Where should the hook be defined?
options: Define the rule in the repository's CLAUDE.md, instructing Claude never to run those commands.
Define the hook in the repository's .claude/settings.local.json alongside the project's other settings.
Define the hook in each engineer's ~/.claude/settings.json, since user settings cover every project.
Define the hook in the repository's .claude/settings.json and commit it to version control.
answer: Define the hook in the repository's .claude/settings.json and commit it to version control.
explanation:
Claude Code hooks are user-defined handlers (shell commands, HTTP endpoints, MCP tools, prompts, or subagents) that fire automatically at lifecycle events. A PreToolUse hook with a Bash matcher runs before a shell command executes and can block it deterministically, which is what makes hooks the right layer for guardrails against irreversible actions such as git push --force or rm -rf. The model never gets a vote once the hook denies the call.

The question is where that hook lives, and the answer follows from how Claude Code layers settings. User settings in ~/.claude/settings.json cover every project on one machine but nothing on anyone else's. Project settings in .claude/settings.json belong to the repository, and once committed they reach every clone, so a single commit puts the guardrail in front of the whole team. Project local settings in .claude/settings.local.json are intended for personal, per-checkout use and are not shared through version control, so they cannot distribute anything. Managed settings deployed by an organization are the tool for machine-wide or organization-wide policy, but for a repository-specific rule the committed project file is the natural home.

One nuance worth knowing: in an interactive session, Claude Code holds back hooks from every settings file until the user accepts the workspace trust dialog for that folder, while -p and SDK sessions treat the folder as trusted and run committed hooks immediately. That is why hooks committed to a repository are also something to review before scripting Claude Code over code you did not write.

The CLAUDE.md option is the classic anti-pattern here.
