CLAUDE.md is for behavioral guidance such as code style and workflow preferences; the documentation explicitly separates it from technical enforcement, which belongs in settings via permissions.deny, sandboxing, or hooks. A sentence asking Claude not to force-push improves the odds, but a hook guarantees the outcome. See Claude Code hooks for event types, matchers, and the settings locations where hooks can be defined.
option_feedback: CLAUDE.md content is behavioral guidance that the model reads and usually follows, but it is probabilistic rather than enforced. Blocking destructive commands is a technical-enforcement concern that belongs in settings-based controls such as hooks or deny rules, not in prose instructions.

The settings.local.json file is meant for personal, per-checkout settings and is intended to stay out of the repository's commits. Because it is not shared through version control, a hook placed there is never distributed to other engineers who clone the repository.

User-level settings apply only to the machine they live on and never reach a teammate's clone or a cloud session. Relying on them means every engineer must configure the hook manually, which is exactly what the team wants to avoid and leaves gaps whenever someone forgets.

Project settings committed to the repository travel with the code, so every engineer who clones it receives the same hooks and permissions. This is the documented way to share guardrails with a whole team, since a single committed file reaches every checkout without per-person setup.

question: An application calls the Messages API directly and needs the tools of a vendor's MCP server that is hosted remotely and reachable over HTTPS. The team needs only tool calling, not MCP prompts or resources, and does not want to run an MCP client. Which approach fits?
options: Reference the server in the request's mcp_servers parameter and govern its tools with an mcp_toolset entry.
Package the server's operations as a Skill so Claude loads the calling instructions only when the task needs them.
Install the MCP SDK, open a client connection from the application, and pass tools through the SDK conversion helpers.
Read the server's tool list once and re-declare each tool as a custom client tool that proxies calls to the server.
answer: Reference the server in the request's mcp_servers parameter and govern its tools with an mcp_toolset entry.
explanation:
The MCP connector exists so that a Messages API caller can consume a remote MCP server without becoming an MCP client itself. You declare the server (type url, its address, and an optional OAuth bearer token) in the mcp_servers array, and you add an mcp_toolset object to tools that names the server and optionally enables, allowlists, or denylists individual tools. Anthropic's side then handles the MCP session: Claude's tool calls come back as mcp_tool_use blocks and their results as MCP tool result blocks inside the same response, so the application never implements the protocol round trip. The feature is in beta (header mcp-client-2025-11-20), supports only tool calling, and is not covered by zero data retention arrangements, which are the boundaries worth checking before choosing it.

The useful mental model is that MCP offers two integration points with very different operational weight. When the server is remote, reachable by URL, and you need only its tools, the connector keeps everything inside a single API request. When you need a local stdio server, MCP prompts, MCP resources, or fine control over the connection lifecycle, you run your own client and use the SDK's conversion helpers to translate MCP types into Claude API types. The client-side path is legitimate, but choosing it here contradicts every stated constraint: the server is remote, only tools are needed, and the team does not want to host a client.

Re-declaring the server's tools as custom client tools and proxying calls is a duplication anti-pattern. Custom tools are the right choice for logic that lives inside your own application, but wrapping someone else's MCP server that way means maintaining a second copy of schemas that will drift as the vendor changes them, plus writing proxy code for each operation. A Skill is the wrong category of extension altogether: Skills are for knowing (procedures, templates, standards, loaded progressively), not for doing, and Skills executed through the API run in a container with no network access, so a Skill cannot reach the vendor's server at all.

See MCP connector for server configuration, toolset patterns, and the client-side helper comparison, and Tool use with Claude for how client and server tools differ in where they execute.
option_feedback: The MCP connector lets a Messages API request connect to a remote MCP server by URL with no separate MCP client, and an mcp_toolset entry in the tools array enables, allowlists, or denylists its tools. This is exactly the documented fit: a remote URL-reachable server where only tool support is needed.

Skills package procedural knowledge and reference material, not live connections to external systems, and Skills running through the API have no network access. Describing how to call a remote service in a Skill gives Claude no mechanism to actually invoke it.

Client-side MCP helpers are the documented path when you need local stdio servers, MCP prompts, MCP resources, or more control over the connection. None of those conditions apply here, and the team explicitly wants to avoid operating an MCP client, so this adds infrastructure the connector already removes.

Hand-copying tool schemas into custom client tools creates a second definition that drifts whenever the server changes its tools, and it forces the application to build and maintain proxying code for every operation. It reproduces what the connector does natively at the cost of ongoing maintenance.

question: A developer commits their own permission allow rules and preferred model for one repository to that repository's .claude/settings.json. After pulling, teammates find these choices applied to their sessions. Where should the developer keep such project-specific personal settings?
options: Add .claude/settings.json to the repository's .gitignore so the file is never pushed to teammates.
Move them into .claude/settings.local.json, the local scope intended to stay untracked by git.
Move them into ~/.claude/settings.json so they take effect across every project on the machine.
Move them into the repository's CLAUDE.md so they load as instructions at the start of each session.
answer: Move them into .claude/settings.local.json, the local scope intended to stay untracked by git.
explanation:
Claude Code resolves configuration from a small hierarchy of settings scopes, and knowing which scope a value belongs in is the core of configuration management for the tool. Organization-wide managed settings sit at the top and cannot be overridden. Below them, a repository has two files that look similar but serve different audiences: .claude/settings.json is the shared project scope, meant to be committed so every contributor runs with the same permission rules, hooks, and defaults; .claude/settings.local.json is the local project scope, meant for one person's overrides in that same repository. User settings in ~/.claude/settings.json apply to every project on the machine.

The local file is the right home for the scenario's values because it is project-specific yet personal. When Claude Code itself creates or writes .claude/settings.local.json, it also adds the file to git's ignore configuration; a developer who creates or moves the file by hand should add it to .gitignore or a global excludes file themselves. Either way, the developer can grant themselves extra allow rules or choose a different model without those decisions propagating through a pull request. How the local values combine with the shared file depends on the type of setting: a scalar setting such as model in the local scope overrides the same key in the shared project scope on the developer's machine, while list settings such as permissions.allow are merged across scopes rather than replaced, and any allow rule still remains subject to deny and ask rules defined in other scopes. In both cases teammates continue to inherit only the committed file. The same split exists for instructions: a committed CLAUDE.md carries team conventions, while CLAUDE.local.md holds personal notes that stay out of the repository.

The alternatives each misplace the configuration. User-scope settings solve the sharing problem but apply the repository-specific choices to every other project the developer opens. Ignoring .claude/settings.json throws away the team's shared configuration channel to fix a scoping mistake. Moving the values into CLAUDE.md confuses guidance with enforcement: CLAUDE.md is context the model reads, not configuration Claude Code applies, and a project CLAUDE.md is committed anyway. The general rule is to ask two questions of any setting: who should it affect, and should it be enforced or merely suggested? Those answers point directly to the correct file. See Claude Code settings for the scope table and precedence rules.
option_feedback: The shared project settings file exists precisely so that team-wide configuration is committed and reviewed together. Ignoring it removes the mechanism for sharing legitimate project settings and does not give the developer a proper place for personal overrides.

Local project settings are the scope designed for one person's preferences within a single repository. When Claude Code itself creates or writes this file it also configures git to ignore it; if the developer creates or moves the file manually, they should add it to .gitignore or a global excludes file so the settings apply only on their machine while the shared .claude/settings.json stays clean for the team.

User settings apply to every repository the developer opens, but the scenario describes choices intended for one project only. Placing repository-specific allow rules and a model preference there leaks them into unrelated work rather than scoping them correctly.

CLAUDE.md holds natural-language guidance for Claude, not enforced configuration, so permission rules and model selection do not belong there. A project CLAUDE.md is also committed and shared, which would reproduce the same problem for teammates.

question: A developer is sizing the context budget for a tool-heavy agent built on the Messages API. Which TWO assumptions about the context window are correct?
options: Budget for tool definitions and every tool result, since both occupy the window alongside the system prompt.
Ignore extended thinking tokens in the budget, since they are billed as output but never occupy the window.
Expect accuracy and recall to degrade as the window fills, so curate content rather than rely on headroom.
Exclude cache-read tokens from the budget, since cached prefixes are not reprocessed on each request.
answer: Budget for tool definitions and every tool result, since both occupy the window alongside the system prompt.
Expect accuracy and recall to degrade as the window fills, so curate content rather than rely on headroom.
explanation:
The context window is the model's working memory for a single request: all the text it can reference while generating, including the response itself. A common mistake is to picture it as just the visible chat history. In practice, a Messages API request loads the system prompt, every entry in messages (user turns, assistant turns, tool results, images, and documents), the tool definitions passed in tools, and then the output Claude produces for the turn, including any extended thinking. For a tool-heavy agent, the tool schemas and the accumulating tool results are often the largest and fastest-growing components, which is why techniques such as tool result clearing, compaction, and deferring tool definitions exist.

The second half of a sound mental model is that more context is not automatically better. As token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot. This is the tradeoff a large window exists to make: it lets you handle long and complex inputs, but attention over irrelevant bulk still degrades. Sizing a budget therefore means deciding what should be in the window at each step, not simply confirming that the total fits under the limit.

The two distractors reflect plausible but wrong shortcuts. Prompt caching changes what you pay and how fast the prefix is processed, but a cached prefix is still part of the prompt; every response's usage field splits input across input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens, and cache_creation_input_tokens, and all three count toward the window. Similarly, thinking tokens are billed as output tokens, but they also consume context during the turn in which they are generated; how earlier turns' thinking blocks are handled afterwards varies by model, so they cannot be treated as costless. To estimate a request before sending it, use the token counting API.

See Context windows for what counts toward the window and how thinking interacts with it, and Prompt caching for the usage field breakdown.
option_feedback: Everything in the request counts toward the context window: the system prompt, all messages including tool results, images, and documents, and the tool definitions themselves. For an agent that carries many tools and accumulates tool results across turns, these components can dominate the budget.

Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens, but they also count toward the context window for the turn in which they are generated, together with the rest of the output. Whether prior turns' thinking blocks remain in later requests depends on the model, so treating them as free of context cost is incorrect.

As token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot. A larger window gives room for longer prompts, but curating what stays in context matters as much as how much space is available.

Prompt caching reduces cost and latency, but cached content still occupies the context window. The input count is split across input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens, and cache_creation_input_tokens, and all three count toward the window.

question: A latency-sensitive chat service moves from Claude Sonnet 4.6 to Claude Sonnet 5 without changing its requests, which have never included a thinking parameter. Output token counts and response times rise sharply. Which change addresses the cause?
options: Raise max_tokens on every request, since Claude Sonnet 5 needs a larger output budget to finish the same answers it produced on Claude Sonnet 4.6.
Opt into fast mode by setting speed to fast, since Claude Sonnet 5 generates output tokens more slowly at standard speed.
Wait for prompt caching support on Claude Sonnet 5 before migrating, since each request currently reprocesses the entire prompt uncached.
Set the thinking configuration and effort level explicitly, because omitting the thinking parameter enables thinking on Claude Sonnet 5.
answer: Set the thinking configuration and effort level explicitly, because omitting the thinking parameter enables thinking on Claude Sonnet 5.
explanation:
A model upgrade changes more than benchmark scores; it can change what a request means when a parameter is left out. On Claude Opus 4.6 through Claude Opus 4.8 and Claude Sonnet 4.6, omitting the thinking parameter leaves thinking off. On Claude Opus 5 and Claude Sonnet 5, the same omission leaves thinking on in adaptive mode, and on Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5 thinking is always on regardless of the parameter. A request body that was implicitly a no-thinking request on Claude Sonnet 4.6 becomes a thinking-enabled request on Claude Sonnet 5 with no code change at all.

The symptoms follow directly. Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens and count toward max_tokens, so output_tokens climbs, and because Claude reasons before it starts the visible answer, time to answer grows. The usage.output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens field shows how much of the billed output was internal reasoning, which is the fastest way to confirm this diagnosis. The right response is to make the configuration explicit rather than rely on defaults: set the thinking parameter deliberately, and use output_config.effort as the calibrated lever for how often and how deeply Claude thinks. At low effort Claude skips thinking on simple turns, which is usually the correct posture for an interactive chat workload where speed dominates.

The distractors each misattribute the cause. Raising max_tokens only widens the ceiling on output and does nothing to cut the reasoning tokens now being generated. Fast mode exists only for Claude Opus 5 and Claude Opus 4.8, and it raises output tokens per second at premium pricing; it does not reduce how many tokens are generated and is unavailable on Sonnet. Prompt caching is supported on every active model, and a caching regression would show up as higher uncached input cost, not as more output tokens.

The broader lesson for model selection is that implicit behavior is part of your contract with a model version. Pin every behavior-affecting parameter explicitly and run the eval suite against the new model before cutover, so that a change in defaults surfaces as a measured difference rather than a production surprise. See Thinking, Effort, and Fast mode.
option_feedback: Raising max_tokens only lifts the ceiling on output; it does nothing to reduce the number of tokens generated or the time to answer. The extra tokens are reasoning that the model now produces by default, not a truncation problem caused by too small an output budget.

Fast mode is available only for Claude Opus 5 and Claude Opus 4.8, not for Claude Sonnet 5, and it changes generation speed rather than how many tokens are produced. A slower per-token rate would not explain a sharp rise in output token counts.

Prompt caching is supported on all active Claude models, including Claude Sonnet 5. Even if caching were lost, that would affect input processing cost and time to first token, not the number of output tokens the model generates.

On Claude Sonnet 4.6, omitting the thinking parameter means thinking is off, while on Claude Sonnet 5 an omitted parameter means thinking is on and adaptive. The migrated requests therefore reason before answering, adding billed output tokens and time to answer; setting the thinking configuration or a lower effort level explicitly matches the workload instead of relying on a default that changed.

question: A multi-tenant document Q&A application uploads each customer's PDFs through the Files API. Its frontend passes the file_id to query in every request, so a customer can supply another customer's file_id. Which change correctly addresses this?
options: Issue a distinct API key to each customer inside the shared Default Workspace so every key can only read the files it uploaded itself.
Instruct Claude in the system prompt to verify that the referenced file belongs to the requesting customer before it answers any question.
Treat file IDs as server-side references, map each user to their files in the application, and isolate tenants with separate workspaces.
Set a short expires_in_seconds value on every upload so that a leaked file_id stops resolving shortly after the original request completes.
answer: Treat file IDs as server-side references, map each user to their files in the application, and isolate tenants with separate workspaces.
explanation:
The Files API scopes uploaded files to the workspace of the API key that uploaded them. Any API key in that workspace can reference any file it contains, and unless keys have been deliberately assigned to separate workspaces, they all share the organization's Default Workspace. The API has no concept of an end user, conversation, or session when it resolves a file_id; it only checks that the file exists in the workspace. This design keeps files reusable across many requests and many keys, which is the point of uploading once and referencing repeatedly, but it means the platform cannot enforce per-user ownership for you.

The consequence for application design is that a file_id must be treated like any other server-side reference to privileged data. The client should identify which document it wants in terms the application controls (its own document ID tied to the authenticated user), and the server should look up the corresponding file_id from a mapping it owns. Accepting a raw file_id from the browser is the classic insecure direct object reference: the identifier is guessable or observable, and the backend performs no ownership check before handing the content to Claude. For applications that serve multiple tenants, the documented approach is to create a separate workspace per tenant so the isolation boundary the platform actually enforces lines up with the trust boundary between customers.

The other approaches confuse different mechanisms for authorization. Asking Claude to verify ownership in the system prompt fails because the file content has already been loaded into the request; the model cannot see who the caller is and cannot be trusted to refuse. Setting a short expires_in_seconds only shortens how long a file lives (with a floor of one hour) and does nothing to stop another customer from referencing it while it is live; expiration is a lifecycle control, not an access control. Minting one API key per customer inside a single workspace sounds like separation, but keys are not the scoping boundary for files, so every key can still read every file in that workspace.

See Files API for the workspace-scoped access warning and Workspaces for how keys and resources are scoped.
option_feedback: Files are scoped to the workspace, not to the API key that uploaded them, so any key in the same workspace can reference any file uploaded there. Per-customer keys within one workspace provide no isolation; only separate workspaces do.

By the time the request reaches Claude, the referenced file has already been resolved and its contents are in the model's context. The model has no reliable knowledge of which user owns which file, and a probabilistic instruction cannot substitute for an authorization check enforced by application code.

Uploaded files are visible to every API key in the workspace, so the Files API does not know which end user owns a file. Authorization must live in the application: the server resolves the caller's identity to the files it owns and never accepts a file_id from the client, and a workspace per tenant gives hard isolation because the workspace is the file scoping boundary.

File expiration is a lifecycle feature, not an access control, and the minimum expiration is one hour, which leaves a wide window for misuse. Any customer whose documents remain live for later questions would still be exposed to another customer supplying their file_id during that time.

question: A team defines a custom Claude Code subagent that reviews pull request diffs and reports findings. The subagent must be unable to modify files, even if a delegated task asks it to. Which configuration enforces this?
options: Restrict the tools frontmatter field to read-oriented tools such as Read, Grep, and Glob.
Set permissionMode to bypassPermissions so the subagent runs without approval prompts.
Enable memory with scope project so the subagent remembers it is a read-only reviewer.
State in the subagent's system prompt that it must never edit, write, or delete files.
answer: Restrict the tools frontmatter field to read-oriented tools such as Read, Grep, and Glob.
explanation:
Subagents in Claude Code are separate agent instances, each with its own context window, its own system prompt, and its own tool access. The frontmatter of a subagent file is where a developer decides what the subagent is able to do, as opposed to what it is asked to do. The tools field is an allowlist: a subagent inherits the built-in and MCP tools of the main conversation only to the extent that field permits. Leaving Edit and Write out of the list means there is no tool call the model can emit to change a file, so the constraint survives any phrasing of the delegated task and any instructions embedded in the diff being reviewed. The documented code-reviewer example uses exactly this shape: a detailed review prompt paired with a narrow tool set. If the reviewer also needs shell access, for example to run git diff, be aware that Bash can modify files too, so decide deliberately whether to include it and, if so, rely on permission rules to bound what it may run.

The mental model is the same one that applies to the main conversation: prompts shape behavior, while configuration enforces it. A sentence in the system prompt saying "never edit files" reduces the probability of edits but leaves the capability in place, which matters most precisely in the cases a reviewer exists to catch, such as a pull request containing text that looks like instructions. permissionMode: bypassPermissions does not enforce anything either: permission mode governs approval prompting rather than tool availability, and a subagent's declared mode may be ignored or inherited depending on the main conversation's permission mode. In no case does it remove the ability to write files. The memory field is a knowledge-persistence feature; enabling it adds Read, Write, and Edit so the subagent can maintain its memory directory, which is a reminder to check what each frontmatter field actually switches on before assuming it constrains anything.

This design choice also pays off in cost and focus. A reviewer limited to read-oriented tools produces fewer surprising side effects, is safe to run in the background, and can be checked into .claude/agents/ and shared across the team without each engineer re-deriving the safety boundary. See Create custom subagents for the frontmatter reference and the read-only reviewer example, and Subagents in the SDK for how the same tool-restriction principle applies when subagents are defined programmatically.
option_feedback: The tools field in a subagent's frontmatter determines which tools the subagent can call at all, so omitting Edit and Write removes the capability rather than merely discouraging it. This is the documented pattern for a read-only reviewer: a focused subagent with limited tool access that can analyze but never accidentally modify files.

Permission mode governs approval prompting, not which tools exist, so it does not enforce read-only access in any direction. Under current subagent rules, a bypassPermissions declaration in frontmatter may be ignored or overridden by the main conversation's permission mode, and in every case the Edit and Write tools remain callable.

The memory field gives a subagent a persistent directory for accumulating knowledge across conversations, and enabling it actually turns on Read, Write, and Edit so the subagent can manage its memory files. It has nothing to do with restricting file modification.

A system prompt instruction is guidance, not enforcement; the Edit and Write tools remain available and the model can still be talked into using them by a poorly phrased task or injected content. Tool restriction is the mechanism that makes the constraint hold regardless of wording.

question: A developer is writing the error-classification layer for a Claude tool-use application. Which TWO practices correctly separate the different failure categories?
options: Classify HTTP error responses as request-processing failures, and read stop_reason only from successful responses.
Treat stop_reason max_tokens as a transport failure and rely on the SDK's automatic retries to resolve it.
Branch on the typed SDK exception class or the error object's type field, not on the message string.
Abort the loop with an exception when a tool's execution fails rather than returning a tool_result marked is_error.
answer: Classify HTTP error responses as request-processing failures, and read stop_reason only from successful responses.
Branch on the typed SDK exception class or the error object's type field, not on the message string.
explanation:
Debugging a Claude application is much easier when failures are sorted into distinct layers, because each layer has its own signals and its own remedies. The first layer is the transport and request layer: the API returns a non-2xx HTTP status together with a JSON body whose error.type names the category (for example invalid_request_error, rate_limit_error, api_error, or overloaded_error) and a request_id that support can use to locate the call. The second layer is the model-output layer: a request that succeeded returns a message whose stop_reason explains why generation stopped, such as end_turn, max_tokens, or tool_use. A stop_reason is never an error in the HTTP sense; it is information about a response you already have.

Within the transport layer, the right way to branch is on the typed SDK exception or the error.type field rather than on message wording. The set of error types is versioned and documented, while message strings are descriptive text that can be reworded at any time. Building conditionals on substrings of the message is a common source of silent regressions when a phrasing changes. The official SDKs already map these categories to exception classes and retry transient ones (connection errors, rate limits, 5xx responses) with backoff, which is why a handler that treats max_tokens as something for the SDK to retry is a category error: nothing failed, so nothing is retried, and the truncated output stays truncated until the application raises max_tokens or continues the response.

The third layer is the integration layer your own code owns, including tool execution. When a tool's underlying operation fails, the documented pattern is to send the failure back inside a tool_result block with is_error: true. Claude reads that flag and the error text, then decides whether to retry with corrected arguments, ask the user for clarification, or explain the limitation. Escalating a tool failure into an API exception collapses the integration layer into the transport layer and throws away the model's ability to recover, which is exactly the behavior an agentic loop is supposed to provide.

See Errors, Handling stop reasons, and Handle tool calls.
option_feedback: HTTP status codes and the JSON error object signal that the request itself failed, while stop_reason is a field on a successful Messages API response that explains why generation ended. Keeping these two categories apart is the foundation of a correct classification layer because each has a different set of remedies.

A response with stop_reason max_tokens arrived successfully; the model simply hit the output ceiling, so there is no transport failure for the SDK to retry. The correct remedy is application logic, such as raising max_tokens or issuing a continuation request, not treating it as an API error.

Error bodies carry a machine-readable type such as rate_limit_error or overloaded_error, and the SDKs surface these as typed exceptions. Message text is free-form and can change, so matching substrings is brittle, whereas the type field and status code are the stable contract.

A failing tool is an integration-layer event, not an API error, and the documented pattern is to return the failure text in a tool_result with is_error set to true. This lets Claude read the error and retry with corrected input or explain the limitation, whereas aborting the loop discards that recovery path.

question: A stakeholder workshop for a Claude-based contract-review tool produces several statements. Before writing the requirements document, the team wants to separate genuine requirements from premature implementation decisions. Which statement is a requirement rather than a design choice?
options: The service shall pin production traffic to a specific dated Claude model snapshot at all times.
The service shall enable prompt caching on the shared clause-library portion of the system prompt.
Reviewers must receive a summary of flagged clauses for each uploaded contract within 90 seconds of upload.
The service shall send contracts that arrive overnight through the Message Batches API for processing.
answer: Reviewers must receive a summary of flagged clauses for each uploaded contract within 90 seconds of upload.
explanation:
Requirements analysis separates what the system must do and how well from how the team intends to build it. A requirement is solution-agnostic: it states an outcome or quality attribute that stakeholders can verify, such as a deliverable per uploaded contract and a 90-second turnaround. Because it does not name a mechanism, it can be satisfied in more than one way, and it survives even if the chosen mechanism later changes.

The other three statements each name a specific Anthropic capability or practice. Prompt caching reuses a stable prompt prefix to cut input cost and latency; model version pinning keeps production on a known snapshot so upgrades become deliberate; the Message Batches API trades immediacy for a per-token discount on latency-tolerant work. All three are legitimate and often correct engineering choices, but they are answers to requirements, not requirements themselves. Writing them into the requirements document too early locks the design before the need is understood. For example, a batch mandate would silently conflict with a 90-second turnaround, and a caching mandate says nothing about the cost or latency threshold that would tell the team whether caching is even worth the complexity.

A practical test when reviewing a statement: ask why. If the answer is another statement about the business or user need, the original was a design decision and the answer is closer to the real requirement. If the answer is simply the business objective, the statement is already a requirement. Capturing the need first and deriving the mechanism second keeps traceability intact and lets the eval and monitoring plan target the outcomes stakeholders actually care about.

See Prompt caching, Batch processing, and the Models overview for the mechanisms named in the distractors, each of which is chosen during design to satisfy requirements like the one in the correct answer.
option_feedback: Model version pinning is a configuration management practice chosen during design and operations. It supports a stability requirement, but the statement itself specifies a mechanism rather than an outcome the business needs.

Prompt caching is a cost and latency optimization technique, which makes this a design decision about how to build the system. The underlying requirement it serves, such as a latency or cost ceiling, is what belongs in the requirements document.

This statement describes what the system must deliver and how quickly, without prescribing any mechanism. It is testable, traceable to the business need, and leaves the design team free to choose the approach that meets it.

Choosing the Message Batches API is a decision about which Anthropic capability to invoke, not a statement of need. The genuine requirement would describe the acceptable turnaround and cost target for overnight contracts, which then justifies or rules out batching.

question: A developer is building an interactive terminal assistant on the Python Agent SDK. Users hold a multi-exchange conversation in one shared context and must be able to interrupt a long-running task mid-execution and redirect it. Which SDK interface fits this requirement?
options: Open a ClaudeSDKClient session, send follow-ups through that client's query() method, and call interrupt() when the user redirects.
Run claude -p as a subprocess for each message and send SIGTERM to the process whenever the user needs to interrupt.
Call the top-level query() function once per user message and resend the entire prior transcript inside each new prompt to preserve context.
Call the top-level query() function once per user message with continue_conversation=True, and cancel the async iterator to interrupt.
answer: Open a ClaudeSDKClient session, send follow-ups through that client's query() method, and call interrupt() when the user redirects.
explanation:
The Python Agent SDK exposes two entry points that share the same underlying agent loop but differ in how they treat a session. The top-level query() function is a one-shot iterator: it creates a fresh session by default, streams messages until the task finishes, and manages the connection for you. It is the right shape for one-off tasks such as a CI job or a scripted refactor, where the caller has no reason to steer mid-flight. ClaudeSDKClient is the stateful counterpart: you open it once, send as many exchanges as you like into the same context, and retain manual control of the connection. That control is what makes interrupts possible, because the client can send a stop signal to the turn currently running and then accept a new instruction.

The mental model is that the SDK spawns and drives a Claude Code process on your behalf. With query(), each call is a self-contained run; continuation is opt-in through continue_conversation or resume, and there is no handle to reach into a run and stop it. With ClaudeSDKClient, the process stays attached to your application, so interrupt() can end the turn, and the client's receive_response() drains what the interrupted turn already produced before the next query's messages arrive. Anthropic's reference describes exactly this split: use the client for chat interfaces or whenever the next action depends on Claude's response.

The alternatives fail for different reasons. Replaying the whole transcript into each prompt reimplements session state the SDK already owns, inflates the context window, and still offers no way to stop a running turn. Cancelling the iterator returned by query() is not a supported interrupt path, so the running turn is not cleanly ended. Driving claude -p as a subprocess and sending SIGTERM kills the process rather than the turn: Claude Code exits with code 143, records no result for the unfinished turn, and only resumes it on a later --continue. The documented guidance for ending a turn is SIGINT or the SDK's interrupt(), which is precisely the capability ClaudeSDKClient provides in-process.

See the Agent SDK Python reference for the comparison of query() and ClaudeSDKClient, and Run Claude Code programmatically for how SIGTERM and SIGINT differ when stopping a run.
option_feedback: ClaudeSDKClient keeps one session open across multiple exchanges, so each follow-up lands in the same context automatically. It is also the only interface that supports interrupts, letting the application stop an in-progress turn and then send a new instruction.

SIGTERM terminates the whole Claude Code process with exit code 143 and leaves the in-progress turn unfinished with no result recorded, which is not the same as ending the turn and redirecting. Spawning a fresh subprocess per message also discards the in-process session handling the Python SDK provides.

Replaying the transcript into every prompt recreates state the SDK already manages through sessions, bloats the context window, and still leaves no interrupt mechanism. It trades a built-in capability for a fragile manual reimplementation.

continue_conversation does let query() pick up a prior session, but the top-level query() function does not support interrupts. Abandoning the iterator is not a supported stop signal, so there is no reliable way to halt the running turn and redirect it within the same session.

question: A content pipeline has Claude produce a draft, critique it against fixed criteria, and then revise it. The team must log each intermediate output and be able to halt the process after the critique step. Which design satisfies these requirements?
options: Enable extended thinking so the critique takes place in thinking blocks, then log those blocks as the audit record.
Run the draft, critique, and revision as separate sequenced API calls, passing each output into the next call.
Spawn the draft and critique as parallel subagents and have a lead agent merge their outputs into the revision.
Send one prompt asking the model to draft, critique, and revise within a single response, then log that whole response.
answer: Run the draft, critique, and revision as separate sequenced API calls, passing each output into the next call.
explanation:
Current Claude models handle most multistep reasoning internally, so a single call with adaptive thinking is often enough for a draft-review-refine loop. The decision to break that loop into explicit prompt chaining, where each stage is a separate Messages API call, is driven by what the application needs rather than what the model can do. Chaining exposes every intermediate output as a real API response that can be logged, scored, or used to branch or stop the pipeline. The most common chaining pattern is exactly the self-correction sequence in this scenario: generate a draft, have Claude review it against criteria, then have Claude refine it based on the review.

This is a workflow-versus-agent tradeoff in miniature. The three steps are fixed and known in advance, so encoding them as sequenced calls buys predictability, per-step validation, and simple debugging, at the cost of extra round trips and orchestration code. Asking the model to do all three phases in one response is cheaper and faster, but the draft and critique become prose inside a single output that has already been revised by the time the application sees it, so there is no halt point. Extended thinking moves the critique into reasoning blocks that the application cannot act on before the answer is produced; it improves quality but is not a control-flow mechanism. Parallel subagents are the right tool for independent workstreams that can run concurrently, but a critique cannot start before the draft exists, so the dependency makes parallelism inapplicable.

The mental model: use internal reasoning when only the final answer matters, and use chained calls when you need to observe, gate, or branch on what happens in between. See Chain complex prompts for stronger performance and the chaining guidance in Prompting best practices.
option_feedback: Thinking content is the model's internal reasoning, not a controlled pipeline stage, and the application cannot intervene between reasoning and the final answer. Extended thinking improves reasoning quality but does not give the application a stopping point or a stable record of each stage.

Explicit prompt chaining makes every stage a discrete API call, so each intermediate output is a real response that can be logged, evaluated, or used as a branch point. Because the critique is returned before the revision call is ever made, the pipeline can stop there deterministically.

The critique depends on the draft, so the two stages cannot run concurrently; a critique subagent started in parallel would have nothing to evaluate. Parallel subagents suit independent workstreams, not a strictly sequential dependency chain.

A single call produces one response, so the draft and critique exist only as text inside that output and the model has already revised before anything can be inspected. There is no point at which the application can halt after the critique step.

question: A team scripts claude -p in CI to review pull requests from external contributors. A contributor's branch adds hooks to the repository's .claude/settings.json. What should the team do so that this untrusted configuration does not execute during the automated run?
options: Add a line to the job's --append-system-prompt text instructing Claude to ignore any hooks defined by the repository under review.
Start the job with --bare or pass a --settings override setting disableAllHooks to true, after reviewing the repository's .claude directory.
Run the job in bypassPermissions mode so that permission prompts triggered by repository hooks cannot interrupt the automated review.
Rely on the workspace trust dialog, which blocks the repository's hooks in a -p session until a maintainer explicitly approves the folder as trusted.
answer: Start the job with --bare or pass a --settings override setting disableAllHooks to true, after reviewing the repository's .claude directory.
explanation:
Repository content is an input to Claude Code, and some of that content is executable configuration, not just text the model reads. A project's .claude/settings.json can define hooks, which are shell commands Claude Code runs deterministically on events such as tool calls, and its .mcp.json can start MCP servers. In an interactive session the workspace trust dialog holds this configuration back until you accept the folder. A -p or SDK session is different: it never shows the dialog and treats the folder as trusted, so hooks committed by whoever wrote the repository run in your CI environment with your credentials. For a pipeline that processes pull requests from strangers, that is a supply-chain hole.

The remedy is to stop the untrusted configuration from being loaded at all. claude --bare starts a session that never reads settings-file hooks, project MCP servers, or other repository-supplied configuration (skills from a directory named with --add-dir are a partial exception), and it authenticates with ANTHROPIC_API_KEY rather than a subscription login, which suits scripted use. Alternatively, --settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}' turns hooks off for that run. Reviewing the repository's .claude/ files before scripting over it is the complementary manual step. Bare mode is the recommended mode for scripted and SDK calls and is slated to become the default for -p.

The distractors fail for structural reasons. The trust dialog is an interactive safeguard that non-interactive sessions skip entirely, so relying on it leaves the hooks running. A system prompt line cannot prevent a hook from executing because hooks fire outside the model's control; that is exactly why hooks are useful for enforcement and exactly why they are dangerous when an adversary defines them. bypassPermissions concerns tool-call approval, not hook loading, and it strips away the remaining approval checks, so it widens the damage a malicious repository could do rather than containing it. The general principle is least privilege at the configuration layer: load only what you trust, and treat everything else in the repository as data.

See Run Claude Code programmatically, What runs before you trust a folder, and Hooks.
option_feedback: Hooks are shell commands that Claude Code executes on lifecycle events outside the model's discretion, so a system prompt instruction has no effect on whether they run. This confuses probabilistic model guidance with a configuration-level control.

A -p session never shows the workspace trust dialog and treats the folder as trusted, so hooks committed in the repository's settings would otherwise run. Bare mode never reads project settings, hooks, or .mcp.json, and the disableAllHooks override switches hooks off for that run, so either keeps contributor-supplied hooks from executing.

Permission modes govern tool-call approval, not whether settings-file hooks execute, so this does nothing to stop contributor hooks from running. It also removes the approval checks that would otherwise limit what an untrusted repository's content can make the agent do, which enlarges the blast radius instead of reducing it.

The trust dialog protects interactive sessions only; a -p or SDK session never shows it and treats the folder as trusted. Hooks committed in the repository's .claude/settings.json therefore run in a non-interactive session with no approval step, so this offers no protection.

question: A service asks Claude for a JSON array of rubric scores and passes the reply text to a parser. Roughly 2% of replies fail to parse; each failing reply is a truncated JSON prefix that cuts off abruptly partway through the final elements. Which change most reliably addresses these failures?
options: Check the response's stop_reason and, when it is max_tokens, raise the limit or request a continuation before parsing.
Move the requests to the Message Batches API so each response is given more time to finish generating.
Add a repair step that appends the missing closing quotes and brackets so the truncated partial JSON can still be loaded.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the model to always emit complete, valid JSON before it stops generating.
answer: Check the response's stop_reason and, when it is max_tokens, raise the limit or request a continuation before parsing.
explanation:
Every successful Messages API response includes a stop_reason that says why generation ended (HTTP error responses are handled separately through status codes and error bodies rather than a stop reason). The values a client will see most often are end_turn (the model finished naturally), max_tokens (the output hit the limit the request set), stop_sequence (a configured stop string was produced), and tool_use (the model is requesting a tool call). Of these, max_tokens specifically means the model ran out of output budget before it was done, so the text should not be parsed as a complete answer; end_turn means the model finished on its own, and stop_sequence can also be an intentional, complete termination depending on the application's contract. A client that reads the content and ignores the stop reason is treating a partial result as if it were whole, which is exactly what produces JSON that is syntactically clean right up to the point where it simply stops.

The engineering fix is to make completeness a checked precondition. Read stop_reason before parsing; when it is max_tokens, either retry with a larger max_tokens value sized for the worst-case payload or ask the model to continue from where it left off and join the pieces. This is the same discipline applied to any external API: the status of a response is part of its contract, and the body is only meaningful in light of it. It also keeps the failure visible in logs and metrics, so a rising truncation rate can be traced back to a change in payload size rather than surfacing as unexplained parse errors.

The alternatives all miss the mechanism. Prompt instructions cannot override a hard output limit, because the cut-off is enforced by the API after the budget is spent, and the failing outputs were correctly structured up to the cutoff. Auto-repairing the JSON by closing quotes and brackets is a genuine anti-pattern: it makes a lossy response indistinguishable from a good one and pushes missing scores downstream as if they were real. Moving to the Message Batches API changes when and at what cost the work runs, not how many output tokens a request may produce, so the same truncation recurs. See Stop reasons and fallback and the Messages API reference.
option_feedback: A reply that is valid JSON up to an abrupt cut-off is the signature of output truncation, and the API reports this explicitly through a stop_reason of max_tokens. Checking that field before parsing lets the client treat a truncated response as incomplete and either allocate a larger output budget or continue the generation, instead of handing a partial document to the parser.

Truncation is caused by the output token limit, not by wall-clock time, so a batch request with the same max_tokens value is cut off at the same point. The Batches API trades latency for cost on asynchronous workloads and does nothing to change how a response ends.

Patching a truncated payload so it parses hides the fact that scores were lost and silently ships incomplete data downstream. It is an anti-pattern that converts a detectable failure into an undetectable one; the correct response to truncation is to obtain the full output, not to fabricate a plausible ending.

The model has no way to comply once the output budget set by max_tokens is exhausted; generation is cut off by the API regardless of instructions. The failing replies are correctly structured right up to the cutoff, so the problem is not the model's formatting but a limit the client imposed and never checked.

question: An Agent SDK application defines a read-only code-reviewer subagent programmatically and runs with permission_mode set to dontAsk and allowed_tools set to Read, Grep, and Glob. Logs show Claude tries to delegate, but every Agent tool call is denied. What resolves this?
options: Add Agent to the subagent's own tools list so it is permitted to run as a subagent.
Set permission_mode to acceptEdits so tool calls no longer require approval.
Mention the subagent by name in the prompt so Claude invokes it explicitly.
Add Agent to the allowed_tools list so subagent invocations are auto-approved.
answer: Add Agent to the allowed_tools list so subagent invocations are auto-approved.
explanation:
In the Claude Agent SDK, a subagent is not a separate channel that bypasses permissions. The main agent reaches it by calling the built-in Agent tool, exactly as it would call Read or Bash. That means the same layered gating applies: a tool listed in allowed_tools (or allowedTools in TypeScript) is auto-approved; anything else falls through to the canUseTool callback if one is registered; and in dontAsk mode, a call that reaches that point with no callback to approve it is simply denied. The Agent tool therefore has to be pre-approved for delegation to happen without a prompt, which is why the SDK examples that define subagents always include Agent alongside the file tools in the allow list.

The design keeps the permission model uniform and auditable. A subagent can read dozens of files, run commands, or edit code, so letting it launch implicitly would create a hole in whatever tool policy the parent enforces. Treating delegation as an ordinary tool call means a PreToolUse hook, a deny rule, or a canUseTool handler can all observe and control it in one place.

The other fields involved do different jobs. The tools list on an AgentDefinition constrains what the subagent itself may do once running; adding Agent there lets the reviewer spawn nested subagents but does nothing for the parent's blocked call. Explicit prompting ("Use the code-reviewer agent to...") addresses the case where Claude never tries to delegate, which the logs rule out. And acceptEdits only widens auto-approval to file modifications, so the Agent call would still land in the same denial path.

See Subagents in the SDK for the troubleshooting guidance on delegation and Permissions for how allowed tools, permission modes, and callbacks interact.
option_feedback: The tools field on an AgentDefinition restricts which tools the subagent may use once it is running; listing Agent there only allows the subagent to spawn subagents of its own. It has no effect on whether the parent's invocation of the subagent is approved.

The acceptEdits mode auto-approves file edits only; it does not grant blanket approval to other tools such as Agent. The invocation would still need to be pre-approved through allowed_tools or handled by a canUseTool callback.

Naming a subagent in the prompt helps when Claude is not attempting to delegate at all. Here the logs show Claude already issues the Agent tool call, so the failure is a permission denial rather than a matching problem.

Claude delegates to subagents by calling the Agent tool, and that call is gated by the same permission system as any other tool. In dontAsk mode, a tool that is not pre-approved through allowed_tools is denied outright, so listing Agent there is what lets the delegation proceed.

question: A team ships three Claude-backed products from a single Console organization and wants each product's credentials to have bounded access and separately controlled spend. Which TWO practices achieve this?
options: Create a separate workspace per product and issue each product's API key scoped to that workspace.
Set spend limits and review usage per workspace instead of relying only on the organization total.
Share one organization-wide key across all products and tag each request with a product identifier for reporting.
Rotate a single shared key on a fixed weekly schedule so any product-level exposure is short-lived.
answer: Create a separate workspace per product and issue each product's API key scoped to that workspace.
Set spend limits and review usage per workspace instead of relying only on the organization total.
explanation:
In the Claude Console, an organization is the billing and administrative root, and workspaces are the unit of isolation beneath it. An API key created for a specific workspace only works in that workspace, and the resources a key touches are scoped the same way: uploaded files are accessible to the whole workspace but not across workspaces, Message Batches are visible only to keys in the workspace that created them, and on the Claude API prompt caches are isolated per workspace. Anthropic's guidance is to use workspaces to segment your API keys and control spend by use case, which is exactly the situation of several products sharing one organization.

The mental model is blast radius. A credential should be able to do only what the workload that holds it needs, and nothing more. Giving each product its own workspace and a key scoped to it means that if one product's deployment leaks its key, the attacker gains that product's access and that product's spend headroom, not the whole organization's. The tradeoff is a little more administrative surface (more workspaces to create, more keys to manage), which is why teams are sometimes tempted to share one key; the security cost of that shortcut is that every product inherits every other product's exposure.

Spend control follows the same boundary. Each workspace has its own configured spend limit, and usage can be reviewed per workspace, so a runaway loop or an abused key in one product is capped and visible on its own rather than blended into an organization-wide total. That per-workspace monitoring is also what makes authorized access monitoring practical: an unexpected spike in a workspace points directly at the product whose credential is misbehaving.

Sharing a single key and attaching a product identifier to requests gives you attribution in your own logs, but attribution is not enforcement; the key still authorizes all products equally and there is no per-product spend ceiling. Scheduled rotation is worthwhile hygiene and complements scoping, but rotating a shared key only shortens how long an exposure lasts; it does nothing to narrow what the exposed key could reach while it was valid. Pair identity-backed, workspace-scoped keys (or Workload Identity Federation where the workload supports it) with per-workspace limits, and rotate on top of that rather than instead of it.

See Authentication, the API overview on using workspaces to segment keys and control spend, and the workspace-scoped access warning in Files API.
option_feedback: Workspaces are the resource and access boundary within an organization: a key created for a specific workspace only works in that workspace, and resources such as uploaded files, batches, and prompt caches are isolated per workspace. Scoping each product's key to its own workspace means a compromised key cannot reach another product's data or usage.

Anthropic documents workspaces as the mechanism for segmenting API keys and controlling spend by use case, with each workspace carrying its own configured spend limit. Monitoring at that granularity lets the team attribute cost and detect anomalous usage for one product without it being masked by the others.

A shared key gives every product identical access, so exposure of any one product's deployment exposes all of them, and request tagging is a reporting convenience rather than an access boundary. Attribution without isolation does not bound access or enforce per-product spend limits.

Rotation is sound hygiene but does not change the scope of what a key can reach; while valid, a shared key still grants every product's access and spend. The requirement is bounded access and per-product control, which scoping provides and rotation alone does not.

question: A research assistant loads a 60,000-token reference corpus into every request with a cache breakpoint on it. Analysts usually send their next follow-up question 15 to 40 minutes after the previous one, and cache_read_input_tokens is almost always zero. Which change most directly restores cache hits?
options: Add additional cache_control breakpoints throughout the corpus so at least one segment survives until the next question.
Route the follow-up questions through the Message Batches API so the discounted rate offsets the repeated cache writes.
Lower max_tokens on each request so response generation consumes less of the cache entry's remaining lifetime.
Set ttl to 1h on the cache_control block, paying the higher write rate so follow-ups within the hour still hit the cache.
answer: Set ttl to 1h on the cache_control block, paying the higher write rate so follow-ups within the hour still hit the cache.
explanation:
Prompt caching stores the processed prefix of a request so later requests with an identical prefix can reuse it instead of paying full input price. The entry is not permanent: by default it has a minimum lifetime of 5 minutes, refreshed at no charge each time it is read. That default is tuned for rapid multi-turn exchanges and tight agentic tool loops, where the next request typically arrives within seconds. Once a workload's natural gap between requests exceeds the lifetime, every request becomes a cache write with cache_read_input_tokens at zero, which is exactly the symptom in the scenario.

Anthropic offers a 1-hour TTL for this case, enabled by adding "ttl": "1h" to the cache_control block. The tradeoff is priced explicitly: a 5-minute write costs 1.25x the base input rate, a 1-hour write costs 2x, and a read under either TTL costs 0.1x. The longer TTL therefore needs two reads to break even against uncached processing rather than one, but for a 60,000-token corpus revisited every 15 to 40 minutes, each hit avoids re-processing the entire corpus at full price, so the economics are strongly in favor of the extended lifetime. Usage reports the split under cache_creation.ephemeral_1h_input_tokens and ephemeral_5m_input_tokens so the team can confirm which writes are happening.

The other options misunderstand what governs expiry. Breakpoints decide where entries are written, not how long they persist, so adding more of them produces more entries that all expire on the same schedule. The Message Batches API is an asynchronous delivery model for latency-tolerant work; it neither extends cache lifetime nor fits an analyst waiting on an answer. Lowering max_tokens targets a real but minor effect, since the lifetime clock starts when the request begins and generation time counts against it, yet that matters only when the follow-up lands moments after expiry, not tens of minutes later. When a caching strategy misses, the first diagnostic question should be whether the request cadence fits inside the TTL, before touching breakpoints or delivery modes.

See Prompt caching and Prompt caching pricing.
option_feedback: Breakpoints control where cache entries are written, not how long they live; every entry written under the default TTL expires after the same 5 minutes of inactivity. Splitting the corpus across more breakpoints leaves all of them expired by the time a follow-up arrives 15 minutes later.

The Batches API returns results asynchronously, which does not suit analysts waiting on a follow-up answer, and it does nothing to extend cache lifetime. The 50% batch discount would also apply to a workload that still re-writes the entire corpus on every request rather than fixing the underlying miss.

The cache lifetime is measured from the start of the request, so generation time does count against it, but that only matters when the follow-up arrives within seconds of the lifetime ending. With 15 to 40 minute gaps, the 5-minute window is exhausted regardless of how quickly the response finishes.

The default cache lifetime is 5 minutes, so gaps of 15 to 40 minutes let the entry expire before the next request arrives. The 1-hour TTL costs 2x the base input price to write instead of 1.25x, but each subsequent read within the hour is billed at 10%, so a single hit on the 60,000-token corpus more than recovers the extra write cost.

question: A long-running agentic conversation is approaching the context window limit, and the team plans to rely on compaction to keep the task going. Which TWO actions are appropriate?
options: Prefer server-side compaction unless the integration specifically needs client-side control over the summarization step.
Let compaction summarize the earlier conversation history and continue the task from that summary in place of the full history.
Configure compaction to drop the oldest tool results one at a time while leaving every other block of the history untouched.
Keep the full uncompacted history resident in the window after compaction so Claude can re-read any earlier turn on demand.
answer: Prefer server-side compaction unless the integration specifically needs client-side control over the summarization step.
Let compaction summarize the earlier conversation history and continue the task from that summary in place of the full history.
explanation:
The context window is a fixed working memory that accumulates every turn, tool result, and tool definition until the conversation can no longer fit. Compaction is the mechanism designed for that boundary: when the conversation grows too large, Claude is asked to write a structured continuation summary (task overview, current state, discoveries, next steps, context to preserve), and the full message history is replaced by that summary. Work then resumes from the summary. The tradeoff is deliberate: fine-grained detail from earlier turns is exchanged for enough distilled state to continue, which is why the default summary prompt emphasizes decisions, failed approaches, and commitments rather than raw transcripts.

There are two implementations. Server-side compaction, configured through the context_management parameter, summarizes on Anthropic's servers and is the recommended approach; it handles token accounting correctly and requires little integration work. SDK compaction runs inside the tool runner helpers, and the compaction_control parameter is deprecated in the TypeScript and Ruby SDKs and removed from the Python SDK. It also has a documented weakness: with server-side tools such as web search, the SDK's token calculation can count accumulated cache reads from internal calls and trigger compaction prematurely. Use SDK compaction only when you specifically need client-side control over the summarization prompt.

It helps to keep compaction distinct from its neighbours. Tool result clearing (the clear_tool_uses context editing strategy) removes the oldest tool results individually and replaces each with a placeholder, leaving the rest of the history intact; that is surgical trimming, not summarization, and compaction cannot be configured to do it. And neither mechanism keeps the removed material available for re-reading: once history is compacted or cleared, it is gone from the window. For facts that must outlive summarization, pair compaction with an external store such as the memory tool, or design the agent to recover state from the filesystem (progress notes, structured status files, git history) when a fresh window starts.

See Context windows and Compaction for the full behaviour and configuration.
option_feedback: Server-side compaction is the documented primary strategy for long-running conversations, with less integration complexity, more accurate token accounting, and none of the client-side limitations of SDK compaction. SDK compaction is positioned only for cases that specifically need client-side control of the summarization step.

Compaction works by having Claude produce a structured continuation summary of the conversation so far, then replacing the accumulated history with that summary. This is what allows a task to continue past the point where the raw history would have exceeded the window.

Selectively clearing old tool results and replacing them with placeholders is the tool result clearing strategy in context editing, not compaction. Compaction operates on the conversation as a whole by summarizing it rather than deleting individual blocks, so it cannot be configured to behave this way.

Compaction exists precisely to stop the full history from occupying the window; after it runs, the detailed earlier turns are no longer in context. Information that must survive summarization needs to be captured in the summary or persisted externally, for example with the memory tool.

question: A developer wants to auto-approve a handful of project-specific shell commands, such as the repository's custom test runner, without committing those permission rules or affecting other projects on their machine. Where should the allow rules go?
options: Add the rules to .claude/settings.local.json in the project, which is meant to stay out of version control.
Add the rules to ~/.claude/settings.json so they apply in every project the developer opens.
Add the rules to .claude/settings.json in the project so they ship with every checkout of the repository.
List the commands in CLAUDE.local.md so Claude knows it may run them without asking each time.
answer: Add the rules to .claude/settings.local.json in the project, which is meant to stay out of version control.
explanation:
Claude Code does not read a single project configuration file. Settings are layered: user settings in ~/.claude/settings.json, shared project settings in .claude/settings.json, project-local settings in .claude/settings.local.json, and managed policy settings deployed by an organization. When the same key appears at several layers, precedence runs from managed settings, through command-line arguments, then project-local, then shared project, then user. Permission arrays such as permissions.allow merge across these layers, which is what makes the hierarchy useful: a team commits the rules everyone needs, and each engineer adds their own on top.

The project-local file is the layer designed for personal, per-project configuration that should not be shared. It is scoped to the repository it lives in, so a rule allowing a custom test runner does not leak into unrelated projects, and it is intended to be kept out of version control so teammates never inherit one person's approval choices. That combination, project-scoped but private, is exactly what the scenario asks for. Putting the same rules in the shared .claude/settings.json would commit them for the whole team, while putting them in ~/.claude/settings.json would apply them to every project on the machine.

The remaining option confuses two different mechanisms. CLAUDE.local.md is part of the memory system: it is loaded into the model's context as instructions, and Claude tries to follow it, but the client never treats it as configuration. Permission prompts are decided by the permission system from settings rules and hooks, regardless of what the model has been told. A useful mental model is that memory files shape what Claude decides to do, while settings files control what Claude is allowed to do without asking. Anything that must hold deterministically, such as auto-approval or a hard block, belongs in settings or hooks rather than in a markdown instruction.

See Claude Code settings for the full list of settings scopes and their precedence.
option_feedback: The project-local settings file exists for exactly this case: personal permission rules and other configuration scoped to one project but not shared with the team. It sits above the shared project file in precedence and is intended to be kept out of the repository.
User-level settings are not scoped to one project; a rule allowing a custom test runner would apply in every repository on the machine. The requirement was to avoid affecting other projects.
The shared project settings file is committed and applies to everyone who clones the repository. That contradicts the stated requirement that the rules remain personal and uncommitted.

CLAUDE.local.md is a memory file that supplies context and instructions to the model; it is not enforced configuration. Permission decisions are made by the client from settings rules, so text in a memory file cannot grant auto-approval.

question: A claims-triage assistant runs with thinking enabled. Its prompt dictates a twelve-step numbered procedure specifying exactly how Claude must reason through every claim, yet eval scores on complex cases remain poor. Which revision is recommended?
options: Replace the prescriptive steps with a general instruction to reason thoroughly and let Claude structure its own thinking.
Expand the procedure into even more granular sub-steps so that no reasoning decision at all is left to the model's discretion.
Move the twelve-step procedure out of the system prompt and into each user message so it sits closer to the claim text.
Lower the temperature to zero so that the model follows the twelve prescribed steps more consistently on every single claim.
answer: Replace the prescriptive steps with a general instruction to reason thoroughly and let Claude structure its own thinking.
explanation:
When thinking is enabled, Claude allocates its own reasoning before producing an answer. The prompting guidance for current models is to prefer general instructions over prescriptive steps: a short directive such as "think thoroughly" or "reason through this carefully" often produces better results than a hand-written, step-by-step plan, because the model's reasoning frequently goes beyond what a human author would have scripted. A rigid twelve-step procedure effectively caps the reasoning at the author's mental model, which is precisely the limitation that hurts on complex, unusual cases.

The useful mental model is that thinking is a capability you steer rather than script. Numbered, sequential instructions remain valuable when order and completeness of concrete actions matter (which tools to call, which fields to fill, what the output must contain). They are far less helpful as a substitute for the model's internal deliberation. If you want to show a reasoning style, the recommended technique is to include <thinking> sections inside a few diverse few-shot examples so Claude generalizes the pattern to its own thinking, rather than dictating each step. Appending a self-check instruction, such as verifying the answer against stated criteria before finishing, is another documented way to improve accuracy without over-prescribing the path.

The other revisions miss the cause. Making the procedure more granular tightens the constraint that is already degrading quality. Lowering the temperature reduces output variability but does nothing about whether the prescribed reasoning path is a good one; it simply makes the model adhere to it more uniformly. Moving the identical procedure from the system prompt into every user turn changes placement, not substance, and restating a long script on each turn adds tokens for no reasoning benefit.

See Prompting best practices and Thinking for the underlying guidance.
option_feedback: With thinking enabled, general guidance such as asking Claude to reason thoroughly often yields better reasoning than a hand-written step-by-step plan. Claude's own reasoning frequently exceeds what a human would prescribe, so a rigid procedure can constrain it on exactly the complex cases where flexibility matters most.

Adding more prescriptive detail moves in the wrong direction; it further constrains a reasoning process that is already stronger when left flexible. Overly granular scripts also bloat the prompt and can misfire on cases the author did not anticipate.

Relocating the same procedure changes where the instructions live, not their content or effect. The problem is over-prescription of the reasoning process, and repeating the script on every turn also adds tokens without addressing that.

Temperature affects sampling variability, not whether a prescribed procedure is the right reasoning approach. Making the model follow a suboptimal script more consistently does not raise reasoning quality on hard cases.

question: A developer adds the web_search server tool to a Messages API request and writes client code that waits for a web_search tool_use block, runs the search, and returns a tool_result. The handler never fires, yet responses already cite search results. What should the developer do?
options: Enable streaming on the request so the tool_use block is delivered to the handler before the rest of the response completes.
Redefine web_search as a client tool with an input_schema so that Claude returns stop_reason tool_use for the handler to act on.
Remove the client-side handler, since server tools execute on Anthropic infrastructure and return results in the same response.
Force the tool with tool_choice set to the web_search tool so that Claude emits the tool_use block the handler is waiting for.
answer: Remove the client-side handler, since server tools execute on Anthropic infrastructure and return results in the same response.
explanation:
The Messages API distinguishes two kinds of tools by where they execute. Client tools, including every user-defined tool and Anthropic-schema tools such as the memory or text editor tools, are executed by your application: Claude emits a tool_use block, the request ends with stop_reason: "tool_use", and your code runs the tool and sends the outcome back as a tool_result block in the next user turn. Server tools such as web_search, web_fetch, and code_execution run on Anthropic's infrastructure with no handler code in your application; the tool call and its results are returned inside the same response, and usage reports the server-side calls under server_tool_use.

This split is deliberate. Client tools give you full control over side effects and access to your own systems, at the cost of implementing an agent loop. Server tools trade that control for zero integration effort on capabilities that are generic and safe to host centrally, like searching the web. The mental model to carry is that stop_reason: "tool_use" is a request for your participation; a server tool never needs it, so a handler waiting for one will idle forever while the response already contains what it was trying to produce.

The other adjustments miss the mechanism. tool_choice influences whether and which tool Claude selects, not where it runs, so forcing web_search still yields server-side execution. Redefining the search as a client tool would work mechanically but obliges the application to implement search itself, throwing away the hosted capability. Streaming only changes response delivery timing and never converts a server tool into a client tool. See Server tools, Web search tool, and Tool use overview.
option_feedback: Streaming changes how the response is delivered over time, not which party executes a tool. A server tool's execution still happens on Anthropic's infrastructure whether or not the response is streamed, so no client-executable tool_use block for web_search will arrive.
