Turning the search into a user-defined client tool would make the application responsible for implementing search itself, discarding the hosted capability the server tool provides. It solves a problem that does not exist, since the server tool is already producing results without any handler.

Server tools such as web_search are executed on Anthropic's infrastructure, so the request does not pause with stop_reason tool_use waiting for the application to act. The search runs and its results are incorporated into the same response, which is why the answers already contain search results while the handler never sees anything to do.

Forcing tool selection does not change where a tool executes; a server tool still runs on Anthropic's side regardless of tool_choice. The handler is waiting for a client-tool handshake that server tools never perform, so this change cannot make it fire.

question: A developer porting a chat backend from another provider places the assistant's persona instructions as the first entry in the messages array with the role set to system. The Messages API returns an invalid request error for that entry. What should the developer do?
options: Place the instructions in an assistant turn at the start of the messages array so Claude treats them as its own prior words.
Prepend the instructions to the first user message with a System: label so the model reads them before the question.
Send the instructions once in a separate preliminary request so the API retains them for every later call in the conversation.
Move the persona instructions into the top-level system parameter so they are in effect from the very first turn.
answer: Move the persona instructions into the top-level system parameter so they are in effect from the very first turn.
explanation:
The Messages API separates what Claude has been told to be from what has been said in the conversation. Standing instructions such as a persona go in the top-level system parameter; the messages array carries the conversation itself, and the models are trained on alternating user and assistant turns (consecutive same-role turns are combined). A system-role entry can appear inside messages only in the supported mid-conversation case, on models that offer it and subject to placement restrictions; it is not a valid opening message. A request that borrows the "system message first" convention from another provider's chat format is therefore rejected as invalid.

This split is deliberate. Keeping start-of-conversation instructions out of the turn structure gives the developer a channel that is clearly distinct from user-supplied content, which supports the content-boundary practices that protect against instructions hidden in pasted data. It also fits the prompt caching hierarchy: cache prefixes are built in the order tools, then system, then messages, so a stable system prompt sits in the reusable part of the prefix while the conversation grows behind it. Mid-conversation system messages exist for the different problem of adding guidance later without disturbing that cached prefix.

The API is also stateless: each request must carry everything Claude should see, so a one-time preliminary request cannot plant instructions that later calls inherit. Labeling text inside a user message as "System:" merely adds user content with no special standing, and writing a fabricated assistant turn misrepresents what Claude actually said rather than instructing it. The correct move is simply to relocate the persona instructions to the system parameter, where they apply from the first turn.

See the Messages API reference and Using the Messages API for the request structure and system prompt guidance.
option_feedback: Assistant turns represent things Claude has already said in the conversation, not standing instructions about how it should behave. Faking prior assistant output to smuggle in persona guidance misrepresents the conversation and is not the mechanism the API provides for system-level direction.

A text label inside a user message is just more user content; the API does not treat it as a privileged instruction channel. This also blurs the boundary between developer instructions and user-supplied data, which is exactly what the separate system parameter exists to keep distinct.

The Messages API is stateless, so nothing from a prior request carries over to the next one. Instructions sent in a preliminary call would be forgotten immediately, and the original request would still be rejected for its invalid opening entry.

Standing instructions that should govern the whole conversation belong in the dedicated top-level system parameter, which is what the Messages API provides for that purpose. A system-role entry inside messages is only accepted in supported mid-conversation positions on certain models, so using one as the opening message is rejected.

question: A team scripts claude -p to draft changelog entries from merged commits. For this one invocation they want to add house formatting rules while keeping Claude Code's default tool guidance and coding conventions intact. Which flag should they use?
options: Start with --bare and place the rules in the project's CLAUDE.md for the run.
Pass the rules with --system-prompt so they become the entire system prompt for the run.
Pass the rules with --append-system-prompt so they are added on top of the default prompt.
Save the rules as an output style and switch to it before the run starts.
answer: Pass the rules with --append-system-prompt so they are added on top of the default prompt.
explanation:
Claude Code builds a substantial default system prompt that gives the model its identity as a coding assistant, explains how each built-in tool should be used, and carries safety instructions and coding conventions. When you customize the prompt from the CLI, the central decision is whether that default identity still fits your task. Claude Code exposes four flags for this: --system-prompt and --system-prompt-file replace the default entirely, while --append-system-prompt and --append-system-prompt-file add to it. The two replacement flags are mutually exclusive, but an append flag can be combined with either.

A changelog script is still coding-adjacent work: Claude needs to read git history, inspect files, and follow the project's conventions, all of which the default prompt already covers. Appending house formatting rules with --append-system-prompt supplies only what differs, and because the flag applies to the current invocation, it is a natural fit for a claude -p call in a script. Replacing the prompt with --system-prompt is the right tool for a different situation: a non-coding agent in an unattended pipeline whose surface, identity, or permission model diverges from Claude Code's. In that case you accept responsibility for re-supplying whatever tool guidance and safety behavior the task still needs, which is exactly the burden this team wants to avoid.

The other two approaches confuse persistence scopes. --bare exists to make scripted runs reproducible by skipping auto-discovery of hooks, skills, subagents, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md, so rules written into CLAUDE.md would be ignored in a bare run; CLAUDE.md is for conventions Claude should follow in every session, not a one-time run. Output styles are persistent personas meant to be switched between and shared across a project, not a delivery mechanism for a single invocation's instructions. See the CLI reference for the system prompt flags and Run Claude Code programmatically for how -p and --bare interact.
option_feedback: Bare mode skips auto-discovery of CLAUDE.md along with hooks, skills, and MCP servers, so rules placed there would never load in that run. CLAUDE.md is also meant for persistent project conventions rather than instructions for a single invocation.

The replacement flag discards the whole default prompt, including tool guidance and safety instructions, and the team would have to supply all of that themselves. That is the opposite of the stated goal of keeping the defaults intact.

The append flag layers the team's rules onto Claude Code's default system prompt, so the built-in tool guidance, safety instructions, and coding conventions stay in place. It applies only to the current invocation, which matches a per-run scripted call.

Output styles are persistent personas you switch between and share across a project, not a mechanism for one-off instructions in a scripted call. They also change how the default prompt is composed rather than simply adding rules on top of it.

question: A prompt for drafting weekly status reports says "use our standard format and follow the usual conventions." The structure of the output varies from run to run, and reviewers reject most drafts. Which prompt change is most likely to fix this?
options: Assign Claude the role of a senior member of the reporting team so that it infers the standard format from the persona.
Restate 'follow the usual conventions' in both the system prompt and every user message so the model treats it as important.
Spell out the exact sections, ordering, and conventions in the prompt, as if briefing a new hire with no company context.
Switch to a larger model, whose broader training data is more likely to include the team's reporting conventions.
answer: Spell out the exact sections, ordering, and conventions in the prompt, as if briefing a new hire with no company context.
explanation:
The failure here is an instruction clarity problem, not a capability or compliance problem. A phrase like "our standard format" is a pointer to knowledge that lives inside the organisation, and the model cannot dereference it. Every run therefore starts from an underspecified request, and the variation reviewers see is simply Claude filling the gap differently each time. The remedy is to move the missing knowledge into the prompt: name the sections, fix their order, state length and tone rules, and give any conventions that differ from what a reasonable default would be.

Anthropic's prompting guidance frames this with a useful mental model: think of Claude as a brilliant but new employee who has none of your team's context. The accompanying golden rule is to show the prompt to a colleague who knows nothing about the task and ask whether they could follow it; if they would be confused, so will Claude. Under that test, "follow the usual conventions" fails immediately. Being specific about the desired output format and constraints, and listing steps in order when order matters, are the concrete techniques that pass it.

The distractors each mistake the nature of the problem. Assigning a role is a real and valuable technique, but it steers behaviour and tone; it cannot conjure facts the model was never given. Repeating an instruction in more places or more emphatically treats the issue as one of attention, yet the instruction is being read and simply cannot be executed. Upgrading the model assumes the conventions exist somewhere in training data, which is false for any organisation's private templates. Only supplying the information itself changes the outcome.

See Prompting best practices for the clarity principles, the new-employee framing, and the guidance on specifying output format and constraints.
option_feedback: A role sharpens tone and focus, but it cannot supply facts Claude does not have. A persona of a senior team member still knows nothing about this team's private report template, so the structure remains a guess.

Repeating an instruction raises its salience but does not add the missing information. The instruction is unclear rather than ignored, so emphasising it more loudly leaves Claude equally unable to know what the conventions are.

Claude has no access to a team's internal norms, so a reference to the standard format gives it nothing to follow and it improvises a different structure each time. Writing the sections, ordering, and rules explicitly removes the ambiguity, which is the clarity principle behind the guidance to treat Claude like a capable new employee who lacks context.
Internal reporting conventions are not part of any model's training data, regardless of size. A more capable model will still have to invent a structure when the prompt does not define one.

question: A team commits a project-level .mcp.json so every developer connects to the same remote HTTP MCP server. The server requires a bearer token in a request header, and the token must never be stored in the repository. How should the header be configured?
options: Base64-encode the token before placing it in the headers field so the committed file never contains the plaintext value.
Write the header value as ${MCP_API_TOKEN} in .mcp.json and have each developer export that variable in their local environment.
Put the token in the project's shared .claude/settings.json env block so the value is loaded automatically for everyone.
Commit the token directly in .mcp.json but rotate it on a fixed schedule so any leaked copy expires before it can be misused.
answer: Write the header value as ${MCP_API_TOKEN} in .mcp.json and have each developer export that variable in their local environment.
explanation:
The principle behind this question is the same one that governs API keys everywhere in the Claude ecosystem: a credential must never be checked into source control, because anything in a repository is copied to every clone, every fork, and every CI runner, and remains recoverable from history even after it is deleted. Configuration that a team shares has to be separated from the secrets that make the configuration work.

Claude Code supports this separation directly. A committed .mcp.json can reference environment variables using ${VAR} or ${VAR:-default} syntax in the command, args, env, url, and headers fields. At load time the placeholder is replaced with the value from the developer's environment, so the shared file describes where the server is and how to authenticate, while each person supplies their own token from a shell profile, a secrets manager, or a git-ignored local file. If the variable is unset and has no default, Claude Code loads the config anyway, warns about the missing variable in claude mcp list, and leaves the literal text unexpanded, which makes a misconfiguration visible without ever requiring a fallback secret in the repository.

The distractors each fail the same test. Committing the token and rotating it accepts a permanent copy in history and a standing exposure between rotations. Base64 encoding is reversible by anyone who can read the file, so it provides no confidentiality. The project .claude/settings.json is, by design, a shared file intended to be committed so teammates receive identical permissions and hooks; putting a token there simply moves the leak to a different tracked file. Per-developer material belongs in the environment or in .claude/settings.local.json, which Claude Code excludes from commits.

Anthropic's broader credential guidance applies the same logic to the Claude API itself: keep keys out of source control, client-side code, and prompts, load them at runtime, and prefer identity-backed credentials such as service account keys or Workload Identity Federation for unattended workloads. See Authentication and the API overview for the documented practices.
option_feedback: Base64 is an encoding, not encryption, and anyone with the file can decode it instantly. The secret is still shipped to every person and system that can read the repository.

Claude Code expands ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} syntax in .mcp.json fields, including headers, at load time. The committed file contains only a placeholder, while the real token lives in each developer's environment or secrets tooling and never touches version control.

The project .claude/settings.json is a shared file meant to be committed so teammates receive the same configuration, so placing the token there stores it in the repository just as directly. Only the per-developer environment or the git-ignored local settings file is appropriate for a personal secret.

Committing a credential puts it in the repository history permanently, where every clone and fork retains it. Rotation shortens the window of misuse but does not remove the secret from source control, and the token is exposed for the entire interval between rotations.

question: A team wants Claude to draft quarterly compliance reports in a house format: fixed section order, a document template, and a validation script for the finished file. No external system is involved, and the guidance is needed only for report requests. Which approach fits best?
options: Package the instructions, template, and script as a Skill that loads when a report task comes up.
Define a custom tool whose description carries the section order, checklist, and template text.
Stand up an MCP server that serves the template and checklist as resources for Claude to fetch.
Place the full formatting guidance and checklist in the system prompt of every request.
answer: Package the instructions, template, and script as a Skill that loads when a report task comes up.
explanation:
The decision between built-in tools, custom tools, MCP servers, and Skills turns on one question: does Claude need to do something in an external system, or does it need to know how to perform a task well? Tools and MCP are the answer to the first case; they give Claude a callable interface whose execution happens outside the model. Agent Skills answer the second case: they package procedural knowledge (workflows, templates, checklists) and optional scripts into a directory that Claude reads from the filesystem when the task calls for it. A house report format with a template and a validation script is procedural knowledge with a deterministic helper attached, which is exactly the shape a Skill is designed to hold.

The mechanism that makes Skills the efficient choice is progressive disclosure. At startup only each Skill's YAML frontmatter (name and description) is placed in the system prompt. When a request matches the description, Claude reads SKILL.md from disk, and only then do the instructions occupy context; additional files such as a template or a validate_report.py script are read or executed only as needed, and an executed script costs only the tokens of its output. This is why the docs describe the context window as a shared resource and recommend scripts for deterministic operations rather than asking Claude to regenerate the logic. See Agent Skills overview and Skill authoring best practices.

The alternatives each solve a different problem. Putting the guidance in the system prompt works functionally but loads it on every turn of every conversation, including ones that never touch a report, and it cannot carry an executable check. A custom tool is an action interface: Claude emits a tool_use block and your application executes it, so a tool whose only content is a long description has no operation behind it and simply becomes an always-loaded prompt fragment with a schema attached. An MCP server is the right choice when a capability must be reached across a process or network boundary and shared by many clients, as described in Tool use with Claude; using it to serve a static template introduces transport, hosting, and connection management for content that has no live source. Matching the mechanism to the nature of the capability, rather than reaching for the most infrastructure-heavy option, is the core of agentic customization.
option_feedback: Skills are filesystem-based packages of instructions, reference material, and optional scripts that Claude uses when a task matches the Skill's description. Only the name and description sit in context until triggered, and the bundled script gives a deterministic check without Claude regenerating validation code each time.

A custom tool exists so Claude can request an action that your application executes, and this scenario has no operation to perform. Stuffing procedural guidance into a description field misuses the schema as a document store and pays its token cost on every request.

MCP is for connecting Claude to systems and data it must reach through a protocol boundary, and here there is nothing external to connect to. Running a server to distribute static procedural knowledge adds a transport, a process, and versioning overhead that a Skill provides directly.

System prompt content is loaded on every turn regardless of whether the task needs it, so guidance for one task type taxes every conversation. It also cannot bundle an executable validation script, so the deterministic check would have to be reimplemented by the model each time.

question: A developer builds a multi-turn chat feature on the Messages API. Each request sends only the newest user message. Users report that Claude does not remember anything said earlier in the conversation. What is the correct fix?
options: Place the earlier turns in the system prompt on the first request so the server keeps them for the whole session.
Pass the id from the previous response so the API can retrieve the earlier turns from its own stored transcript.
Enable prompt caching on the request so the server retains the earlier turns for the model between successive calls.
Keep the history client-side and resend the accumulated user and assistant turns in the messages array each call.
answer: Keep the history client-side and resend the accumulated user and assistant turns in the messages array each call.
explanation:
The Messages API is a stateless REST endpoint: every POST /v1/messages call is a self-contained request, and the model reasons over exactly the tokens in that request. There is no server-side session, conversation object, or transcript that a later call can reference. This is why the request body carries a messages array rather than a single string. A multi-turn conversation is expressed by alternating user and assistant entries, and the application is responsible for appending each exchange and replaying the whole history on the next call.

The engineering consequence is that your application owns conversation state. In practice that means persisting the turn list per user or session in your own storage, appending the model's returned content as an assistant turn, and then appending the next user input before calling the API again. Because the full history is sent each time, input token usage grows with the conversation, which is exactly why context window management and prompt caching matter for long chats. Caching makes replaying an identical prefix cheaper, but it is an optimization layered on top of the stateless model, not a substitute for sending the history.

The distractors all assume state that does not exist. A response id is a correlation identifier, not a pointer to stored turns. The system prompt is scoped to the request it arrives in and is intended for instructions, not dialogue. Prompt caching changes cost, not visibility: content absent from the request is invisible to the model regardless of cache configuration. The Using the Messages API guide covers the multi-turn pattern and shows how history is passed on each call.
option_feedback: There is no session on the Messages API; the system prompt applies only to the request it is sent with. Content sent once is not carried forward, and the system field is meant for instructions rather than dialogue history.

The Messages API does not keep a server-side transcript keyed by response id, and no request parameter accepts one for continuation. The id is an identifier for logging and correlation, not a handle to stored conversation state.
Prompt caching reduces the cost and latency of reprocessing an identical prefix, but it does not change what the model sees. If the earlier turns are not in the request, a cache cannot supply them.

The Messages API is stateless: each request is evaluated only on the content it carries, so prior turns must be included in the messages array for Claude to see them. Maintaining the history in the application and replaying it on each call is the documented multi-turn pattern.

question: An agent harness on Claude Sonnet 4.6, with no beta headers, caches a system prompt and tools for a long session. It lowers output_config.effort on routine turns and raises it on planning turns, but cache_creation_input_tokens spikes on every switch. What should the developer change?
options: Move the cache breakpoint onto the newest user message so the effort setting sits outside the cached prefix.
Switch to manual extended thinking and vary budget_tokens per turn, since only the effort value is rendered into the prompt.
Keep the effort level fixed for the whole session and steer thinking per turn by appending guidance to the user message.
Extend the cache_control ttl to 1h so the cached prefix survives the effort changes between consecutive turns.
answer: Keep the effort level fixed for the whole session and steer thinking per turn by appending guidance to the user message.
explanation:
Prompt caching works by hashing the rendered prompt prefix up to a breakpoint and reusing the server-side representation when a later request produces the identical prefix. The important mental model is that the prefix is not just the text you send: request configuration that shapes how Claude reasons is rendered into the prompt too. That includes the thinking configuration (mode, and budget_tokens in manual mode) and the resolved output_config.effort value. Changing any of these between requests changes the prefix, so message-level breakpoints miss and, on models that render the configuration ahead of tools and system content, those caches miss as well. The symptom is exactly what the harness observed: cache_creation_input_tokens jumping on every switch as the prefix is written again at the premium write rate.

The remedy in this context is to separate the two levers. On Claude Sonnet 4.6, effort is a request-level setting rendered at the front of the prompt, so the practical rule is to pick the level that matches the workload's default balance of quality and latency and hold it constant while relying on cache hits. Per-message steering is the turn-level lever: appending a phrase such as "Please think hard before responding" on planning steps or "Answer directly without deliberating" on routine confirmations changes only the newest user turn, which sits after every earlier breakpoint and therefore leaves the cached prefix intact. Steering is wording-sensitive and should be measured on representative traffic, but it is the mechanism available here for varying thinking within one conversation without paying cache write costs each time. Setting effort explicitly to the model's default is equivalent to omitting it and does not break the cache, so a harness that wants an explicit value can safely pin the default.

The distractors each misunderstand where invalidation comes from. Repositioning the breakpoint cannot help because effort is not a content block; it changes the rendered prompt wherever the marker sits, and a breakpoint on a per-turn user message would never match anyway. Swapping to budget_tokens trades one rendered value for another with identical invalidation behavior, on a mode that is deprecated or rejected on current models. Extending the TTL addresses entries expiring between requests, which is a different failure mode: a longer lifetime keeps a matching entry alive but does nothing when the prefix hash no longer matches.

See Effort, Steering thinking, and Prompt caching.
option_feedback: Effort is not a message block that can be positioned behind a breakpoint; it is a request-level setting rendered into the prompt. An effort change always invalidates message-level cache blocks regardless of where the breakpoint is placed, and a breakpoint on the varying user message would itself never produce a hit.

The budget_tokens value is also rendered into the prompt, and changing it between requests invalidates cache breakpoints in exactly the same way. Manual extended thinking is additionally deprecated on the 4.6 models and rejected on later ones, so this would not restore cache hits.

On this model and without beta features, the resolved effort value is rendered into the prompt, so changing it between requests invalidates cache breakpoints and forces a fresh cache write. Per-message steering phrases appended to the newest user turn sit after the cached prefix, so they adjust thinking on that turn without breaking earlier breakpoints.

The TTL governs how long an entry stays alive between requests, not whether a new request matches it. An effort change alters the rendered prompt prefix so the hash no longer matches, and a longer lifetime cannot make a mismatched prefix hit; it would only add write cost.

question: A team structures a coding assistant as a lead agent that delegates review, test execution, and lookup tasks to specialist subagents. Which TWO advantages does this hierarchy provide beyond context isolation?
options: Every subagent inherits the lead agent's full conversation history, so shared context never needs restating.
Subagent outputs become deterministic across runs because each runs a fixed system prompt.
Routine subtasks can be assigned to a faster, lower-cost model than the one the lead agent uses.
Each subagent's tool access can be limited to what its task requires, reducing the risk of unintended actions.
answer: Routine subtasks can be assigned to a faster, lower-cost model than the one the lead agent uses.
Each subagent's tool access can be limited to what its task requires, reducing the risk of unintended actions.
explanation:
A subagent is a separate agent instance with its own context window, its own system prompt, an optional tool allowlist, and its own model choice. The lead agent invokes it through the Agent tool by writing a task prompt; the subagent works independently and only its final message flows back into the lead's conversation. That design makes each subagent definition a small, self-contained policy boundary, and two of the levers it exposes are the ones this question turns on.

The first lever is tool restriction. Because the tools field can be set per subagent, a code reviewer can be given only Read, Grep, and Glob so it can analyze but never edit, while a test runner is separately granted Bash. When the field is omitted, the subagent inherits every tool available to subagents, so the restriction is an opt-in allowlist rather than a default. Granting the minimum each role needs limits the blast radius of a confused or misdirected subtask, which is harder to achieve when a single agent holds every tool for every phase of the work. The second lever is model selection. The model field lets the lead reason on a more capable model while routine lookups or summaries run on a faster, cheaper model such as Haiku; the docs list controlling cost this way as one of the core reasons to use subagents.

The distractors reflect two common misunderstandings. Subagents do not inherit the lead's conversation; a non-fork subagent begins with its system prompt, the delegation message, and startup material such as CLAUDE.md, so the lead must restate whatever the task requires. This is the flip side of context isolation: the subagent's exploration stays out of the lead's window precisely because the two contexts are separate. Nor does delegation make outputs deterministic; a subagent is still a sampled model call, and anything that must happen identically every time belongs in hooks or application code rather than in a prompt.

See Create custom subagents and Subagents in the SDK for the per-subagent fields and what a subagent's context contains at startup.
option_feedback: A non-fork subagent starts with a fresh context containing its own system prompt and the delegation message the lead writes, not the lead's conversation history. Anything the subagent needs must be stated in that task prompt, which is why context isolation works in the first place.

A fixed system prompt narrows behavior but does not make sampling deterministic; subagents remain LLM calls with the same variability as the lead. Determinism where it is required comes from hooks and code, not from delegation.

A subagent definition includes a model field, so simple lookups can run on Haiku while the lead reasons on a more capable model. Routing by task difficulty is one of the documented ways subagents control cost.

A subagent definition can include a tools allowlist, so a reviewer can be restricted to Read, Grep, and Glob while a test runner gets Bash; if the field is omitted, the subagent inherits every tool available to subagents. Least-privilege tool grants at the subagent level bound what any single delegated task can do to the codebase.

question: A coding agent works on a software project across many separate sessions spread over several weeks. Each new session re-explores the codebase from scratch and sometimes rebuilds features an earlier session already completed. Which pattern most directly addresses this?
options: Switch to a model with a larger context window so the whole project history can be kept inside one long session instead of being split across many sessions.
Have the first session create a progress log and feature checklist as memory files, and have each later session read them at start and update them before ending.
Enable server-side compaction so a summary of each finished session is produced and carried automatically into the context window of the next session.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent to remember what earlier sessions completed and to skip any feature that has already been finished.
answer: Have the first session create a progress log and feature checklist as memory files, and have each later session read them at start and update them before ending.
explanation:
A Claude conversation is the only working memory the model has, and every new session starts with an empty one. Anything an agent learned or finished in a previous session is gone unless the harness deliberately wrote it somewhere durable and reads it back. This is why long-horizon agent work is designed around externalized state rather than around making any single conversation bigger.

The documented multisession pattern makes that state explicit. An initializer session sets up the memory files before substantive work begins: a progress log recording what has been done and what comes next, a feature checklist defining the scope, and a pointer to any setup or initialization script the project needs. Every subsequent session opens by reading those files, which restores project state without re-exploring the codebase or retracing decisions, and closes with an end-of-session update so the next session has an accurate starting point. A key discipline is to work on one feature at a time and mark it complete only after end-to-end verification, so the log never claims work that is not actually finished. The memory tool is a natural place to keep these files, since it is a client-executed tool whose reads and writes your application performs and persists, consistent with how tool use works in general: the model requests the operation, your code carries it out.

The distractors each misunderstand where continuity comes from. A larger context window helps within a session but does nothing for a session that begins empty, and no window holds weeks of work. Server-side compaction is a within-conversation mechanism: it summarizes earlier turns so that conversation can keep going, but it does not hand state to an unrelated later session. A system prompt telling the agent to remember earlier sessions cannot conjure information the model never receives; at best it produces confident guesses about what was finished, which is exactly the failure the team is trying to eliminate.
option_feedback: A larger context window only delays the problem; a multi-week project still exceeds any single window, and the scenario already involves separate sessions that start empty. Cross-session continuity has to come from state persisted outside the conversation, not from a bigger conversation.

This is the multisession memory pattern: an initializer session writes durable state (what is done, what remains, how to start the project), every later session reads that state before working, and each session records its progress before it ends. Because the state lives in files outside any single conversation, a fresh session recovers where the last one stopped instead of re-exploring or redoing finished work.

Compaction summarizes earlier turns within a conversation so that conversation can continue past the context limit. It does not transfer state between separate sessions, so a new session would still begin with no knowledge of what the previous one completed.

The model is stateless between sessions and has no access to earlier conversations unless the application supplies them. Instructing it to remember cannot create memory that does not exist and invites it to guess or fabricate what was done.

question: A team plans to consume Claude through Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud instead of the first-party Claude API. Which TWO actions correctly account for what changes?
options: Skip per-feature verification because every Claude API feature ships on the cloud platforms at the same time.
Configure the application to authenticate with the cloud provider's IAM credentials instead of an Anthropic API key.
Rewrite the production prompts to compensate for the reduced-capability model build the cloud platforms serve.
Track the chosen cloud platform's own model retirement schedule when planning model migrations.
answer: Configure the application to authenticate with the cloud provider's IAM credentials instead of an Anthropic API key.
Track the chosen cloud platform's own model retirement schedule when planning model migrations.
explanation:
Claude is offered both through Anthropic's first-party Claude API and through cloud platforms. The platforms fall into two groups: Anthropic-operated platforms (Claude Platform on AWS and Microsoft Foundry) and partner-operated platforms (Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud). The design goal of the partner platforms is to let an organization keep its existing cloud commercial, governance, and network arrangements while still using Claude. The tradeoff is that the cloud provider, not Anthropic, controls several operational levers.

Two things change in practice. First, authentication and billing move to the cloud provider: requests are authorized through the provider's IAM and credentials, and usage appears on the cloud bill rather than an Anthropic invoice. The application uses the provider's endpoints and SDK configuration, and model identifiers take a platform-specific form (a Bedrock ID or a Google Cloud ID) rather than the Claude API alias. Second, model lifecycle is owned by the platform: Anthropic's retirement commitments cover only Anthropic-operated platforms, while Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud publish their own dates. A team that pins a model snapshot on Bedrock must watch Bedrock's schedule, not Anthropic's, to plan a controlled upgrade.

What does not change is the model itself. The same Claude models are served, so prompts, evals, and system instructions carry over without rewriting; the idea that cloud platforms receive a diminished build is a misconception. Equally wrong is the assumption that feature parity is automatic. Availability and timing vary by platform, so before committing, a team should confirm that the specific features it relies on (for example, particular caching options, thinking modes, or beta headers) are supported on the chosen platform.

See Claude in Amazon Bedrock, Claude on Vertex AI, and the Models overview for platform IDs and lifecycle details, and the Messages API reference for the first-party request shape.
option_feedback: This is incorrect. Feature availability and timing vary by platform, and each platform's documentation lists what it supports. Some features arrive later or behave differently on partner-operated platforms, so the team must verify each feature it depends on.

This is correct. Partner-operated platforms integrate Claude with the cloud provider's own identity, access management, and billing, so the application configures the provider's SDK and credentials instead of sending an x-api-key header to Anthropic.

This is incorrect. The cloud platforms serve the same Claude models under platform-specific model IDs, so prompts and evals carry over unchanged. What differs is the invocation mechanics, not the model's behavior, so a rewrite based on this premise is wasted effort.

This is correct. Anthropic's retirement commitments apply to Anthropic-operated platforms, while Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud set their own model lifecycle dates. Teams on those platforms must follow the platform's schedule when planning migrations.

question: A custom Skill developed and tested in claude.ai runs pip install for a parsing library and downloads a reference dataset from a public URL at runtime. Used through the Claude API with the code execution tool, its script fails. Which change fixes this?
options: Raise max_tokens and set the Skill version to "latest" so the container has time to finish installing packages.
Bundle the dataset inside the Skill's files and rewrite the script to use only packages pre-installed in the container.
Re-upload the Skill with type set to "anthropic" instead of "custom" so it inherits pre-built Skill privileges.
Add the web fetch server tool to the same request so scripts running inside the container can reach the public URL.
answer: Bundle the dataset inside the Skill's files and rewrite the script to use only packages pre-installed in the container.
explanation:
The same Skill can behave very differently depending on which surface runs it. In claude.ai, the code execution environment can install packages from npm and PyPI and pull from GitHub, so a Skill that fetches resources on the fly works. Through the Claude API, Skills run inside the code execution tool container, which is deliberately isolated: no network access and no runtime package installation, with only the pre-installed package set available. A script that calls pip install or reaches an external URL fails there by design.

The design implication is that Skills intended for the API must be self-contained. Bundle reference data, schemas, and examples as files in the Skill folder; they cost no context tokens until Claude reads them, so there is little penalty for including them. List required packages in SKILL.md and verify each one against the code execution tool's documented package list before relying on it. This is why the Skill authoring best practices warn against assuming tools are installed and against Skills that fetch from external URLs, which also carry prompt-injection risk when fetched content changes over time.

The other approaches misunderstand where things run. The web fetch tool executes on Anthropic's servers and hands content back to the model as a tool result; it does not give code inside the sandbox an outbound connection. The anthropic Skill type simply identifies Anthropic's pre-built Skills and cannot be applied to a custom upload, and those Skills operate under the same sandbox rules. Adjusting max_tokens or the version field changes output length and which revision loads, not the environment's capabilities. See the Agent Skills overview for the full list of environment constraints across surfaces.
option_feedback: max_tokens bounds the model's output and the version field selects which Skill revision loads; neither affects the container's environment. The failure is a hard environment constraint, not a timeout or a stale version.

Skills invoked through the API run in the code execution container, which has no network access and no runtime package installation. Shipping the data with the Skill and relying on the pre-installed package set is the only way the script can run there.

The anthropic type refers to Skills Anthropic publishes, such as pptx or xlsx, and cannot be assigned to your own upload. Pre-built Skills run in the same sandbox with the same constraints, so there are no extra privileges to inherit.

Web fetch is a server tool that retrieves pages on Anthropic's infrastructure and returns them as tool results to the model. It does not open network access for code running inside the sandboxed code execution container, so the script's own download and pip install still fail.

question: A long-horizon coding agent keeps progress notes and test status in files and commits each step to git. Its context window is nearly exhausted mid-task. Which approach best lets it continue with a clean, uncluttered context?
options: Start a fresh context window and direct the agent to reorient from progress.txt, tests.json, and the git log before resuming.
Replay the entire prior transcript into a new context window so the agent regains every earlier detail before it resumes work.
Delete the progress and test-status files before resetting so stale state cannot confuse the fresh session's rediscovery.
Raise max_tokens on the next request so the remaining work fits inside the current window without any reset.
answer: Start a fresh context window and direct the agent to reorient from progress.txt, tests.json, and the git log before resuming.
explanation:
The mental model to hold is that the context window is working memory, not durable storage. Everything in it (system prompt, messages, tool results, thinking, and the response itself) competes for the same finite space, and as that space fills, accuracy and recall degrade through context rot. Anything that must survive beyond a single window therefore has to be written somewhere outside it: files, structured status documents, or a git history. Once an agent is disciplined about externalizing state, the window itself becomes disposable.

That is why the prompting guidance for long-running agents suggests that when a window is cleared you should consider starting with a brand-new context window rather than compacting. Current Claude models are very effective at discovering state from the local filesystem, so a fresh session that is told to pwd, review progress.txt, tests.json, and the git log, and run a basic integration test before adding features can pick up cleanly. The tradeoff versus compaction is favorable here: a summary is a lossy compression produced by a model that is already operating in a degraded, overfull window, whereas on-disk state is exact and was recorded incrementally while the work was fresh. Compaction remains the right tool when state has not been externalized and the conversation itself is the only record.

The other approaches fail for distinct reasons. Replaying the entire transcript into the new window reproduces the bloat that caused the problem, so the agent hits the limit again and continues to reason over stale tool payloads. Raising max_tokens addresses output length only; it does not enlarge the window or reclaim consumed input space. Deleting the progress and test files destroys the externalized state that a fresh start depends on, turning rediscovery into rework. The general principle for long-horizon work is to use structured formats for state data, freeform notes for progress, and git for checkpoints, then treat any individual context window as replaceable.

See Prompting best practices for the guidance on starting fresh versus compacting and on state management, and Context windows for how the window fills and why curation matters more than headroom.
option_feedback: Because the task state already lives on the filesystem and in git, a brand-new window can recover everything it needs by reading those artifacts, with no accumulated noise and no summarization loss. Being prescriptive about how to start (review the progress file, the test status file, and the git log) is the documented pattern for this situation.

Replaying the full transcript simply recreates the exhausted window in a new session, including every spent tool result and dead end. The agent would be back at the limit almost immediately and would suffer the same accuracy degradation from an overfull context.

Those files are exactly the externalized state that makes a fresh start viable; removing them forces the agent to redo work or guess at what was completed. State on disk is current by construction because the agent updates it as it works, so there is nothing stale to protect against.

max_tokens caps the output Claude may generate in a single response; it does not enlarge the context window or free any of the space already consumed by history. Raising it does nothing to relieve a window that is nearly full of input.

question: An agent occasionally needs one of a dozen large internal API reference documents. Placing all of them in the system prompt consumes most of the context window on every request. Which approach keeps the references available without that cost?
options: Ask the model to skim the references once and retain only the relevant parts for future turns.
Bundle the references as files in a Skill so each one is read into context only when a task needs it.
Keep all references in the system prompt and add a cache breakpoint so they no longer occupy the window.
Move the references into the first user message instead of the system prompt to free system space.
answer: Bundle the references as files in a Skill so each one is read into context only when a task needs it.
explanation:
The right mental model for the context window is a single, finite working memory that the model attends over on every request. The system prompt, every entry in messages (including tool results, images, and documents), tool definitions, and the generated output all draw from the same pool, and as the pool fills, accuracy and recall degrade (context rot). The goal of context engineering is therefore not to fit as much as possible but to keep the window full of material relevant to the current step.

Progressive disclosure is the technique that fits this situation. A Skill bundles instructions and reference files on a filesystem; at startup only the Skill's name and description enter the system prompt, SKILL.md is read when the Skill is relevant, and any reference file is read only when a specific task calls for it. Files that are never opened cost zero tokens, so a Skill can carry a dozen large API references with no per-request penalty. Scripts inside a Skill behave the same way: only their output enters the window, not their source. On the Claude API this requires the code execution tool, whose container the Skill files live in; in Claude Code and the Agent SDK the same on-demand loading applies through the local filesystem.

The distractors each misunderstand what actually consumes the window. Prompt caching is a cost and latency optimization: a cached prefix is cheaper to process, but it is still processed and still occupies context on every request. Asking the model to skim and retain only what matters assumes the model can edit its own context by instruction, which it cannot; the application decides what is sent. Moving documents from the system prompt into a user message shifts their position without changing their token count, since there is no separate allowance for system content. Only the Skill-based approach removes the unused documents from the window while keeping them one file read away.

See Context windows and Agent Skills overview.
option_feedback: The model has no ability to selectively remember or discard parts of its own context by instruction; whatever is sent in the request occupies the window. Retention across turns happens only through what the application chooses to include, not through a request to the model.

Skills use progressive disclosure: only the Skill's name and description are loaded at startup, and bundled reference files consume no context tokens until Claude actually reads them. The agent can navigate to exactly the document a task requires, so the other eleven never enter the window.

Prompt caching reduces the cost and latency of reprocessing a repeated prefix, but cached content still counts fully toward the context window. Every request would still carry all twelve documents into the model's working memory, so the bloat and its effect on attention remain.

There is no separate budget for the system prompt versus messages; the context window is a single pool covering the system prompt, every message, tool results, and tool definitions. Relocating the documents changes their position, not the number of tokens they consume.

question: An application implements the memory tool's file operations against per-user storage on its own servers. Which TWO safeguards should the application's handler enforce for production use?
options: Canonicalize every requested path and reject any that resolves outside the memory directory before executing the command.
Add a system prompt instruction telling Claude never to include parent-directory sequences in memory file paths.
Rely on the API to validate memory paths server-side, since the memory tool's file operations run on Anthropic's infrastructure.
Run validation that strips or blocks sensitive data such as credentials before the handler writes a memory file.
answer: Canonicalize every requested path and reject any that resolves outside the memory directory before executing the command.
Run validation that strips or blocks sensitive data such as credentials before the handler writes a memory file.
explanation:
The memory tool gives Claude persistent files under a /memories prefix, but the tool is client-side: Claude emits a tool_use request such as create or view with a path, and your application performs the operation against real storage and returns a tool_result. That design keeps user data on infrastructure you control, which is a privacy advantage, but it also means every security property of the store is yours to implement. The API does not execute the filesystem operation or validate the path against your storage layout for you.

The first consequence is path traversal. A path like /memories/../../secrets.env is syntactically valid and, if mapped naively onto a filesystem, escapes the memory directory. The correct handler resolves each path to its canonical form (for example with Python's pathlib.Path.resolve() and relative_to()), confirms it still lies under the memory root, and rejects traversal sequences including URL-encoded variants. This check belongs in code on every command, because the request may originate from injected instructions rather than from the user's intent. A system prompt asking Claude to avoid .. only lowers the odds of a bad request; it does not stop one.

The second consequence is data minimization. Claude generally refuses to store secrets in memory, and that is useful, but a production store should not depend on it. Adding validation that strips or blocks credentials, tokens, and other sensitive fields before the write happens turns a model tendency into a guarantee. The same secure-by-design mindset extends to capping file sizes, limiting how much view returns, and expiring stale memory files.

The mental model is that the model proposes and your code disposes. Anything that must hold every time, such as staying inside a directory or keeping secrets out of durable storage, is enforced at the execution boundary, layered on top of whatever guidance you give the model. See Memory tool for the full list of recommended safeguards.
option_feedback: The memory tool is client-side, so a malicious or mistaken path such as /memories/../../secrets.env reaches whatever storage the handler maps it to. Resolving paths to canonical form and verifying they remain under the memory directory is the documented defense against directory traversal, and it should run on every command.

A prompt instruction is advisory and can be undermined by injected content in conversation or retrieved data. Path traversal must be blocked in code at the point of execution, not left to the model's compliance.

This misunderstands where the memory tool executes. Claude only requests file operations, and the application executes them against storage it controls; Anthropic does not perform the filesystem operation or provide server-side path validation for your storage handler, so any path check has to live in your own code.

Claude usually declines to write sensitive information to memory, but that is a probabilistic behavior, not an enforceable control. Adding deterministic validation in the write path gives a stronger guarantee that secrets and personal data never land in persistent storage.

question: An organization wants every Claude Code session on all developer machines, across every repository, to load the same data-handling reminders and code style guidance, and individual developers must not be able to exclude it. How should this be configured?
options: Commit a CLAUDE.md to the root of every repository and ask each team to keep it synchronized with the central version.
Encode the guidance as permissions.deny rules in managed settings so the constraints are technically enforced in every session.
Deploy a managed CLAUDE.md to the machine's managed policy location through MDM or another configuration management tool.
Have each developer paste the guidance into their personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so it applies across all of their projects.
answer: Deploy a managed CLAUDE.md to the machine's managed policy location through MDM or another configuration management tool.
explanation:
Claude Code layers instruction files by scope. A managed CLAUDE.md lives at a fixed policy location (for example /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/CLAUDE.md on macOS or /etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md on Linux), a user CLAUDE.md lives in ~/.claude/, and a project CLAUDE.md lives in the repository. The managed file loads before the user and project files, applies to every session on the machine regardless of repository, and cannot be excluded by individual settings. Organizations distribute it with whatever they already use to manage developer machines: MDM, Group Policy, Ansible, or similar. The claudeMd key in managed-settings.json offers the same effect without a separate file, and is honored only at the managed and policy settings level.

The mental model to hold is that CLAUDE.md is context, settings are enforcement. Instructions in any CLAUDE.md enter the context window and shape behavior, which is exactly what code style guidance and compliance reminders need; they are guidance the model follows, not gates the harness applies. permissions.deny, sandbox.enabled, and similar keys in managed settings are technical controls that block tools, commands, or paths deterministically, but they have no way to express "prefer this naming convention" or "remember the data classification policy." Choosing the wrong layer either leaves a hard constraint unenforced or tries to force soft guidance into a mechanism that cannot carry it.

The repository-scoped approach fails on both coverage and control: each team must copy and maintain the file, and developers can skip project CLAUDE.md files with claudeMdExcludes. The personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md approach fails for the same reason a shared spreadsheet fails as version control: it relies on every individual doing the right thing and keeps the file entirely under that individual's control. Only the managed layer gives a central owner, a repeatable delivery path, and immunity from local overrides.

See Manage Claude's memory for the CLAUDE.md scopes and the managed policy locations, and Deploy managed settings for how organization-wide configuration reaches developer machines.
option_feedback: A project CLAUDE.md is scoped to a single repository, so coverage depends on every team copying and maintaining it. It also can be excluded by developers through claudeMdExcludes, so it does not satisfy the requirement that individuals cannot opt out.

Permission deny rules block specific tools, commands, or file paths; they cannot express code style guidelines or compliance reminders. Managed settings are the right place for technical enforcement, but behavioral guidance belongs in a managed CLAUDE.md.

A managed CLAUDE.md at the managed policy location applies to every Claude Code session on the machine in every repository and cannot be excluded by individual settings. Distributing it with MDM, Group Policy, or Ansible is the documented way to deliver organization-wide behavioral guidance.
The user-level CLAUDE.md is a personal file each developer controls and can edit or delete at will. It provides no central delivery mechanism and no guarantee that the guidance stays in place.

question: A team is writing the requirements document for a Claude-based assistant that translates incoming customer messages for a multilingual support desk. Which of the following statements is a non-functional requirement?
options: The assistant shall translate each incoming message into the handling agent's configured language.
The translation prompt should include a few-shot example for each language the desk supports.
The assistant must be available 99.9% of the time during the published support hours.
The company intends to extend support coverage to four additional regional markets next year.
answer: The assistant must be available 99.9% of the time during the published support hours.
explanation:
Requirements analysis separates several kinds of statements that stakeholders tend to mix together. A business objective states the outcome the organisation wants (expanding into new markets). Functional requirements state what the system must do for a given input (translate each message). Non-functional requirements state the qualities the system must exhibit while doing it: performance, availability, security, data isolation, and similar attributes. Design decisions (how the prompt is structured, which model is chosen) come later and should be justified by the requirements, not confused with them.

An availability target is a classic non-functional requirement. It says nothing about translation itself, but it constrains the architecture in concrete ways: the client must handle transient 429 and 529 responses with backoff, the team must decide what happens when a request fails (queue it, degrade to a fallback, or surface an error), and the service must be monitored against the target during the hours that matter. Writing the target as a measurable percentage over a defined window is what makes it verifiable rather than aspirational.

The translation statement is functional because it can be tested by sending a message and checking the output language. The market-expansion statement is the business driver, which is why it belongs in the project charter rather than the requirements list. The few-shot prompt statement describes an implementation approach; it may well be a good one, but it should be recorded as a design decision that traces back to a quality requirement (for example, translation accuracy), not written into the requirements document as if it were a constraint the stakeholders imposed.

Keeping these categories distinct matters for Claude applications in particular because prompt design, model selection, and integration mechanics are all flexible and are easy to lock in too early. See Using the Messages API for the integration surface these requirements ultimately constrain, and Rate limits for the capacity and error-handling behaviour an availability target has to account for.
option_feedback: This describes a specific behaviour the system performs for a given input, which makes it a functional requirement. Functional requirements define what the system does, not the quality or constraints under which it does it.

This is a premature implementation decision about how the prompt will be built, not a requirement. Design choices like prompt structure belong to the system design phase and should be traceable back to requirements rather than written as requirements.

Availability is a quality attribute that constrains how the system must behave rather than what it does, which is the defining trait of a non-functional requirement. It shapes design decisions such as retry handling, fallbacks, and monitoring without describing any single feature.

This is the business objective that motivates the project, not a requirement placed on the system itself. Business goals sit above the requirements and are what functional and non-functional requirements exist to serve.

question: A repository already contains an AGENTS.md that several other coding agents read. The team wants Claude Code to follow those same instructions, plus a few Claude-specific rules, without maintaining two copies of the shared content. What should they do?
options: Create a CLAUDE.md that imports the existing file with @AGENTS.md and add the Claude-specific rules below the import.
Rename AGENTS.md to CLAUDE.md and append the Claude-specific rules, since Claude Code recognizes only that file name.
Copy the shared instructions and the Claude-specific rules into the project's .claude/settings.json so they load each session.
Rely on Claude Code reading AGENTS.md automatically and place the Claude-specific rules in a gitignored CLAUDE.local.md.
answer: Create a CLAUDE.md that imports the existing file with @AGENTS.md and add the Claude-specific rules below the import.
explanation:
Claude Code loads its persistent project instructions from CLAUDE.md at the start of every session; it does not look for AGENTS.md. Rather than copying content between two files that will inevitably drift, CLAUDE.md supports imports using @path/to/file syntax. An imported file is expanded and loaded into context at launch alongside the CLAUDE.md that references it, and anything written below the import is appended afterward. A CLAUDE.md consisting of @AGENTS.md followed by a short Claude-specific section therefore gives Claude Code the shared instructions and the extra rules while other agents keep reading the unchanged AGENTS.md. A symlink from CLAUDE.md to AGENTS.md is an alternative when no Claude-specific content is needed, though on Windows creating one needs elevated privileges, so the import form is the more portable choice.

The mental model is that CLAUDE.md is context, not configuration: it is delivered to the model as instructions, and imports are simply a way to compose that context from multiple files. Relative import paths resolve against the file containing the import, and paths wrapped in backticks are left literal. After setting this up, running /context and checking the list under Memory files confirms that CLAUDE.md loaded and pulled in the imported content. Note that imported files still consume context at launch, so the usual guidance about keeping instruction files concise applies to AGENTS.md as well.

The distractors each break a different part of the requirement. Renaming AGENTS.md satisfies Claude Code but strands every other tool that reads the original name, and it forces Claude-only rules into a file those tools consume. Pasting the instructions into .claude/settings.json confuses the two files' roles: settings files are strict JSON that hold configuration such as permission rules, hooks, and environment variables, not the prose conventions Claude reads as project context, and copying the text there would duplicate the shared content anyway. Assuming Claude Code reads AGENTS.md automatically is simply false, and CLAUDE.local.md is designed for private, gitignored per-project preferences, so team-wide rules placed there would never reach other engineers. See How Claude remembers your project for the CLAUDE.md and import mechanics, and Claude Code settings for what belongs in settings files instead.
option_feedback: Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md, not AGENTS.md, and CLAUDE.md supports @path imports that are expanded into context at session start. Importing AGENTS.md keeps a single source of truth for the shared instructions while the CLAUDE.md body carries the Claude-only additions.

Renaming the file would make Claude Code read it, but the other coding agents that depend on AGENTS.md would lose their instructions. It also mixes Claude-specific rules into a file other tools consume, which is the duplication and coupling the team wants to avoid.

The project settings.json holds configuration such as permission rules, hooks, and environment variables; it is strict JSON and is not where Claude Code reads project instructions or conventions from. Copying the shared content there would also create the second copy the team wants to avoid.

Claude Code does not read AGENTS.md on its own, so the shared instructions would never load. A gitignored CLAUDE.local.md is also the wrong home for team-wide Claude rules, because it stays on one engineer's machine rather than traveling with the repository.

question: An application consumes Claude responses that contain both tool_use blocks and a classification field constrained by a JSON schema enum. Which TWO consumption practices are correct?
options: Find tool calls by iterating the response content and selecting blocks whose type is tool_use, not by scanning prose.
Detect a tool invocation by matching a fixed lead-in phrase such as 'I will now call' in the text block that precedes it.
Add enum values that differ only in capitalization so that exact and near matches map to distinct downstream code branches.
Compare the returned enum label against the allowed values case-insensitively, since exact capitalization is not guaranteed.
answer: Find tool calls by iterating the response content and selecting blocks whose type is tool_use, not by scanning prose.
Compare the returned enum label against the allowed values case-insensitively, since exact capitalization is not guaranteed.
explanation:
The mental model for consuming a Claude response is that content is a typed list of blocks, not a single string. Text, tool_use, and thinking blocks can appear together in one assistant turn, and each block type has its own contract. A client tool call is signalled by stop_reason: "tool_use" and one or more tool_use blocks with id, name, and input; the application answers with tool_result blocks keyed by tool_use_id. The natural-language narration Claude produces before a call ("I'll check the weather first") exists for the human reader. It is generated text like any other, its phrasing varies, and Tool use with Claude is explicit that code should not rely on specific formatting conventions in it. Iterating blocks and dispatching on type is therefore the defensive pattern; matching a lead-in phrase is brittle by construction.

Structured outputs tighten the contract on the JSON itself. Both JSON outputs (output_config.format) and strict tool use (strict: true) work by grammar-constrained sampling, so the shape, required fields, and types are enforced during generation rather than checked afterwards. The tradeoff is that the grammar governs structure, not every character-level detail: Structured outputs documents that the exact capitalization of string enum and const values is not guaranteed. The practical consequence is twofold. When designing the schema, do not create enum members that differ only by case, because the consumer cannot reliably distinguish them. When consuming the value, normalise case before comparing, so a label that comes back as Refund instead of refund still routes correctly.

Together these habits reflect the broader discipline of defensive consumption: read what the API actually returns (typed blocks, documented fields, documented caveats) rather than what a fluent response appears to say, and validate at the boundary before any downstream system acts on it.
option_feedback: A response is a list of typed content blocks, and client tool calls arrive as tool_use blocks carrying an id, name, and input. Selecting blocks by type is the reliable way to consume them; the surrounding narration is ordinary generated text with no fixed format.

Claude often comments on what it is about to do before calling a tool, but the wording varies and no particular phrasing is promised. Code should treat that text like any other assistant prose and rely on the tool_use block type instead of formatting conventions.

Because capitalization of enum strings is not guaranteed exactly, two values that differ only by case cannot be told apart reliably. This design invites misrouting; the documented guidance is to avoid case-only distinctions in enums.

Constrained decoding keeps the output within the schema, but the documented caveat is that the exact capitalization of string enum and const values is not guaranteed. Comparing case-insensitively, or avoiding values that differ only by case, keeps downstream branching from breaking on a cosmetic difference.

question: A team runs claude -p in CI to summarize failing test output. Results differ across runners because each machine's ~/.claude holds different hooks, plugins, and CLAUDE.md content that the run picks up. Which flag makes the startup context identical on every runner?
options: Add --system-prompt with a fixed prompt so the runner's CLAUDE.md and hook configuration are not applied.
Add --setting-sources user so only the settings under each runner's home directory are loaded.
Add --disable-slash-commands so the run stops loading custom commands and skills from the runner's directories.
Add --bare so the run skips loading hooks, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md from the runner.
answer: Add --bare so the run skips loading hooks, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md from the runner.
explanation:
Without --bare, a claude -p invocation loads the same startup context an interactive session would: it reads the working directory and ~/.claude for hooks, skills, custom commands, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md. That behavior is a feature for a developer at a terminal, because their personal setup travels with them. In a pipeline it is a liability: two runners with different home directories build different prompts, run different hooks, and may connect different MCP servers, so the same commit is processed with different inputs.

Bare mode addresses this directly. Passing --bare skips auto-discovery of that host-specific configuration, which reduces startup time and gives the run a consistent starting context on every machine. Whatever the job actually needs is then supplied explicitly on the command line: --append-system-prompt or --append-system-prompt-file for instructions, --settings for settings, --mcp-config for MCP servers, --agents for custom agents, and --plugin-dir for a plugin. The useful mental model for CI is that the run's inputs should come from the repository and the flags, not from whichever runner happened to pick up the job. Because bare mode does not rely on a logged-in session, set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the environment for the Anthropic API.

The alternatives each touch one slice of the problem. --disable-slash-commands only affects slash commands and directory watching, leaving hooks, plugins, MCP servers, and CLAUDE.md in place. A replacement --system-prompt swaps out Claude Code's default instructions, but CLAUDE.md still loads through the message flow and hooks configured in settings still fire. --setting-sources user restricts settings to the user tier, which is the very tier that differs from runner to runner. Only bare mode removes runner-local configuration as an input. See Run Claude Code programmatically and the CLI reference.
option_feedback: Replacing the system prompt changes Claude Code's instructions but does not stop configuration discovery. CLAUDE.md content still loads through the normal message flow, and hooks and plugins from the runner's settings still run.

Restricting setting sources to user settings loads precisely the per-machine configuration that is causing the differences. It narrows where settings come from but does nothing to make the machines consistent with each other.

This flag only turns off slash commands and stops Claude Code from watching the command and agent directories. Hooks, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md still load from the runner, so the machines continue to diverge.

Bare mode skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, custom commands, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md, so configuration on the host machine does not reach the run. This makes the CI job independent of whatever runner-local Claude Code configuration happens to be present.

question: An application enables adaptive thinking on a current Claude model but keeps the max_tokens value of 1,024 that its earlier non-thinking responses fit within. Many responses now return stop_reason max_tokens with the final answer cut off. What is the appropriate fix?
options: Set thinking display to omitted so hidden reasoning stops consuming the output budget that the response text needs.
Enable fast mode so the model generates output quickly enough to complete the answer within the existing cap.
Retry the same request unchanged, since thinking tokens are billed separately and the truncation is likely transient.
Raise max_tokens so the cap leaves room for both the thinking tokens and the final response text.
answer: Raise max_tokens so the cap leaves room for both the thinking tokens and the final response text.
explanation:
The mental model to hold is that max_tokens is a single hard ceiling on everything Claude emits for a request. When thinking is active, the reasoning Claude does before (and, with interleaved thinking, between) its visible output is generated as output tokens, billed as output tokens, and counted against that same ceiling. Nothing is generated past it. A value of 1,024 that comfortably fit a direct answer becomes far too small the moment Claude decides a request warrants reasoning, because the thinking alone can consume most or all of the budget and the response text is cut off when the cap is hit.

This is by design. With adaptive thinking there is no separate thinking budget to configure: max_tokens is the hard cost bound, and the effort parameter is soft guidance on how much of that output Claude allocates to reasoning. Effort shapes behavior but does not guarantee a token count, so the only true limit is the cap. That gives you two remedies when you see stop_reason: "max_tokens". If the truncated requests genuinely needed the reasoning, raise max_tokens so both the thinking and the answer fit. If they were over-thought, lower effort so Claude reasons less and leaves more of the budget for response text. The right choice depends on whether quality on those requests matters more than the tokens saved.

The distractors each confuse a different dimension for token count. The display setting is purely about visibility: omitted thinking still exists, still counts toward the cap, and is still billed. Thinking tokens are not tracked outside max_tokens, and a max_tokens stop reason is an ordinary, deterministic outcome of hitting the cap rather than a transient error, so retrying the unchanged request just reproduces it. Fast mode affects output tokens per second at premium pricing; a token limit is not a time limit, so generating faster cannot make more tokens fit.

See Steering thinking for the cost-control mechanics of adaptive thinking, Effort for how the effort levels change thinking behavior, and the Models overview for per-model maximum output limits.
