Reducing max_tokens on Opus trims output spend but keeps its higher per-token price and latency. Extended thinking adds latency per ticket, the opposite of the target. A nightly batch sacrifices the responsiveness that live support triage requires. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/choosing-a-model

question: A document-extraction pipeline at Cendrix began emitting a different field layout overnight even though no code was deployed. The team discovers its configuration references the Claude model by an alias name. What prevents this class of regression going forward?
options: Set the anthropic-version header so responses keep the earlier behavior
Lower the temperature so new releases sample the same token sequences
Add a system instruction that locks the output layout across releases
Reference a dated model snapshot and migrate to new releases deliberately
answer: Reference a dated model snapshot and migrate to new releases deliberately
explanation: An alias automatically tracks the newest snapshot of a model, so a new release can change production behavior without any deploy, while a dated snapshot keeps the model fixed until the team validates an upgrade on its own schedule. The anthropic-version header versions the API request and response shapes, not model behavior. Temperature settings do not make two different model versions behave alike. A prompt instruction has no power to hold output stable when the underlying model changes. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/model-deprecations

question: Bramblewood's assistant sends a 20,000-token block of policy text and fifteen tool definitions with every request, followed by a short user question. Input spend dominates the bill even though the large block never changes between requests. Which two request changes cut the input cost? Choose 2.
options: Mark the end of the stable policy block with a cache_control breakpoint
Place the user's question ahead of the policy text so it is stored too
Order the request so tools and stable content precede the variable turns
Trim max_tokens on each request so the large block bills at a lower rate
answer: Mark the end of the stable policy block with a cache_control breakpoint
Order the request so tools and stable content precede the variable turns
explanation: Prompt caching bills reads of a cached prefix at a small fraction of the base input price, so marking the stable block with a cache_control breakpoint lets every later request reuse it. Because caching matches from the start of the prompt, tools and stable content must come before the variable turns for the prefix to stay identical. Putting the changing question ahead of the policy text alters the prefix on every request and defeats reuse. max_tokens governs output length and has no effect on how input tokens are priced. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching

question: Meridian Ledger ingests customer PDFs whose extracted text ranges from one page to three hundred pages. Finance wants a reliable per-document cost projection before each document is submitted to Claude, and rough character-based estimates have been off by 40 percent. What should the engineering team use?
options: A heuristic of four characters per token applied to the extracted text
The token counting endpoint to measure each prompt before submission
A one token max_tokens request whose usage field reveals the input size
The average of previously billed input tokens across recent documents
answer: The token counting endpoint to measure each prompt before submission
explanation: The token counting endpoint returns the exact token count for a prospective Messages request without incurring model charges, which turns tokens into an accurate cost projection before anything is submitted. Character heuristics vary with content type, which is exactly why the current estimates miss badly. Sending a real request capped at one output token still bills the entire input just to measure it. Averages over past documents say little about a specific document whose length varies three hundredfold. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/token-counting

question: A developer at Brightlark Insurance is building a document intake pipeline with Claude: every submission is classified, key fields are extracted, and a templated summary is written. The steps never vary and each step has clear pass criteria. The team is debating how to structure the integration. Which approach fits this task best?
options: A single autonomous agent that plans its own steps with a general tool set
A workflow that chains fixed prompt steps with validation between each stage
A supervisor agent that routes each document to specialized worker agents
An agent loop that continues until the model stops requesting tool calls
answer: A workflow that chains fixed prompt steps with validation between each stage
explanation: The task decomposes into fixed, predictable steps with verifiable checkpoints, which is the defining signal for a workflow built from predefined code paths rather than an agent. Chaining prompts with validation gates between stages gives consistent results at lower cost. An autonomous planning agent adds latency and variability the task does not need, a supervisor hierarchy is designed for dynamic delegation across unpredictable subtasks, and an open-ended loop that runs until tool calls stop suits tasks whose step count cannot be known in advance. Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

question: Kestrelworks is building a Claude system that answers broad competitive research questions for its analysts. The subtasks cannot be predicted ahead of time: each question demands a different mix of searches, comparisons, and syntheses, and some questions need many parallel threads while others need only one. Which architecture handles this variability best?
options: A fixed chain of prompts that repeats the same research steps per question
A routing step that classifies each question and sends it to one prompt template
A parallel fan-out that runs one identical searcher per configured data source
A lead agent that breaks each question into subtasks and delegates them to workers
answer: A lead agent that breaks each question into subtasks and delegates them to workers
explanation: When subtasks cannot be predicted in advance, an orchestrator structure fits: a lead agent decomposes each question dynamically, delegates the pieces to worker agents, and synthesizes their results. A fixed chain applies identical steps regardless of what the question needs. A routing classifier selects a single downstream path, which cannot cover questions that require several kinds of work at once. Fanning out one identical searcher per source is static parallelization and cannot adapt the number or type of subtasks to the question. Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

question: Moxa Freight's engineering team uses Claude Code to audit large repositories. Exploratory searches return thousands of lines of output, and after several audits in one session the assistant starts overlooking findings from early in the conversation because the transcript is crowded with raw search results. How should the team restructure the work?
options: Delegate exploration to subagents that report back only their conclusions
Raise the max_tokens setting so responses can restate every earlier finding
Repeat earlier searches whenever the assistant appears to lose track
Paste prior findings into CLAUDE.md so they load with each prompt
answer: Delegate exploration to subagents that report back only their conclusions
explanation: Subagents run in their own isolated context windows, so the noisy exploration happens outside the main transcript and only a concise conclusion returns to the parent session. Raising max_tokens changes how long responses can be, not how much history the window holds. Repeating searches burns turns and adds even more raw output to the crowded transcript. CLAUDE.md content loads into context at session start, so pasting findings there consumes the same budget the team is trying to protect. Reference: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents

question: Parlan Systems runs a coding agent built on Claude Code. Policy requires the unit test suite to run after every file edit the agent makes. An instruction in CLAUDE.md is followed most of the time but is occasionally skipped during long sessions. What guarantees the tests always run?
options: Rewriting the CLAUDE.md instruction with stronger and more explicit wording
Adding a Skill that documents the test procedure for the agent
Configuring a PostToolUse hook that executes the suite after edits
Prompting the agent to confirm test completion before each response
answer: Configuring a PostToolUse hook that executes the suite after edits
explanation: Hooks are shell commands the harness executes deterministically at lifecycle events, so a PostToolUse hook fires after every file-editing tool call regardless of what the model decides to do. Stronger CLAUDE.md wording and confirmation prompts both still depend on the model choosing to comply, which is exactly the failure mode observed on long sessions. A Skill supplies procedural instructions when the task calls for them but does not guarantee that any command actually executes. Reference: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks

question: A developer at Quillbay wrote a custom agent loop directly against the Messages API. The agent completes its assigned task correctly but then keeps invoking tools for several extra turns, adding cost to every run. Reviewing the loop code, what is the most likely omission?
options: A retry wrapper that backs off when the API returns a 429 status
A check that ends the loop when the response contains no tool_use blocks
A cache_control block that stops repeated tool definitions from being re-sent
A streaming handler that closes the connection after the final content event
answer: A check that ends the loop when the response contains no tool_use blocks
explanation: A custom loop needs an explicit exit condition: when a response arrives with no tool_use blocks and the stop_reason is end_turn, the task is finished and the loop should stop re-prompting. Without that check the harness keeps giving the model chances to act, which produces the extra turns observed. A 429 retry wrapper governs rate-limit recovery, not termination. cache_control lowers the cost of repeated prefixes but does not shorten the run. A streaming handler manages delivery within a single turn, not across turns. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/implement-tool-use

question: Verdane Labs wants to embed a coding assistant inside its desktop product. The team wants the iteration structure, tool execution, and context handling provided for them, while everything still runs inside their own application process. They already use the Anthropic Python client for simple completions. What should they build on?
options: The Anthropic client library with a hand-written loop around it
The Messages API called through raw HTTP requests per turn
The Message Batches API to process the assistant turns asynchronously
The Claude Agent SDK running inside their application process
answer: The Claude Agent SDK running inside their application process
explanation: The Claude Agent SDK packages the same agent loop that powers Claude Code, including iteration, tool execution, and context management, and it runs inside the host application's own process, which matches both requirements. The client library and raw HTTP calls would each require Verdane to build and maintain that harness themselves. The Message Batches API processes large asynchronous jobs and cannot drive an interactive in-product assistant. Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-agents-with-the-claude-agent-sdk

question: A long-horizon Claude agent at Fennelcore processes support escalations in sessions that run dozens of turns. Around turn thirty, the agent slows down and begins repeating tool calls it already made. Token metrics show the context window is nearly full of old tool results. Which two changes reclaim headroom while preserving task continuity? Choose 2.
options: Switch the session to a model alias so the window resets automatically
Prune tool results from older turns once their content has been used
Raise max_tokens on every request so the model can finish sooner
Compact the conversation into a summary that preserves key decisions
answer: Prune tool results from older turns once their content has been used
Compact the conversation into a summary that preserves key decisions
explanation: Pruning consumed tool results and compacting the history into a summary each free window space while carrying forward the decisions the agent still needs, which restores tool selection quality without losing the task thread. A model alias only controls which snapshot serves the request and does nothing to the accumulated transcript. Raising max_tokens expands the output ceiling and leaves the crowded input context untouched. Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents

question: A scheduling agent at Ostrafield helps clinicians reserve imaging equipment. Every session starts fresh, and users complain that the agent re-asks for the same site preferences every day. The team wants those preferences available in future sessions without users re-entering them. Which pattern addresses this?
options: Extend the context window so past sessions remain inside the transcript
Cache prior conversations with cache_control so they persist across sessions
Persist preferences to memory files stored outside the conversation context
Embed each user preference into the tool schemas the agent loads
answer: Persist preferences to memory files stored outside the conversation context
explanation: With the memory pattern the agent writes durable facts to files stored outside the context window, then reads them back at the start of any later session before acting, so preferences survive across conversations. A context window does not span separate sessions no matter its size. Prompt caching with cache_control is a cost and latency optimization for repeated prefixes that expires quickly, so it cannot serve as durable storage. Tool schemas describe capabilities, not per-user state. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool

question: A developer at Harborline Analytics sends three lengthy vendor contracts, about 150K tokens combined, in a single Messages API request, asking the question first and appending the contracts after it. Claude's answers frequently miss clauses buried deep in the third contract, though the same question against any single contract succeeds. What prompt restructuring should the developer try first?
options: Move the question to the end of the prompt so it follows the contract text
Split each contract into separate requests and merge the three answers afterward
Raise max_tokens so the model has more room to reason across all three contracts
Add a few-shot example that demonstrates answering from a short sample contract
answer: Move the question to the end of the prompt so it follows the contract text
explanation: Anthropic's long-context guidance is to place longform documents near the top of the prompt with the query after them, which measurably improves recall of details deep in the input. Asking first forces the model to carry the question across 150K tokens of contract text, degrading retrieval of late clauses. Splitting contracts into separate requests loses cross-contract comparison and adds merge complexity without fixing in-context recall. Raising max_tokens expands the response budget, not how well the input is read. A few-shot example shapes answer format rather than deep-document retrieval. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/long-context-tips

question: Peltrow Insurance runs a long-lived claims-processing agent that calls document-lookup tools hundreds of times per session. Sessions eventually fail because earlier tool results, most of which are never referenced again, consume nearly the entire context window. The team wants to keep sessions running without rebuilding the agent. Which API capability should they enable?
options: Context editing, so stale tool results are cleared automatically as the conversation grows
Prompt caching, so repeated tool results are stored and no longer counted as input
The Message Batches API, so long sessions are processed asynchronously with higher limits
Streaming responses, so partial output is delivered before the window limit is reached
answer: Context editing, so stale tool results are cleared automatically as the conversation grows
explanation: Context editing automatically clears older tool results from the conversation once they exceed a configured threshold, reclaiming window space while the session continues. Prompt caching lowers cost and latency for repeated prefixes, but cached tokens still occupy the context window. The Message Batches API serves asynchronous bulk workloads and does not change per-conversation context limits. Streaming changes how output is delivered, not how much accumulated input the window can hold. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing

question: Quillsona ships a compliance-review assistant built on the Messages API. The persona and tone rules are currently pasted at the top of every user message. In long conversations where users paste large document excerpts, the assistant increasingly ignores those rules and adopts the tone of the pasted material. What is the most effective fix?
options: Repeat the persona rules at both the top and bottom of every user message
Reduce the excerpt size users can paste so the rules stay proportionally prominent
Add a final user turn after each excerpt reminding the assistant of its persona
Move the persona rules into the system prompt instead of the user messages
answer: Move the persona rules into the system prompt instead of the user messages
explanation: The system prompt is the designated place for persona and role instructions, and Claude treats it as standing guidance that persists across turns rather than as content competing with pasted material. Repeating rules inside user messages, or appending a reminder turn after each excerpt, still mixes instructions with conversational content and degrades as the conversation grows. Restricting excerpt size limits the product's usefulness without addressing where the instructions live. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/system-prompts

question: Orvin Software's extraction service asks Claude for a JSON object, but responses often begin with a short introductory sentence that breaks the downstream parser. The team wants every response to start with the opening brace, without adding a post-processing step. Which technique achieves this?
options: Set temperature to zero so the model stops generating conversational openings
Prefill the assistant turn with an opening brace so output continues from it
Add a rule at the end of the system prompt that forbids any prose
Lower max_tokens so the model has no budget left for introductory sentences
answer: Prefill the assistant turn with an opening brace so output continues from it
explanation: Prefilling the assistant message with an opening brace forces generation to continue from that character, so the reply cannot begin with prose. Temperature zero makes output more deterministic but does not remove openings the model considers appropriate. A system-prompt rule reduces preamble yet does not guarantee the first character, which is what the parser requires. Lowering max_tokens truncates the JSON itself rather than eliminating the introduction. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/prefill-claudes-response

question: Kestrel Data uses Claude to extract vendor names, invoice totals, and due dates from emailed invoices. Outputs vary from run to run: field names change, dates appear in mixed formats, and sentences inside the emails are sometimes treated as instructions. Which two prompt changes best address these problems? Choose 2.
options: Raise the temperature so the model explores until it settles on one consistent format
Add several example invoice inputs paired with outputs in the exact desired format
Split each email across multiple requests so the model handles one field at a time
Wrap the email body in XML tags so it is clearly separated from the instructions
answer: Add several example invoice inputs paired with outputs in the exact desired format
Wrap the email body in XML tags so it is clearly separated from the instructions
explanation: Paired input-output examples show Claude the exact field names and date formats expected, which is the most reliable way to standardize structure across runs. XML tags around the email body separate document text from the instructions, so sentences inside emails stop being followed as directives. Higher temperature increases variability, the opposite of the goal. Splitting fields across requests multiplies cost and still leaves each request without a format specification. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/multishot-prompting

question: Marrowfield Legal uses Claude to answer questions over uploaded case files, quoting passages as support. Reviewers discover that some answers cite page numbers and quotations that read convincingly but do not appear anywhere in the uploaded files. Which safeguard most directly addresses this failure mode?
options: Verify each quotation against the source documents programmatically before showing the answer
Instruct the model to sound less confident whenever it is quoting from the files
Raise the thinking budget so the model reasons longer before producing each citation
Ask the model to rate its own confidence and discard answers scoring below a threshold
answer: Verify each quotation against the source documents programmatically before showing the answer
explanation: Fabricated quotations read fluently and confidently, so the reliable defense is programmatic verification that each quoted passage actually appears in the source before the answer is released. Telling the model to sound less confident changes tone without changing accuracy. A larger thinking budget improves reasoning but does not prevent a plausible citation from being invented. Self-reported confidence scores are themselves model output and can be confidently wrong. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations

question: Lumavia Systems' summarization service intermittently returns JSON that fails to parse. Logs show the malformed responses are always the longest ones and are cut off mid-string, while shorter responses parse cleanly. The engineer inspects the raw API responses to isolate the cause. Which response field confirms this diagnosis?
options: The usage object, which reports how many input tokens the request consumed
The model field, which shows whether an alias resolved to a newer snapshot
The stop_reason field, which reports max_tokens when output hits the configured limit
The request-id header, which links the failing call to server-side error logs
answer: The stop_reason field, which reports max_tokens when output hits the configured limit
explanation: A stop_reason of max_tokens shows the response ended because it reached the configured output limit, which explains JSON that is cut off mid-string only on the longest responses. The usage object reports token counts, but input consumption does not truncate output. The model field identifies which snapshot served the request and is unrelated to truncation. The request-id header helps when reporting server errors to support, not when diagnosing an output limit. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/handling-stop-reasons

question: A developer at Brightlyn Analytics wires Claude to an internal inventory lookup tool. When the inventory service times out, the harness currently drops the failed call and sends Claude a fresh user message saying the data is unavailable, and conversations often derail. What should the harness return instead so Claude can recover within the same tool-use loop?
options: A stop_sequence entry that ends the turn when the service fails
A new system prompt that tells Claude the inventory service is unreliable
A tool_result block that describes the timeout and sets is_error to true
A tool_choice parameter set to none while the inventory service recovers
answer: A tool_result block that describes the timeout and sets is_error to true
explanation: Returning a tool_result block with is_error set to true answers the pending tool_use request and keeps the failure inside the loop, so Claude can acknowledge the problem, retry, or adjust its plan. A stop_sequence only controls where text generation halts and cannot report a tool failure. Swapping in a new system prompt leaves the outstanding tool_use block unanswered, which breaks the expected request structure. Setting tool_choice to none merely blocks future calls and still fails to resolve the pending one. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/implement-tool-use

question: Verdana Logistics gives Claude twelve custom tools for shipment operations. In testing, Claude frequently calls the rate-quote tool when users ask for delivery-status updates, and it sometimes guesses parameter values. Every JSON schema validates correctly. Which change most directly improves Claude's tool selection?
options: Expand each tool description to state its purpose and when it applies
Lower the temperature so the model selects between tools more deterministically
Reorder the tools array so frequently used tools appear before the others
Shorten each description so the model relies on the schemas instead
answer: Expand each tool description to state its purpose and when it applies
explanation: Description quality is the highest-leverage factor in tool selection: stating what a tool does, when it applies, and what its parameters mean lets Claude distinguish overlapping tools and supply real values. Temperature changes sampling variability but does not improve the model's understanding of which tool fits a request. Position in the tools array carries no priority semantics. Trimming descriptions removes exactly the context the model depends on, because a schema alone does not convey intent. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/implement-tool-use

question: Cartwheel Books builds a citation-extraction endpoint where every response must arrive through a record_citation tool the team defined, never as plain prose. During tests Claude occasionally answers in text without calling the tool. Which request change guarantees the tool is invoked?
options: Add a system prompt line that tells Claude to respond through the tool
Mark the tool itself as required inside its input_schema parameter definition
Send the request with parallel tool use disabled so text answers stop
Set tool_choice to the specific tool by name in each request
answer: Set tool_choice to the specific tool by name in each request
explanation: Setting tool_choice with type tool and the tool's name forces Claude to call that tool, which is the only mechanism that guarantees invocation on a request. A system prompt instruction raises the likelihood of a call but the model can still reply in prose. The required field inside input_schema governs which parameters must be supplied once the tool is called, not whether it is called at all. Disabling parallel tool use limits how many calls happen in one turn and does nothing to prevent text answers. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/implement-tool-use

question: A platform team at Quillhaven prototyped an MCP server that runs as a subprocess on each developer laptop and communicates over standard input and output. They now need the same capabilities served from one central host so hundreds of engineers can connect without installing anything locally. Which change fits this requirement?
options: Keep the stdio transport and mount the server binary on a network drive
Migrate the server to a streamable HTTP transport on the shared host
Package the stdio server as a container that each engineer runs locally
Convert the server's tools into MCP prompts so no transport is needed
answer: Migrate the server to a streamable HTTP transport on the shared host
explanation: Remote MCP servers use a streamable HTTP transport, which lets many clients connect over the network to a single hosted endpoint. Stdio ties the server's lifecycle to a locally launched subprocess, so placing the binary on a network drive still requires every machine to spawn it. A container preserves the install-per-laptop model the team wants to eliminate. Prompts are a separate MCP primitive for reusable message templates and still require a transport to reach the server. Reference: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/concepts/transports

question: An enablement lead at Ferndale Studio wants Claude to follow the company's multi-step brand-review checklist, consult bundled style-guide documents, and produce a scored report, both in Claude Code and in the Claude apps. No external system needs to be called. Which approach fits best?
options: A custom tool whose input schema encodes the checklist steps
A built-in tool invoked with the style guides pasted as arguments
A Skill that packages the checklist instructions and style-guide files
An MCP server that exposes the checklist as a resource endpoint
answer: A Skill that packages the checklist instructions and style-guide files
explanation: A Skill bundles procedural instructions and supporting files into a reusable package that Claude loads on demand, and it works across Claude Code and the Claude apps, which matches a workflow that needs guidance and reference material rather than external calls. A custom tool exists to execute code against outside systems, and encoding steps in a schema does not teach the procedure. Built-in tools cover capabilities like search and code execution, not company checklists. An MCP server adds hosting and transport overhead that buys nothing when there is no external system to integrate. Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/equipping-agents-for-the-real-world-with-agent-skills

question: Halverton Freight built internal APIs for shipment tracking and customs paperwork. The developer platform team must expose these operations to Claude Code, Claude Desktop, and a custom Claude API application that different teams maintain. Which two factors make an MCP server the right integration layer here? Choose 2.
options: One server definition serves each MCP-capable client without per-app tool code
Server-hosted tools run on Anthropic infrastructure so the team hosts nothing
Servers can expose prompts and resources alongside tools from one endpoint
Tool schemas become optional because clients discover behavior from traffic
answer: One server definition serves each MCP-capable client without per-app tool code
Servers can expose prompts and resources alongside tools from one endpoint
explanation: An MCP server is defined once, and any MCP client, including Claude Code, Claude Desktop, and API applications using the MCP connector, can consume it, which removes duplicated integration code across teams. The protocol also lets a single server publish prompts and resources in addition to tools, so shared templates and reference data ride along. MCP servers are hosted and operated by their authors, not by Anthropic. Declared input schemas remain mandatory, because clients rely on them rather than on observed traffic to call tools correctly. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector

question: A consultant works across many client repositories in Claude Code and wants their personal coding conventions loaded into every session on their machine, without committing any file to a client repo. Where should these instructions live?
options: In a CLAUDE.md committed at each repository root
In the user memory file at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
In the allow list of each project's settings.json
In a custom slash command invoked at session start
answer: In the user memory file at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
explanation: The user-level memory file at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md loads into every Claude Code session for that user across all projects and never touches a client repository. A CLAUDE.md at a repository root must be added project by project and would be visible to each client team. The settings.json allow list controls tool permissions, not prose guidance. A custom slash command runs only when explicitly invoked, so the conventions would not load automatically each session. Reference: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory

question: A team lead at Osprey Labs wants two behaviors enforced in every Claude Code session on a shared repository: the project formatter runs automatically after Claude edits any source file, and attempts to modify files under config/production/ are stopped before they execute. Which two configurations meet these requirements? Choose 2.
options: A CLAUDE.md rule asking Claude to format code and avoid the directory
A PostToolUse hook that runs the formatter after file edits
A subagent that reviews the session diff once work concludes
A PreToolUse hook that rejects edits targeting the protected directory
answer: A PostToolUse hook that runs the formatter after file edits
A PreToolUse hook that rejects edits targeting the protected directory
explanation: Hooks execute deterministic shell commands at fixed lifecycle points: a PostToolUse hook can run the formatter after each successful edit, and a PreToolUse hook can inspect a pending tool call and block it before anything touches the protected path. A CLAUDE.md instruction is guidance the model may weigh, but it is not enforced on every action, which fails the requirement for guaranteed behavior. A subagent reviewing the diff afterward acts only once changes have already landed, so it neither formats on each edit nor prevents the modification. Reference: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks

question: Brightvale Insurance runs a public chatbot that produces instant policy quotes. Its system prompt embeds the company's confidential underwriting thresholds so quotes stay accurate. Screenshots are circulating online showing users coaxing the bot into reciting those thresholds despite an instruction to keep them private. Which change best protects the thresholds?
options: Append a final instruction telling the model to refuse any request that asks about its configuration
Move the proprietary thresholds into server-side code that applies them after the model responds
Lower the temperature to zero so the model produces the same safe response for each user
Pin the deployment to a model snapshot with stronger resistance to disclosure requests
answer: Move the proprietary thresholds into server-side code that applies them after the model responds
explanation: Confidential business logic should not live in the model's instructions at all: relocating the thresholds into server-side code that runs after the model responds removes the secret from anything a user can extract through conversation. A refusal instruction can be bypassed by novel phrasings, as the circulating screenshots already demonstrate. Zero temperature changes sampling variability, not what the model is willing to reveal. Pinning a snapshot stabilizes behavior across model updates, but no snapshot is immune to extraction prompts when the secret remains in the prompt. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-prompt-leak

question: Lumera Health is preparing to launch a patient-facing assistant that can reschedule appointments through a records tool. Before launch, the security team must harden the deployment so that a malicious or manipulated conversation cannot cause unauthorized record changes. Which two practices best achieve this? Choose 2.
options: Rely on the model's built-in safety training to turn away harmful appointment requests
Run each user message through a fast screening model before the assistant acts on it
Concentrate the policy rules in one comprehensive system prompt to keep behavior consistent
Scope the records tool's credentials to the specific operations the workflow needs
answer: Run each user message through a fast screening model before the assistant acts on it
Scope the records tool's credentials to the specific operations the workflow needs
explanation: Screening each incoming message with a fast model adds an independent detection layer that catches injection and abuse attempts before the assistant acts, and scoping the tool's credentials to just the operations the workflow needs limits the damage any attack that slips through can cause. Safety training provides a useful baseline, but it is not sufficient on its own when a tool can modify patient records. Concentrating the rules in a single system prompt creates one point of failure instead of layered defenses. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/mitigate-jailbreaks

question: Engineers at Ferrowood Analytics use Claude Code across a shared monorepo. Last week an agent session executed a shell command that dropped a staging database table, even though the repository's guidance files warn against destructive commands. The platform team wants a safeguard that executes independently of the model's own judgment on every tool call. Which approach delivers this?
options: Add a strongly worded rule to CLAUDE.md instructing the agent to avoid destructive commands
Enable plan mode so the agent presents its approach before touching project files
Configure a Stop hook that reviews the transcript for risky commands after each turn
Register a PreToolUse hook that inspects each shell command and blocks matches before execution
answer: Register a PreToolUse hook that inspects each shell command and blocks matches before execution
explanation: A PreToolUse hook runs as the team's own code before a tool call executes, so a blocking response stops the command deterministically regardless of what the model intended. CLAUDE.md guidance shapes model behavior, but the incident shows that instructions alone can fail. Plan mode inserts a review step, yet it depends on session settings and per-session approval rather than firing on every tool call. A Stop hook fires after the turn completes, which is too late for a command that has already run. Reference: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks

question: Quillbrook Retail sees a sudden spike in Claude API spend from unrecognized traffic. The investigation finds one API key copied onto developer laptops, into the CI pipeline, and into the production service, and pasted into an internal troubleshooting document. The team must shut down the abuse without an outage. Which change makes that containment possible?
options: Issue a separate key for each environment so one credential can be revoked in isolation
Rotate the shared key on a fixed monthly schedule and announce each new value internally
Store the single key in a managed secrets vault that the environments read at startup
Encode the key before committing it so the raw value stays hidden from repository readers
answer: Issue a separate key for each environment so one credential can be revoked in isolation
explanation: With one credential shared across laptops, CI, and production, revoking it would take every consumer down at once, so separate keys per environment are what make containment possible: the abused key can be killed immediately while production continues on its own credential. Rotating a still-shared key leaves the same blast radius between rotations, and announcing values internally widens exposure. A secrets vault improves storage hygiene, but a single stored key still cannot be revoked selectively. Encoding is not encryption, since anyone with repository access can decode and reuse the value. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/getting-started

question: Torvane Systems is adding a feature where warehouse staff photograph damaged parcels and Claude writes a damage description for the claims record. The developer must include each photo in the Messages API request. Which two methods supply the photo correctly? Choose 2.
options: Send the photo as base64 data in an image content block
Attach the photo as multipart form data on the Messages request
Point an image content block at a publicly reachable image URL
Write the photo's local file path into an image content block
answer: Send the photo as base64 data in an image content block
Point an image content block at a publicly reachable image URL
explanation: The Messages API accepts images through image content blocks whose source is either base64 encoded data or a publicly accessible URL, so both of those methods deliver the photo to the model. Multipart form uploads are not part of the Messages request format, which is a JSON body. The API also has no access to the caller's filesystem, so a local file path cannot be resolved into image data. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/vision

question: Mosswick Analytics generates long research summaries through the Messages API. A few responses end mid-sentence, and the cut-offs became more frequent after the team lowered a request parameter to control spend. What should the client code check to detect these truncated responses?
options: Compare the response length against the average of previous responses
Inspect the stop_reason field for a max_tokens value on each response
Watch for an HTTP 413 status code returned with the truncated body
Scan the output text for a truncation marker appended by the API
answer: Inspect the stop_reason field for a max_tokens value on each response
explanation: When generation halts because the output token limit was reached, the response reports stop_reason max_tokens, so the client can detect the truncation and retry with a higher limit or continue the turn. Response length varies naturally between summaries, so comparing against an average produces false alarms and misses. The API returns a normal 200 status with the shortened completion rather than an HTTP error, and it appends no marker text to cut-off output. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/handling-stop-reasons

question: Rundleford Insurance submits 5,000 claim documents to the Message Batches API each night and writes each result back to its claim record by position, first result to first request. Some summaries land on the wrong claims. What is the correct fix?
options: Split the nightly job into smaller batches so ordering is preserved
Sort the downloaded results file by creation timestamp before writing back
Resubmit mismatched requests through the synchronous Messages endpoint
Assign a custom_id per request and join results on that identifier
answer: Assign a custom_id per request and join results on that identifier
explanation: Batch results can come back in any order, so position-based matching is unreliable no matter how the work is divided. Each batch request accepts a custom_id that is echoed back on its result, which is the supported way to correlate outputs with source records. Sorting by timestamp still does not reconstruct submission order, and rerouting work through the synchronous endpoint gives up batch pricing without repairing the correlation logic. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing

question: Peltwater Media generates chapter-length drafts with a large output budget. Requests that run past several minutes intermittently fail with connection timeouts before any content arrives, even though shorter drafts complete without trouble. Which change makes the long generations reliable?
options: Request the response as a stream and assemble it from incremental events
Raise the client's socket timeout so the connection waits indefinitely
Retry each failed request with exponential backoff until a draft succeeds
Split each draft into sentence-length requests to keep calls short
answer: Request the response as a stream and assemble it from incremental events
explanation: Long-running requests are vulnerable to idle connection drops from network intermediaries, so Anthropic recommends streaming for them: incremental events keep data flowing over the connection and deliver output as it is generated. Raising the client's own timeout does not stop proxies or load balancers from closing a connection that looks idle. Backoff retries just repeat the same long silent wait. Sentence-length requests fragment one coherent draft and multiply per-request overhead. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/streaming

question: Ivorydale Legal's assistant answers repeated questions about the same 80 page compliance manual. Every API call re-encodes the manual and sends it again, so each request carries a multi-megabyte payload and uploads are slow on office connections. Which change removes the repeated transfer?
options: Compress the manual with gzip before encoding it into each request
Cache the manual client side and attach it on alternating requests
Upload the manual once and reference its file ID in later requests
Shrink the manual to a summary and send that in place of it
answer: Upload the manual once and reference its file ID in later requests
explanation: The Files API stores a document once and lets subsequent Messages requests reference it by file ID, which eliminates re-encoding and re-uploading the manual on every call. Gzip compression does not change what the Messages request body must contain. Attaching the manual on alternating requests leaves half the calls without their source document. Substituting a summary changes the content the assistant reasons over and can degrade answer accuracy. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/files

question: Bellcrest Retail's shopping chatbot must keep a consistent stylist persona. Developers prepend the persona text to every user message, yet after a few turns the tone drifts, and users who argue with the persona can talk the bot out of it. Where should the persona instructions live?
options: In the first user message of every conversation, sent once at the start
In the system parameter of each request, separate from user turns
In a tool description that the model reads before answering each turn
In an assistant message inserted after each user turn to restate the tone
answer: In the system parameter of each request, separate from user turns
explanation: The system parameter is the designated channel for role and persona instructions, and content placed there is treated as standing guidance distinct from conversational input, which keeps the persona stable and harder for users to argue away. Persona text inside user messages competes with everything else users say, and a single opening message loses influence as history grows. Tool descriptions steer tool selection rather than conversational tone. Injected assistant restatements clutter the transcript without carrying system-level authority. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/system-prompts

question: Three product teams at Quenmark Software copy the same custom slash commands, subagents, and hooks between their repositories by hand. The copies have drifted apart, and a fix applied in one repository rarely reaches the other two. How should these customizations be managed?
options: Move them into each repository's CLAUDE.md so they load automatically
Store them in one engineer's user-level directory as the reference copy
Post them to an internal wiki page that teams copy from quarterly
Package them as a plugin that teams install from a shared marketplace
answer: Package them as a plugin that teams install from a shared marketplace
explanation: Plugins bundle slash commands, subagents, hooks, and MCP configuration into one versioned package, and a shared marketplace lets every team install and update from a single source, which ends the copy drift. CLAUDE.md holds project instructions for the model, not executable command or hook definitions. A user-level directory configures only one engineer's machine. A wiki page still depends on manual copying, which is the failure mode the teams already have. Reference: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins

question: Harrowfen Logistics stores chat history by saving one plain text string per turn and rebuilding the messages array from those strings on the next request. After tool use was enabled, replayed conversations began failing validation on the request that follows a tool call. What should the persistence layer store instead?
options: Each message's complete content block array with tool_use and tool_result preserved
Each turn's text plus a running summary of tool activity
The final assistant text of each turn with role labels attached
A transcript rendered to markdown that is reparsed into messages later
answer: Each message's complete content block array with tool_use and tool_result preserved
explanation: Tool interactions are represented as structured content blocks, and a replayed history must keep each tool_result paired with its matching tool_use, so the schema has to persist every message's block array intact. Text plus a tool summary, final assistant text alone, and a reparsed markdown transcript all discard those structured blocks, producing rebuilt histories that fail validation as soon as a tool call appears in the conversation. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/messages

question: At Cindermill Press, three engineers edit the production prompt for a headline generator directly in a shared admin screen. After a quality drop, nobody can say what the prompt looked like the week before or restore it. Which practice prevents a repeat?
options: Limit prompt edits to a single owner so changes stay coordinated
Duplicate the prompt into a backup row before each edit session
Manage prompts in version control with reviewed, tagged releases like code
Snapshot the admin database nightly so earlier prompts can be recovered
answer: Manage prompts in version control with reviewed, tagged releases like code
explanation: Prompts change model behavior the way code changes application behavior, so they belong in version control where each edit is reviewed, attributable, diffable, and tagged for rollback. A single owner narrows who can edit but still leaves no history of what changed. Backup rows and nightly snapshots capture scattered states without review or diffs, and none of them tie a specific prompt version to the quality observed in production. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

question: Ostergate Health is rolling out Claude Code to forty engineers. The lead wants identical permission rules for everyone working in the repository, while letting individuals keep personal preferences that never enter version control. Which two configuration practices achieve this? Choose 2.
options: Have each engineer maintain the team rules in their user settings file
Commit the team's shared permission rules in the project level .claude/settings.json
Encode the permission rules as bullet points inside the repository CLAUDE.md
Keep each engineer's personal overrides in .claude/settings.local.json, which stays untracked
answer: Commit the team's shared permission rules in the project level .claude/settings.json
Keep each engineer's personal overrides in .claude/settings.local.json, which stays untracked
explanation: The project level .claude/settings.json is checked into source control, so everyone working in the repository inherits the same permission rules, while .claude/settings.local.json holds personal preferences and is excluded from version control by default. User settings files live per machine, so asking forty engineers to maintain team rules there reintroduces the drift the lead wants to avoid. CLAUDE.md provides guidance text to the model, not enforced permission configuration. Reference: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings

question: Vexley Robotics is scoping an assistant that answers questions over field manuals ranging from 2 to 900 pages. A business requirement states that a technician's upload must not fail after they hit submit. Which functional requirement should the developer derive from this?
options: A retry queue that resubmits failed uploads until the request succeeds
A pre-submission check of each manual's token count against the context window
A file size cap of ten megabytes enforced by the upload form
A compression step that shrinks each manual before it is transmitted
answer: A pre-submission check of each manual's token count against the context window
explanation: Requests whose input exceeds the model's context window are rejected, and page count is a poor predictor of tokens, so the reliable control is counting each manual's tokens with the token counting endpoint before submission and handling oversized manuals up front. A retry queue resubmits a request that will fail again for the same reason. A megabyte cap measures bytes rather than tokens. Compression changes transfer size, not the token total the model receives. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/token-counting

question: Bramblehurst Travel's product owner sets one business requirement for a fare assistant: a quoted fare must match the price in the booking system at the moment of the question, and prices change hourly. Which technical requirement follows from this?
options: Refresh the system prompt with a full fare table at each deploy
Fine tune the model monthly on the latest fare history
Embed the fare catalog in a vector store refreshed every night
Expose a fare lookup tool the model calls during each conversation
answer: Expose a fare lookup tool the model calls during each conversation
explanation: A freshness requirement measured at the moment of the question points to tool use: the model calls a fare lookup tool against the booking system during the conversation, so each quote reflects live data. A fare table refreshed at deploy time and a nightly vector store both serve stale prices between refreshes, and periodic retraining bakes historical fares into the model rather than exposing current ones. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/implement-tool-use

question: Silverquay Finance pushes prompt edits and model snapshot upgrades straight to production as configuration flips, while application code follows a staged release process. A snapshot upgrade just regressed their document classifier in production. How should these changes be handled going forward?
options: Promote them through staging behind an evaluation suite before production release
Schedule them for quarterly windows so regressions surface less often
Apply them to production during low traffic hours with monitoring active
Document them in the change log after each production flip
answer: Promote them through staging behind an evaluation suite before production release
explanation: Prompt and model changes alter system behavior just as code changes do, so they belong in the same lifecycle: promoted through staging, where an evaluation suite has to pass before the change reaches production. Quarterly batching delays regressions without preventing them. Low traffic timing with monitoring shrinks the blast radius but still lets the defect ship. A change log records what happened and gates nothing. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests

question: Norvath Tools wraps every non-200 response from the Messages API in the same exponential backoff retry loop. A deploy with a malformed request body retried silently for six hours before anyone noticed the feature was down. What should the error handling do instead?
options: Alert on the first failure and pause the deployment pipeline
Cap the backoff loop at ten attempts regardless of error class
Fail fast on invalid_request errors and keep retries for transient statuses
Route failed requests to a dead letter queue for overnight replay
answer: Fail fast on invalid_request errors and keep retries for transient statuses
explanation: A 400 invalid_request_error means the request itself is malformed, so an identical retry can never succeed; the client should surface it immediately so the payload gets fixed. Retries belong to transient conditions such as 429 rate limits and 529 overloads. A universal attempt cap still delays detection and treats permanent and transient failures alike. Pausing deployments on any first failure overreacts to transient errors, and overnight replay of a malformed request simply fails again. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/errors

question: Duskfield Labs calls the Messages API through a handwritten HTTP wrapper. The team maintains its own retry logic, auth header code, and response typing, and each API evolution has broken the wrapper in a different place. What is the most maintainable path forward?
options: Adopt the official client SDK instead of the handwritten HTTP wrapper
Generate a client from the API's OpenAPI specification at build time
Freeze the wrapper against the current API version and stop upgrading
Split the wrapper into one module per endpoint to isolate breakage
answer: Adopt the official client SDK instead of the handwritten HTTP wrapper
explanation: The official client SDKs wrap the REST API with typed responses, authentication, and built-in retry behavior, and Anthropic maintains them as the API evolves, which removes the class of breakage the team keeps repairing by hand. A generated client still leaves retries, streaming helpers, and upgrades to the team. Freezing on the current API version defers the problem until an upgrade is forced. Splitting modules reorganizes the same self-maintained code without reducing it. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/client-sdks

question: Tarrowbeck Energy submits 2,000 meter reports to the Message Batches API, then immediately requests the results and receives none. The engineer confirms the submission itself succeeded. How should the consuming job obtain the results?
options: Reopen the original HTTP connection and wait for the server push
Poll the batch's processing status and fetch results after it ends
Resubmit the same batch with a flag that makes it synchronous
Stream the batch through server-sent events as items finish processing
answer: Poll the batch's processing status and fetch results after it ends
explanation: Batch processing is asynchronous: the consuming job checks the batch's processing status until it reaches the ended state, then downloads the output from the results URL. Results are not pushed back over the original submission connection. No flag converts a submitted batch into a synchronous request. Batch output is delivered as a downloadable results file, not as a server-sent event stream of items as they finish. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing

question: A platform engineer at Lorwyn Digital ports a working SDK integration to a lightweight edge runtime using raw HTTP calls. Requests carry the correct API key and a valid JSON body yet are rejected with a 400 error citing a missing required header. Which header must the raw requests add?
options: An anthropic-beta header opting the request into the Messages endpoint
A content-length header matching the byte size of the request body
An anthropic-version header pinning the API behavior the client expects
An accept header requesting the response in the JSON media type
answer: An anthropic-version header pinning the API behavior the client expects
explanation: API requests are required to include the anthropic-version header, which pins the API behavior the client was built against; the SDKs add it automatically, so it is easy to miss when hand-rolling HTTP. The anthropic-beta header is needed just for opting into beta features, not for the standard Messages endpoint. Content-length is set by HTTP clients automatically, and the API returns JSON without requiring an accept header. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/versioning

question: Corvale Systems bills enterprise customers for a Claude-powered contract summarizer. Finance wants per-customer spend figures derived from live traffic, but the team's character-count estimates have drifted 25 percent from the actual invoice. What is the most accurate source for these figures?
options: A word-count multiplier applied to each prompt and reply
The token counts reported in each API response's usage data
The monthly invoice totals divided across customers by request volume
A pre-request estimate from the token counting endpoint applied uniformly
answer: The token counts reported in each API response's usage data
explanation: Every Messages API response reports exact input and output token counts in its usage data, which can be logged and aggregated per customer for precise spend attribution. Word-count multipliers and character heuristics drift because tokens do not map cleanly onto words. Dividing invoice totals by request volume ignores large differences in request size between customers. Pre-request counting measures the input alone, missing output tokens that bill at a different rate. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/messages

question: An assistant at Ardexa sends a fixed 8,000-token instruction block, then a product catalog that refreshes hourly, then the user's question. The team placed a single cache marker after the catalog, and every hourly refresh re-bills the entire prefix at cache-write rates. Which adjustment keeps the stable portion cached across refreshes?
options: Move the catalog ahead of the instruction block in the request
Shorten the catalog so the rewritten prefix costs less each hour
Add a second cache marker at the end of the instruction block
Switch the cache to the one-hour lifetime so refreshes land inside it
answer: Add a second cache marker at the end of the instruction block
explanation: Caching matches the request prefix, so placing a marker at each stability boundary lets the unchanged instruction block keep serving cache reads while only the catalog segment is rewritten each hour. Moving the volatile catalog earlier would invalidate even more of the prefix on every refresh. Shortening the catalog lowers the rewrite cost but still re-bills the stable instructions hourly. A longer cache lifetime does not help because any byte change in the prefix invalidates the entry regardless of remaining time. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching

question: Nuvexa's support assistant runs on a Claude model with reasoning enabled. Deep analysis is worth the wait on complex refund disputes, but simple order-status questions now take several seconds and spend heavily on reasoning tokens. The team wants both paths served by the same model. Which approach fits?
options: Lower the effort setting on the routine question route
Cap the output limit tightly so answers return sooner
Route simple questions through the batch processing endpoint
Trim the system prompt so short queries process faster
answer: Lower the effort setting on the routine question route
explanation: The effort setting controls how much reasoning the model performs per request, so dialing it down on routine traffic cuts latency and token spend while the dispute route keeps deep analysis on the same model. A tight output cap risks truncating answers rather than reducing reasoning depth. Batch processing is asynchronous and increases turnaround time instead of shortening it. A shorter system prompt trims input tokens but does not change how long the model reasons. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/extended-thinking

question: Pellenor Analytics extracts line items from vendor invoices into JSON. Short invoices parse cleanly, but long invoices consistently come back with JSON that ends mid-array. Retries reproduce the cutoff at roughly the same output length every time. What should the team examine first?
options: The sampling settings that control randomness in generation
The model's context window against the invoice input size
The stop reason on the response and the output token ceiling
The JSON instructions in the prompt for a missing close rule
answer: The stop reason on the response and the output token ceiling
explanation: A cutoff that recurs at a consistent output length points to the response hitting its output token limit, which the response's stop reason reports explicitly, and raising the ceiling or streaming resolves it. Sampling settings affect wording variety, not repeatable truncation at a fixed length. An input that exceeded the context window would fail validation rather than truncate output mid-array. Prompt instructions cannot force closing brackets once generation halts at the ceiling. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/handling-stop-reasons

question: Brightloom Media generates five headline options per article using a Claude model that accepts sampling controls. Across runs the five headlines come back nearly identical in wording and structure, even though the prompt already asks for variety. Which request change most directly increases variation?
options: Raise the output token limit so richer options can emerge
Increase the temperature setting toward the top of its range
Add example headlines in a single house style as guides
Lower the top-p value to sample from fewer candidate tokens
answer: Increase the temperature setting toward the top of its range
explanation: Higher temperature flattens the sampling distribution so less probable tokens are chosen more often, producing more varied phrasing across generations. A larger output limit changes how much can be written, not how differently it is written. Example headlines in one style anchor outputs toward that style and reduce diversity. Lowering top-p narrows sampling to the most likely tokens, which makes outputs more uniform rather than less. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/messages

question: Halbrook Freight summarizes multi-day dispatch logs with Claude. For the largest logs the API rejects the request with a validation error about token limits, even though the log itself measures under the model's advertised window. The request also sets a very large ceiling for the summary output. What explains the rejection?
options: The window covers input and requested output tokens combined
The window shrinks when responses stream instead of returning whole
The tokenizer expands log text well beyond its character count
The system prompt is measured separately from the user message
answer: The window covers input and requested output tokens combined
explanation: The context window is shared between the input and the tokens reserved for output, so a near-window input combined with a large output ceiling exceeds the limit and fails validation. Streaming changes how the response is delivered, not how much room the window provides. Tokenization can inflate counts relative to characters, but this log already fits the window on its own. System prompts count inside the same window as user messages rather than in a separate allocation. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows

question: Setterfield Labs runs an agentic code-migration service on a mid-tier Claude model. Small repositories convert cleanly, but the largest multi-step migrations drift off plan and make inconsistent decisions late in the run. Latency is flexible and the budget has room. Which adjustment best targets the failure?
options: Raise the output ceiling so runs finish in fewer turns
Split each large migration across many fastest-tier workers
Rerun failed migrations with identical settings until they pass
Route the largest migrations to the most capable model tier
answer: Route the largest migrations to the most capable model tier
explanation: Sustained planning and consistent decisions across many dependent steps are exactly where the top capability tier outperforms mid-tier models, and this workload tolerates its higher latency and cost. A larger output ceiling changes how much one response can contain, not the quality of multi-step decisions. Fanning the work across fast-tier workers fragments shared context and worsens consistency. Repeating a run with unchanged settings replays the same capability gap. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/choosing-a-model

question: Vantergrove Systems runs a production document pipeline on an earlier Claude Sonnet release. A newer release is available, and a past upgrade quietly changed output formatting downstream. The team wants the newer model's gains without a repeat incident. Which two practices reduce the upgrade risk? Choose 2.
options: Run the existing evaluation suite against the newer release first
Point production at a general alias so upgrades apply automatically
Assume prompt behavior carries over because releases stay compatible
Compare outputs on a small slice of live traffic before full cutover
answer: Run the existing evaluation suite against the newer release first
Compare outputs on a small slice of live traffic before full cutover
explanation: Model releases can change behavior in breaking ways, so replaying an existing evaluation suite surfaces format and quality regressions before customers see them, and a limited live-traffic comparison catches issues that offline evaluations miss under real inputs. Pointing at a general alias hands upgrade timing to the platform and removes the chance to test before the switch. Assuming prompt behavior transfers ignores the documented breaking changes that appear between releases. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/migration-guide

question: Ostwind Digital calls Claude through the official Python SDK. An engineer proposes a wrapper that catches throttling and server errors and immediately re-sends each failed call in a loop. During traffic spikes the wrapper hammers the API and deepens the throttling. What makes most of this wrapper redundant?
options: A server-side queue that replays throttled requests once capacity returns
An automatic downgrade to a faster model tier during overload
A billing credit issued for any request refused with a throttle
Built-in retries with exponential backoff for transient error responses
answer: Built-in retries with exponential backoff for transient error responses
explanation: The official SDKs retry rate-limit and server errors automatically with exponential backoff, and the retry count is configurable, so hand-rolled immediate re-sends duplicate this while removing the backoff that eases pressure during spikes. The API rejects throttled requests rather than holding and replaying them server-side. No automatic model downgrade happens during overload. Throttled requests are refused before billing, so a credit mechanism is not involved. Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/errors

question: Lumenreef Media generates product descriptions with Claude in three fixed steps: draft an outline, expand it into copy, then translate the copy into two languages. Bad outlines occasionally slip through and waste the expansion and translation calls downstream. The order of the steps never changes. Which design fixes this?
options: Decompose the task into sequential Claude calls with a programmatic check that validates each intermediate output before the next step runs
Replace the fixed sequence with a single autonomous agent that decides which step to perform next based on intermediate results
Run the three steps concurrently in separate requests and merge the outputs when the calls return
Combine the three steps into a single request so the model catches outline problems while writing the final copy
answer: Decompose the task into sequential Claude calls with a programmatic check that validates each intermediate output before the next step runs
explanation: Decomposing a fixed sequence into chained calls with programmatic checks between steps catches a bad outline before the expansion and translation calls spend tokens on it. An autonomous agent adds nondeterministic pathing to a task whose steps are already enumerable, which increases complexity without adding capability. Running the steps concurrently does not work because each step consumes the previous step's output. A single combined request removes the intermediate boundaries entirely, so nothing can validate the outline before the final copy is written. Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

question: Support tickets at Vantabrook Software fall into clearly separable groups: billing disputes, password resets, and deep technical escalations. A single Claude prompt currently handles them, and each improvement the team makes for escalations degrades the short scripted replies for resets. Which restructuring addresses this?
options: Consolidate the instructions into one longer system prompt that covers each ticket group in its own labeled section
Hand each ticket to an autonomous agent that selects tools until it judges the reply complete
Classify each ticket first, then dispatch it to a separate downstream prompt specialized for that ticket group
Generate three candidate replies for each ticket and return the one a judge model scores highest
answer: Classify each ticket first, then dispatch it to a separate downstream prompt specialized for that ticket group
explanation: Classifying each ticket and dispatching it to a specialized downstream prompt lets the team tune escalation handling without touching the reset script, because the categories are cleanly separable. One longer sectioned prompt keeps the groups coupled in a single instruction set, which is exactly what causes the cross-category regressions. An autonomous tool-selecting agent adds cost and unpredictability to traffic that is mostly scripted. Generating three candidates with a judge multiplies spend on each ticket without separating the competing instruction sets. Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

question: Quenholt Legal builds a Claude workflow in which one model call drafts a contract clause and a second call critiques the draft against a checklist, looping until the critique passes. An architect asks when this two-call loop actually earns its extra cost over a single well-prompted call. Which two conditions justify it? Choose 2.
options: The task carries a strict latency budget on each individual request
Draft quality measurably improves when critique feedback is applied across iterations
The clause format is fixed enough that one templated call reliably produces it
Clear evaluation criteria exist that a model can apply reliably to each draft
answer: Draft quality measurably improves when critique feedback is applied across iterations
Clear evaluation criteria exist that a model can apply reliably to each draft
explanation: A generate-and-critique loop earns its cost when clear evaluation criteria exist for the reviewing call to apply and when applying that feedback measurably improves the draft across iterations. Those are the two published fit conditions for pairing a generator with an evaluator. A strict per-request latency budget argues against extra round trips rather than for them. A format so stable that one templated call reliably produces it needs no iterative refinement in the first place. Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

question: Corvellan Health is building a Claude agent that files insurance claims containing protected health information. Compliance requires that conversation state never persist on infrastructure outside the company's covered environment. The engineers also want the agent loop, context management, and tool scaffolding provided rather than hand-written. Which construction approach satisfies both requirements?
options: Define the agent as a hosted resource that Anthropic executes and streams results back to the application
Run the agent on the Claude Agent SDK inside the company's own environment where session state stays local
Write the loop directly against the Messages API so no library code touches the claim data
Split the claim data across two hosted agents so neither one stores a complete patient record
answer: Run the agent on the Claude Agent SDK inside the company's own environment where session state stays local
explanation: Building on the Claude Agent SDK gives the team the loop, context management, and tool scaffolding while the agent process and its session state run entirely inside the company's covered environment. Defining the agent as an Anthropic-executed hosted resource stores session state server side, which breaks the residency requirement. Writing the loop directly against the Messages API satisfies residency but forfeits the provided scaffolding the engineers asked for. Splitting records across two hosted agents still persists conversation state on outside infrastructure. Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-agents-with-the-claude-agent-sdk

question: Ostermile Robotics built its dispatch agent on a graph-based agentic framework. In production the agent intermittently picks the wrong branch, and the team cannot tell what instructions the model actually received because the framework assembles them at runtime. What should the team do first?
options: Inspect the raw prompts and responses beneath the framework layer to see what the model is actually being sent
Migrate the agent to a different abstraction framework that ships with a larger library of prebuilt graph nodes
Raise the reasoning budget on each node so the model can compensate for imperfect assembled instructions
Add more branches to the graph so each dispatch category has a narrower and more specific path
answer: Inspect the raw prompts and responses beneath the framework layer to see what the model is actually being sent
explanation: Agentic frameworks assemble prompts at runtime, so the first debugging move is to inspect the raw requests and responses underneath the abstraction and confirm what the model actually received. Anthropic's guidance is to understand the underlying prompts and code before relying on added layers, because extra abstraction is a common source of hidden misbehavior. Switching to a framework with more prebuilt nodes replaces one opaque layer with another. Raising reasoning budgets or adding narrower branches both tune a system the team cannot yet observe. Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
